items.title: Restart, stop or start Windows services (Windows only)
items.text:
Pick services in a table, then the action to apply to them. Script: examples/pick-service.ps1; it supports -WhatIf and -Confirm. Changing services needs an elevated PowerShell. This recipe has no Linux counterpart (systemctl units would be the equivalent).

Real capture on Windows Server 2022 with the released packages.

The examples run in the examples folder of a clone of this repository and were run against the released CLI 0.1.2 in Windows PowerShell 5.1 by scripts/test-docs.ps1 (how).
path: Restart, stop or start Windows services (Windows only)

items.title: Run it
items.text:
.\pick-service.ps1 -Name 'w*'

The table shows Name, DisplayName, Status and Start type. After a Submit a second window offers Restart, Stop and Start. With -WhatIf nothing is changed:

.\pick-service.ps1 -Name 'w*' -WhatIf

[{"Name":"W32Time","DisplayName":"Windows Time","Status":"Running","Start type":"Manual"}]

Restart

What if: Performing the operation "Restart service" on target "Windows Time".

No match: the script exits 0 without a window:

.\pick-service.ps1 -Name 'no-such-service-*'

No service matches no-such-service-*.
path: Restart, stop or start Windows services (Windows only)

items.title: How it works
items.text:
ConvertTo-Json writes enums such as Status as numbers, so the script turns them into strings first:

$rows = @(Get-Service -Name $Name | Sort-Object DisplayName | Select-Object -First 2000 |
    Select-Object Name, DisplayName, @{ n = 'Status'; e = { "$($_.Status)" } }, @{ n = 'Start type'; e = { "$($_.StartType)" } })
$picked = @(ConvertFrom-Json -InputObject ($rows | ConvertTo-Json -Compress |
    Invoke-Picker select --multi --input-format json --output-format json --title 'Services') | ForEach-Object { $_ })
$action = 'Restart', 'Stop', 'Start' | Invoke-Picker select --title "Action for $($picked.Count) service(s)"

A one-liner for a quick look at running services:

Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Running' |
    Select-Object Name, DisplayName, @{ n = 'Status'; e = { "$($_.Status)" } } |
    ConvertTo-Json -Compress | nativehtmlkit view --input-format json --title 'Running services'

items.title: Choose a time zone in a light theme (Windows)
items.text:
Choose one value from a long list in a window restyled with --css, and use it in the next command. Script: examples/pick-timezone.ps1 with css/light.css.

Real capture on Windows Server 2022 with the released packages.

The examples run in the examples folder of a clone of this repository and were run against the released CLI 0.1.2 in Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7 by scripts/test-docs.ps1 (how).
path: Choose a time zone in a light theme

items.title: Run it
items.text:
.\pick-timezone.ps1

The table lists every time zone of the system (Id, Offset, Name); on Windows the ids are Windows names such as Tokyo Standard Time, in PowerShell 7 on Linux IANA names such as Asia/Tokyo. The script prints the chosen id:

[{"Id":"Tokyo Standard Time","Offset":"+09:00","Name":"(UTC+09:00) Osaka, Sapporo, Tokyo"}]

Tokyo Standard Time

Use the choice for the next command:

$zone = .\pick-timezone.ps1
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit $LASTEXITCODE }
$now = [TimeZoneInfo]::ConvertTimeBySystemTimeZoneId([DateTime]::UtcNow, $zone)
'{0:HH:mm} in {1}' -f $now, $zone
path: Choose a time zone in a light theme

items.title: How it works
items.text:
The rows are .NET TimeZoneInfo objects reduced to three strings, sent as JSON, with a style sheet; single choice is the default, so exactly one row comes back:

$json = $rows | ConvertTo-Json -Compress |
    nativehtmlkit select --input-format json --output-format json --title 'Time zone' `
        --css (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'css/light.css')
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit $LASTEXITCODE }
(ConvertFrom-Json -InputObject ($json -join "`n"))[0].Id

The same with plain strings:

'Europe/Prague', 'Europe/London', 'America/New_York', 'Asia/Tokyo' |
    nativehtmlkit select --title 'Time zone' --css css/light.css

Asia/Tokyo

css/light.css overrides the page's colour custom properties and a few fixed colours (CSS and forms).

items.title: Tutorials (Windows)
items.text:
Build a complete shell tool step by step.

  • Tutorial: build a project picker
  • Tutorial: a Git branch picker

items.title: Concepts
items.text:
These pages explain why NativeHTMLKit behaves the way it does. They contain no step-by-step instructions; for those see the tutorials and how-to guides (PowerShell).

Page Read it when you want to understand… Architecture which component owns windows, rendering, language APIs and UI helpers Process and lifecycle model why your script runs twice, what ready and shutdown mean, how quitting is negotiated Threading and callbacks where your callbacks run, what may block, how to do background work safely Documents and stale handles windows vs documents, why an old handle suddenly raises a stale error Security model what is trusted, what is escaped, what the host refuses Why native? the trade-offs compared with Electron or an embedded browser

All statements describe the released packages: Core 1.0.3, CLI 0.1.2, Python SDK 0.1.2, PowerShell SDK 0.1.2 and UI 0.1.1.

items.title: Accessibility basics
items.text: NativeHTMLKit builds a native accessibility tree from your HTML (AccessKit, exposed through AT-SPI on Linux and UI Automation on Windows). Screen readers see roles, names and states derived from your markup, so ordinary semantic HTML is the most important tool.

items.title: Checklist
items.text:
• Use real elements. <button> for actions, <a href> for links, <input>/<select>/<textarea> for input, headings in order, lists for lists, <table> with <th> for tables. A <div> with a click handler is neither focusable nor announced as a button.
  • Name every control. Use <label for="id"> (or wrap the control in <label>); add aria-label only where no visible label exists, such as a search field.
  • Announce status changes. Put status text in an element with role="status" (polite) or role="alert" (important), and update it with set_text. The UI libraries' alert component uses role="status".
  • Keep keyboard paths. Everything must work with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space. Forms submit with Enter; modal <dialog>s close with Escape. Move focus deliberately after actions (document.focus(id), Set-NativeHTMLKitFocus), as the todo tutorial does after adding an item.
  • Do not rely on colour alone. Pair colour with text or icons (for example, show a service state as text inside a coloured pill).
  • Respect preferences. Style for prefers-color-scheme and prefers-reduced-motion; Style with the supported CSS shows how.
  • Give images text. Every <img>, including live bitmaps, needs a meaningful alt; keep values you draw in a chart available as HTML text too (Live bitmap charts).

items.title: Check what assistive technology sees
items.text:
The get_accessibility_tree document operation returns the tree the host exposes (roles, names, states, relations, bounds). Read it to confirm, for example, that the fields of a sign-up form are named "E-mail" and "Repeat password":

tree = doc.command("get_accessibility_tree")["tree"]
names = [(node["role"], node["name"]) for node in tree["nodes"] if node["name"]]

PowerShell: Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand -Document $doc -Operation get_accessibility_tree.

This is a quick structural check, not a substitute for testing with a screen reader (Orca on Linux, Narrator or NVDA on Windows).

items.title: Known limitations
items.text: Screen-reader coverage is still being qualified. Core 1.0.3 has a reported Orca issue with collapsed <select> announcements on Linux, and UI-library-specific screen-reader coverage is incomplete; see limitations.

items.title: Architecture — who owns what?
items.text:
flowchart TD
  APP[Your Python or PowerShell program] --> UI[UI library, optional<br/>nativehtmlkit_ui / NativeHTMLKit.UI]
  APP --> SDK[Language SDK<br/>nativehtmlkit / NativeHTMLKit]
  UI --> SDK
  SHELL[Shell script or pipeline] --> CLI[Native CLI<br/>nativehtmlkit / nhk]
  SDK -->|wire protocol v1<br/>local authenticated IPC| HOST[Core native host<br/>nativehtmlkit-host, Rust]
  CLI -->|wire protocol v1| HOST
  HOST --> OS[Linux KDE Wayland / Windows desktop]

NativeHTMLKit is not a website in a hidden browser tab. A Rust native host parses HTML and CSS, lays out and draws the page, owns the native windows, handles keyboard, pointer, IME, accessibility and native dialogs, and reports events to your program. Your program — the backend — contains the application logic and sends commands such as “set this element's text” back to the host.

items.title: Components
items.text:
Component Owns Does not own Core (nativehtmlkit-host) Native windows, HTML/CSS engine, input, rendering, native dialogs, clipboard, live bitmaps, the wire protocol Application logic, language APIs Python SDK (nativehtmlkit) Python API for applications, windows, documents, nodes, bitmaps; launching the bundled host; diagnostics Rendering, widgets PowerShell SDK (NativeHTMLKit) The same host-level features as exported functions; the event pump and background tasks for PowerShell Rendering, widgets UI library (nativehtmlkit_ui, NativeHTMLKit.UI) Reactive state, computed values, a compact component set (layout, text, buttons, inputs, select, checkbox, lists, conditional regions) and themes Anything the SDK does not expose; native dialogs, extra windows and bitmaps stay SDK calls CLI (nativehtmlkit, alias nhk) select, view, form and doctor commands for shell pipelines, with a stdin/stdout/exit-status contract General event subscription or scripting

Each SDK wheel/module and the CLI archive ship the native host they were released with, so a normal install needs no separate Core download.

items.title: The boundary rule
items.text:
• The UI libraries call only the public API of their language SDK. They never talk to Core directly. Your application can mix both: build the main window with the UI library and use the SDK for file dialogs, clipboard, a second window or a live bitmap.
  • The CLI is independent of the language SDKs: it implements its own protocol v1 client and bundles its own host.
  • A feature that Core does not expose cannot be added in a UI library or an application through private calls; it belongs in Core and the SDKs.

items.title: The wire protocol
items.text:
SDKs and the CLI talk to the host over a private local channel (a Unix-domain socket on Linux, a named pipe on Windows), authenticated with a per-launch token. Messages are length-prefixed JSON-RPC 2.0. Protocol v1 is the public, stable contract since Core 1.0.3: within v1, framing, method and operation names, parameter names and types, error codes and lifecycle ordering never change; new methods, operations, optional parameters and result members may be added, and clients must ignore what they do not know. The authoritative description is the Core protocol README.

Most applications never see the protocol: they use the SDK. Low-level escape hatches exist (Document.command(op, ...) in Python, Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand in PowerShell) for documented document operations that have no convenience wrapper.

items.title: Where to read more
items.text:
• Core architecture
  • Process and lifecycle model · Threading and callbacks · Security model
  • Reference index for each repository's API documentation

items.title: Windows and documents
items.text:
A window is a native top-level window owned by the host. It shows at most one document: the HTML you loaded with app.open_html(...) / window.load_html(...) / window.load_file(...) in Python, or Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml / Open-NativeHTMLKitFile in PowerShell. Loading new HTML into the same window atomically replaces its document; unloading (doc.unload() / Remove-NativeHTMLKitDocument) leaves the window open and empty.

An inline HTML source is limited to 1 MiB. Relative stylesheet, image and font URLs resolve against an asset root: the folder of a loaded file, or the folder you pass as asset_root / -AssetRoot.

items.title: Handles are generation-bound
items.text:
Every object the SDK gives you — Window, Document, Node, live bitmap, event subscription — refers to one specific host object. The host gives each document a new identity (generation) when it is loaded, so a handle can never silently point at a different page.

A document handle becomes stale when:

  • its window loaded another document (the old document handle is retired, the new one is live),
  • the document was unloaded,
  • its window closed, or
  • the application shut down (app.shutdown retires every window and document handle at once).

Using a stale handle fails locally, before anything is sent:

Python PowerShell Stale window or document nativehtmlkit.StaleDocumentError (a StaleHandleError) NativeHTMLKit.StaleObjectException App is shutting down (new window/document refused) ApplicationShutdownError — (handles are already retired) The host itself reports a gone object RpcError with code == -32004 NativeHTMLKit.RpcException with Code -32004 Operation no longer valid (invalid state, e.g. during shutdown) RpcError with code == -32008 NativeHTMLKit.RpcException with Code -32008

The UI libraries treat these errors as “the document is gone” and dispose themselves quietly instead of reporting a corrupted UI.

Practical rule: after replacing a document, re-register event handlers on the new document object, and never cache document handles in long-lived workers without handling the stale error. Handlers, nodes and bitmaps of the old document are released with it.

items.title: Elements, ids and nodes
items.text:
Most commands address an element by its HTML id (doc.set_text("status", "…"), Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText -Element status). For elements without an id, doc.query_nodes(selector) / Get-NativeHTMLKitNodes return opaque node references that are bound to the same document generation; they become stale with it. doc.query(selector) returns only the ids of matching elements that have one.

Several changes can be applied as one host transaction with doc.batch([...]) / Invoke-NativeHTMLKitBatch.

items.title: Events and delegation
items.text:
Event handlers are registered on the document: doc.on("click", callback, element="save") / Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Type click -Element save. The event object carries the type, the nearest identified target element, and path — the ids of identified elements on the event's route. A handler registered with an element id fires when that id is the target or appears on the path, so one handler on a list container can serve all its rows (delegation). Without element, the handler receives every event of that type.

  • Events arrive after native dispatch. To stop a supported default action (for example a key's default editing), register it in advance with doc.prevent_default(...) / Set-NativeHTMLKitPreventDefault; a callback cannot cancel it afterwards.
  • Control events carry the current value / checked; key events carry key and code.
  • A document accepts at most 256 handlers.
  • Programmatic changes are not user input: set_value, set_checked and set_selected_values fire no events, while request_submit runs validation and fires invalid / submit, and replace_control_range goes through the native editor and fires input.

items.title: Live bitmaps
items.text:
A live bitmap (doc.create_bitmap(id, w, h) / New-NativeHTMLKitLiveBitmap) is a bounded RGBA8 image surface for <img src="ui4me-bitmap://ID">, shared with the host through a private memory-mapped file. Presenting a frame waits until the host has taken it, so there is no unbounded frame queue. A bitmap belongs to its document and is released when the document is replaced, unloaded or its window closes. See live bitmap charts (PowerShell).

Related: Update the page (PowerShell) · Handle events (PowerShell) · Threading and callbacks

items.title: Process and lifecycle model
items.text:
A NativeHTMLKit application is two cooperating processes: the native host, which owns the windows, and your script, which owns the logic. The SDK hides most of this, but knowing the model explains several rules you will meet in every tutorial.

sequenceDiagram
  participant L as Launcher run (uv run app.py / pwsh -File app.ps1)
  participant H as Native host
  participant B as Backend run (same script, second time)
  L->>H: start host with a private manifest
  H->>B: start the same script again, with endpoint + token
  B->>H: authenticate, create windows, load documents
  B->>H: app.ready
  Note over H,B: events flow to the backend, commands flow to the host
  H->>B: app.shutdown (last window closed or quit accepted)
  B-->>H: backend exits
  H-->>L: host exits; the launcher exits with the host's status

items.title: Your script runs twice
items.text:
When you run uv run app.py, Application.start() notices that it was not started by a host. It writes a private temporary manifest, starts the bundled host and waits; it never returns in that first run — the process ends with the host's exit status. The host then runs the same Python command again (the project's interpreter with the same script and arguments) as its supervised backend. In that second run Application.start() connects to the host and returns the Application.

PowerShell works the same way: Start-NativeHTMLKitScript in a script run with pwsh -File app.ps1 (or powershell.exe -File app.ps1 on Windows) starts the host, which re-runs the script with the same PowerShell edition and arguments; the call returns the connected application only in the backend run. Script arguments are forwarded to the backend run.

Consequences:

  • Everything above Application.start() / Start-NativeHTMLKitScript runs twice. Keep imports, constants and function definitions there; put side effects (reading files, creating folders, network calls) below the call or inside main().
  • Python examples use if __name__ == "__main__": main() and keep work inside main().
  • Application.start() must run from a script file or a module (uv run app.py, uv run -m package.module); it refuses an interactive interpreter, python -c and standard input, because it could not re-run them. Command-line arguments are passed to the backend run unchanged.
  • A Python backend started with uv run -m nativehtmlkit run module:main (or by a host manifest) only connects; it is not relaunched.

items.title: Starting up: ready
items.text:
After connecting, the backend creates at least one window, loads its document and registers event handlers, then announces ready:

  • Python: app.run() sends ready and then waits for shutdown (or call app.ready() yourself earlier).
  • PowerShell: Set-NativeHTMLKitReady -Application $app (the UI library's Start-NHKUi does this for you unless you pass -NoReady), then Wait-NativeHTMLKit -Application $app -UntilShutdown.

The backend must authenticate and become ready before the manifest's startup deadline (startup_timeout_ms / -StartupTimeoutMilliseconds, default 30 seconds), otherwise the host gives up.

items.title: Single or multiple instances
items.text: instance="single" (Python) / -Instance single (PowerShell) is the default: launching the same app again forwards the launch to the running instance instead of opening a second copy. The identity is the app_id / -AppId (a reverse-DNS name such as org.example.Notes); without one, a stable identity is derived from the script path. Use "multiple" for tools where several copies make sense.

items.title: Closing windows and quitting
items.text:
Closing is a negotiation, because a window may have unsaved work:

  1. The user closes a window (or your code calls window.request_close() / Close-NativeHTMLKitWindow).
  2. If you installed a before-close policy (window.on_before_close(callback) / Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeClose), the host asks it; returning false keeps the window open. In PowerShell the scriptblock's last output decides ($true allows).
  3. The window emits close_requested and then closed window events, and its handles become stale.

Quitting the whole application is negotiated the same way: app.request_quit() / Request-NativeHTMLKitQuit asks the before-quit policy (app.on_before_quit(callback) / Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeQuit).

When the last window closes, or a quit is accepted, the host sends app.shutdown. In Core 1.0.x there is no closed window event for that last window — app.shutdown follows close_requested directly, and it implies that every window is closed. The SDKs therefore retire all window and document handles when shutdown arrives.

items.title: Shutting down
items.text:
• Python: app.run() delivers the events that arrived before app.shutdown (for up to two seconds), runs app.on_shutdown(...) callbacks in the thread that called run(), and returns normally. It raises DisconnectedError if the host disappeared instead of shutting down in order. Leaving the with Application.start(...) block closes the connection.
  • PowerShell: Wait-NativeHTMLKit -UntilShutdown returns after shutdown (or after your own Close-NativeHTMLKit) and throws NativeHTMLKit.DisconnectedException if the host vanished first. Put Close-NativeHTMLKit (and Stop-NHKUi) in a finally block.

After app.shutdown, the backend has the manifest's shutdown timeout (shutdown_timeout_ms, default 5 seconds) to finish and exit.

items.title: Exit status and teardown
items.text: The launcher exits with the host's status. If the Python launcher is interrupted by a signal it stops the host (bounded) and returns the conventional 128 + signal status, for example 143 for SIGTERM and 130 for Ctrl+C. The host supervises the backend, and the launcher keeps the host tied to its own lifetime (on Windows through a job object, on Linux by watching the launcher process), so stopping the launcher does not leave orphaned host or backend processes.

items.title: Headless test mode
items.text:
Set NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 before running a Python or PowerShell app, and the SDK starts the host with --headless (the CLI uses NATIVEHTMLKIT_CLI_TEST_HEADLESS=1). The host then runs the complete protocol and lifecycle — documents are parsed, styled and laid out, commands and queries work, events produced by document operations (for example request_submit firing submit, or replace_control_range firing input) are delivered — but no window is shown and:

  • there is no user input: nothing clicks or types for you;
  • the clipboard and native file dialogs are unavailable (the calls fail with RPC error -32001), as is opening external targets;
  • desktop preferences report no observed values.

Headless mode is meant for continuous integration and automated checks that an app starts, renders, reaches ready and shuts down cleanly. It never proves real input, focus or accessibility behaviour; those need an interactive desktop.

Related: Threading and callbacks · Documents and stale handles · Troubleshooting (PowerShell)

items.title: Security model
items.text: NativeHTMLKit is a local desktop toolkit. Its security model is about keeping the host channel private, keeping untrusted text from becoming markup, and keeping the renderer away from the network and from arbitrary files.

items.title: A private, authenticated channel
items.text:
• The host creates a random token for each launch and gives the backend the endpoint and token through environment variables (UI4ME_ENDPOINT, UI4ME_TOKEN). The backend must authenticate with host.hello before anything else.
  • The endpoint is local only: a Unix-domain socket on Linux, a named pipe on Windows. On Linux the host's runtime files are created private to the user (directories 0700, files 0600).
  • The SDKs remove the connection variables from their own environment right after connecting, so programs your app starts do not inherit the secret and can launch their own NativeHTMLKit apps.
  • The launcher's temporary manifest (which names the program, script, arguments and working directory) lives in a private temporary folder — mode 0700 on Linux; on Windows the per-user temporary folder's permissions apply — and is removed when the launcher ends.

items.title: No JavaScript, no network
items.text:
There is no JavaScript engine, so <script> content and on… attributes do nothing. The resource loader always denies network URLs (http:, https:, ftp:, ws: …) as well as javascript: and blob: URLs for stylesheets, images and fonts. Pages can use:

  • local files inside the document's asset root (the folder of a loaded file, or the asset_root / -AssetRoot you pass) — paths outside every allowed root are refused before they are opened,
  • ui4me-res:// bundles you register from code, and ui4me-bitmap:// live bitmaps.

Activating a link is reported to your program as a link_activated event; what happens next is your code's decision (for example open_external).

items.title: Trusted and untrusted content
items.text:
The one rule you must follow: markup APIs take trusted HTML only.

Safe for any text (never parsed as HTML) Trusted markup only doc.set_text, Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText, doc.set_value, Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentValue, doc.set_attribute, UI text/heading/badge/alert/text_list and their PowerShell equivalents doc.replace_html, doc.insert_html, Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml, open_html / Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml, UI raw_html / Add-NHKUiHtml

When you build HTML from data — file names, process names, user input, log lines — escape every value first: html.escape(value) in Python, [System.Net.WebUtility]::HtmlEncode($value) in PowerShell. Every tutorial and example on this site does this. The UI libraries escape all bound text and list items and reject unsafe attribute names (on…); generated element ids cannot be overridden.

items.title: Desktop services
items.text:
• open_external / Open-NativeHTMLKitExternal accepts only http, https, mailto and file URIs or absolute local paths. On Windows, local targets whose file type would be executed rather than opened (executables, scripts, shortcuts) are refused. Revealing a file requires a bounded absolute local path. Both are unavailable in headless mode.
  • Clipboard access is explicit (clipboard_text / set_clipboard_text, Get-/Set-NativeHTMLKitClipboard). Clipboard editing commands are deferred and report completion through events.

items.title: The CLI
items.text: nativehtmlkit select and view treat their stdin data as untrusted: it is escaped before display and bounded (UTF-8, up to 8 MiB, 2,000 rows and 32 columns in the 0.1.x line). The HTML passed to nativehtmlkit form --html and CSS passed with --css are trusted developer input — never feed them user-supplied content. Results are written to stdout only on success (exit 0). See the CLI reference.

items.title: What this model does not cover
items.text:
NativeHTMLKit runs with the permissions of the user who starts it; it is not a sandbox for untrusted code. Your Python or PowerShell program can do anything that user can. Treat example scripts like any other script you run.

Related: Architecture · Update the page (PowerShell) · Distribute your app (PowerShell)

items.title: Threading and callbacks
items.text: The host renders and handles input on its own threads; your program only receives events and sends commands. Where your callbacks run differs between Python and PowerShell, and it decides what you may block on.

items.title: Python SDK
items.text:
flowchart LR
  HOST[Native host] -- socket/pipe --> R[Receiver thread<br/>never runs your code]
  R --> Q[Ordered event queue]
  Q --> E[Event worker thread<br/>your document/window callbacks, in order]
  R --> C[Completion threads<br/>Future done-callbacks]
  R --> L[Lifecycle workers<br/>before_close / before_quit policies]
  M[Main thread] -->|app.run waits for shutdown| M
  • The transport reader never runs application code. Callbacks may therefore make synchronous calls to the host (doc.set_text(...) inside a click handler is normal).
  • Document and window events are delivered in order on one event worker thread. A slow handler delays every later event. The queue is bounded (128 queued notifications); events the SDK had to drop because a callback blocked are counted in app.rpc.dropped_notifications, and events the host dropped because the process stopped reading appear in app.host_diagnostics()["dropped_notifications"].
  • Close/quit policies are answered on separate request workers, so a busy event handler does not stall lifecycle control.
  • call_async futures complete on their own short-lived nativehtmlkit-completion thread. Done-callbacks may call the host synchronously or wait for other futures.
  • SDK calls are allowed from any thread, including your own threading.Thread workers. Use that for long work: compute in a worker and push results with doc.set_text(...) and friends.

Native dialogs inside an event handler. window.open_files(), save_file() and choose_folder() wait for the user by default (wait=True, no deadline). Called from an event handler, that blocks the event worker — every later click waits until the dialog closes. Pass wait=False to get a Future and handle the result in future.add_done_callback(...); future.cancel() asks the host to close the dialog. See file dialogs (PowerShell).

The optional async_adapter() exposes the same connection to an asyncio loop; it does not change who renders.

items.title: Python UI library
items.text:
• Build the component tree on the main thread before ui.mount(app); afterwards the tree is fixed and you change it only through state.
  • Each mounted UI has one owner thread that performs all runtime DOM writes. SDK event workers only enqueue events for it, and state changes are batched into few document updates.
  • State.set(...) may be called from any thread; bindings marshal the resulting DOM update to the owner. ui.post(fn, *args) runs a function on the owner thread (it raises if the bounded queue is full).
  • Known limitation: a computed(...) value can race when several threads change its dependencies at the same time. Change related state from one thread (for example, post results to the owner with ui.post). See limitations.
  • ui.diagnostics reports update counts, dropped events, errors and whether the DOM may be out of sync after a failed write.

items.title: PowerShell SDK
items.text:
PowerShell has one runspace per script and no background event thread. The SDK runs everything on your runspace through an event pump:

  • Wait-NativeHTMLKit -Application $app -UntilShutdown pumps messages and runs your scriptblocks until shutdown. Without -UntilShutdown it handles what is queued (waiting up to -TimeoutMilliseconds) and returns, which lets you write your own loop.
  • Every waiting SDK call also pumps. While a command such as Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText or a blocking Show-NativeHTMLKitFileDialog waits for its reply, host requests (close/quit policies) are still answered.
  • Callbacks never nest. A notification that arrives while one of your callbacks is running is deferred and delivered after it returns (up to 128 deferred notifications; further ones are dropped and counted). A blocking file dialog inside a click handler is therefore safe for lifecycle, but other clicks wait until it closes.
  • Callback nesting is limited to 32 levels; break/continue used outside a loop inside a callback is stopped at the callback boundary.

items.title: Scriptblock scope
items.text: A scriptblock written at script level resolves variables when it runs, in the script scope, so it can use $doc and a shared state object defined there. Assigning $count = $count + 1 inside a callback creates a local variable — keep mutable state in an object ($state.Count++). Inside a function, pass ({ ... }.GetNewClosure()) to capture the function's local variables. The UI library's -Data parameter passes context explicitly to -OnClick handlers instead.

items.title: Background work
items.text: Start-NativeHTMLKitTask -Application $app -ScriptBlock { ... } -ArgumentList ... -OnCompleted { ... } -OnFailed { ... } runs work in an isolated runspace without your variables or modules. Pass plain data only: SDK objects (application, window, document, bitmap, ...) are refused as arguments. -OnCompleted / -OnFailed run later on your runspace, during the normal pump and never inside another callback, so they may update the document. At most 8 tasks per application (32 per process) run at once; -TimeoutMilliseconds and Stop-NativeHTMLKitTask only request cancellation, and a worker that ignores it keeps its slot until it ends. Close-NativeHTMLKit requests stop of unfinished tasks and runs no further callbacks. See background work (PowerShell).

items.title: PowerShell UI library
items.text:
NativeHTMLKit.UI uses the same runspace. It records the owning runspace in Start-NHKUi and refuses updates from any other runspace — update state in -OnCompleted callbacks of SDK tasks, not inside the task scriptblock. Changes made inside an event callback are written in one batch when the callback returns; use Invoke-NHKUiBatch for many changes made elsewhere.

Related: Process and lifecycle model · Documents and stale handles

items.title: Why native instead of Electron or an embedded browser?
items.text: NativeHTMLKit targets local tools and small desktop applications where you want the familiar structure of HTML and CSS and the convenience of Python or PowerShell — without shipping a JavaScript engine, a browser process or a local web server.

items.title: What you gain
items.text:
• One language for the logic. Event handlers are ordinary Python functions or PowerShell scriptblocks. There is no front-end/back-end split, no bundler and no IPC layer for you to design.
  • Small, self-contained installs. The SDK wheel or module bundles the native host; uv add nativehtmlkit or Install-Module NativeHTMLKit is the whole runtime. The CLI is a single archive.
  • No network surface. There is no HTTP server and the renderer never fetches remote resources (see the security model).
  • Real native windows and services. Native file and folder dialogs, clipboard, multiple windows, window state, desktop preferences, accessibility integration and live RGBA bitmaps are host features, not browser emulations.
  • Scripts become apps. A PowerShell admin script or a shell pipeline can ask the user a question in a proper window (nativehtmlkit select, form) and continue with the answer.

items.title: What you give up
items.text:
• A subset of the web platform. The engine implements a large part of HTML and CSS layout, forms, dialogs and popovers, but it is not a complete browser. There are no JavaScript or browser APIs (fetch, canvas, web components, routing), no video/audio playback, and CSS support is defined by the engine's own profile and compatibility tests. Check the capability matrix and styling guide (PowerShell) instead of assuming Chrome behaviour.
  • No existing web component ecosystem. React/Vue widgets, charting libraries in JavaScript and similar packages cannot run. Build charts with live bitmaps (PowerShell) or server-free HTML/CSS.
  • Platform scope. The current targets are Linux with KDE Plasma on Wayland and Windows (x64). The Linux Python wheel needs glibc 2.39 or newer. See limitations.
  • Young UI library. nativehtmlkit_ui / NativeHTMLKit.UI 0.1.1 is an early release with a deliberately small component set.

items.title: When to choose something else
items.text:
• You need a complex single-page web application, existing JavaScript libraries, or exact browser rendering: use a browser-based stack.
  • You need macOS today: it is not a target of the current releases.
  • You need rich native widget toolkits (tree views with virtualization, docking, rich text editors): consider a native toolkit such as Qt.

If your app is a form, a dashboard, a picker, a settings dialog, a log viewer or a small utility written in Python or PowerShell, NativeHTMLKit is designed for exactly that. Start with Getting started.

items.title: Screenshots and media
items.text:
Every screenshot on this site is a real capture. Each example was started unchanged with the released packages (Core 1.0.3, Python SDK 0.1.2, PowerShell SDK 0.1.2 on PowerShell 7.7, UI 0.1.1, CLI 0.1.2) on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland (1280×800, 100% scaling) and its window captured with KDE Spectacle (active window only). Nothing was retouched. Windows looks the same apart from the window frame. Every example page shows its own capture; the four capability galleries are below.

Python SDK Python UI PowerShell SDK PowerShell UI

items.title: Capturing a new screenshot
items.text:
1. Install the exact released packages on the target desktop and note the OS, runtime and versions.
  2. Run the example unchanged from a neutral working directory (and a scratch HOME if the example shows a file path), so no personal paths appear in the window.
  3. Exercise what the page describes. Never present a capture of a broken state as working.
  4. Capture only the window (KDE: spectacle -b -n -a -o shot.png; Windows: Win+Shift+S, window mode).
  5. Save it in the owning repository under docs/images/examples/ with that repository's naming (py-sdk-<file>.png, ps-sdk-<file>.png, ui-py-<file>.png, ui-ps-<file>.png) and re-run scripts/import-docs.py here.

items.title: Install and first steps
items.text:
NativeHTMLKit shows native desktop windows whose content is plain HTML and CSS. Your program, written in Python or PowerShell (or a shell script using the CLI), owns the logic; a small native host process draws the window and sends you the user's events. There is no browser, no JavaScript and no local web server.

Just looking?

Install the demo to click through every example and read its source first: uvx nativehtmlkit-demo or Install-Module NativeHTMLKit.Demo. See Try the demo.

items.title: Pick your path and install
items.text: Choose the layer you want to work with, then the language (or, for the CLI, your system). Each tab has the complete install command and a quick check that it worked. Python uses uv: each app is a uv project, and you run its files with uv run app.py (uv provides Python 3.10 or later if needed).

items.title: UI library: reactive components (start here)
items.text:
PythonPowerShell 
uv init --app myapp && cd myapp      # a project for your app
uv add nativehtmlkit_ui              # also installs the nativehtmlkit SDK
uv tree                              # both installed, with versions

Next: Python UI library: getting started

Install-Module NativeHTMLKit.UI -Scope CurrentUser   # also installs the NativeHTMLKit SDK
Get-Module NativeHTMLKit, NativeHTMLKit.UI -ListAvailable | Select-Object Name, Version

Next: PowerShell UI library: getting started

items.title: SDK: your own HTML and CSS, full control
items.text:
PythonPowerShell 
uv init --app myapp && cd myapp      # a project for your app
uv add nativehtmlkit
uv run nativehtmlkit-python version  # SDK, protocol and bundled host versions

Next: Python SDK: getting started

Install-Module NativeHTMLKit -Scope CurrentUser
Get-NativeHTMLKitHostPath           # the bundled native host for this system

Next: PowerShell SDK: getting started

items.title: CLI: one question to the user from a shell script
items.text:
LinuxWindows 
curl -fLO https://github.com/nativehtmlkit/nativehtmlkit-cli/releases/download/v0.1.2/nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-linux-x64.tar.gz
tar -xzf nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-linux-x64.tar.gz
cd nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-linux-x64
./nhk doctor

Next: CLI on Linux (checksums, putting it on PATH, first command)

Invoke-WebRequest -OutFile nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-windows-x64.zip `
    https://github.com/nativehtmlkit/nativehtmlkit-cli/releases/download/v0.1.2/nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-windows-x64.zip
Expand-Archive .\nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-windows-x64.zip -DestinationPath "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs"
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-windows-x64\nativehtmlkit.exe" doctor

Next: CLI on Windows (checksums, adding it to PATH, first command)

Not sure which to pick? Read Choose an entry point. Before installing, check the platform requirements and the few Linux and Windows differences.

items.title: What happens when you run an app
items.text:
1. You run your script normally (uv run app.py, pwsh -File app.ps1).
  2. The SDK starts the bundled native host, and the host starts your script a second time as its backend, connected over a private local channel. That is why every example keeps its work after Application.start() / Start-NativeHTMLKitScript. See Process and lifecycle.
  3. Your code opens windows, loads HTML, subscribes to events and announces that it is ready.
  4. Events (clicks, typing, form submits) arrive in your callbacks; you change the page with document commands such as "set this element's text".
  5. When the user closes the last window, the host shuts the application down and your script ends.

items.title: After the first window
items.text:
• Build a complete app: the tutorials in your section (UI, SDK, CLI).
  • Understand the model: Concepts.
  • Look up exact APIs: Reference (each package documents its own API).

Every example on this site is a program in the repository that owns its API, run automatically against the released packages; see Examples and verification.

items.title: Choose an entry point
items.text:
All entry points use the same native host and the same HTML/CSS renderer. They differ in who writes the page and how much control you get.

Your job Best entry point Why A Python program needs a window, and you are happy to write HTML Python SDK Full control: windows, documents, events, dialogs, clipboard, live bitmaps A Python tool needs a form-like window quickly Python UI Reactive state()/computed(), inputs, lists and layout without writing HTML A PowerShell admin script needs a dashboard or a dialog PowerShell SDK The same features as cmdlets, plus background tasks in isolated runspaces A PowerShell script needs a settings form or a small reactive UI PowerShell UI Add-NHKUi* components bound to New-NHKUiState values A shell pipeline needs the user to pick rows or fill a form CLI One command, stdin in, stdout out, exit status tells what happened

items.title: How they relate
items.text:
• The UI libraries are small layers built only on the public SDK of the same language. They do not wrap everything: native file dialogs, HTML <dialog>, clipboard, extra windows and live bitmaps are used through the SDK, next to the UI library, in the same app.
  • The CLI is a standalone program. It does not need Python or PowerShell, and scripts cannot subscribe to individual events; a window ends with one result.
  • You can start with the UI library and drop down to the SDK at any time: ui.document (Python) and the document of the window returned by Start-NHKUi (PowerShell) are ordinary SDK objects.

items.title: Rules of thumb
items.text:
• Prefer the SDK when the page is your own HTML/CSS design, when you show tables or logs, or when you need dialogs, several windows or bitmaps.
  • Prefer the UI library for settings, forms and small tools where state should drive the page automatically. It is an early (0.1.1) release; check its limitations.
  • Prefer the CLI when the rest of the program is a shell script and you need a single decision from the user.

Feature-by-feature availability is in the capability matrix.

items.title: Try the demo
items.text:
The quickest way to see what NativeHTMLKit can do: install one package and get a window that lists every example from these docs. Each example shows its Python, PowerShell, HTML and CSS source, and starts with one click as its own native window.

Real capture: NativeHTMLKit Demo 0.1.1, KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland. The Counter example was started with Run Python and clicked three times.

items.title: Install and start
items.text:
PythonPowerShell 
uvx nativehtmlkit-demo                    # run it without installing
uv tool install nativehtmlkit-demo        # or install the command, then:
nativehtmlkit-demo

Needs uv (it provides Python 3.10 or later if needed). The demo comes with the nativehtmlkit SDK and nativehtmlkit_ui, which its Python examples use.

Install-Module NativeHTMLKit.Demo -Scope CurrentUser
Start-NativeHTMLKitDemo

Works in PowerShell 7 (Linux and Windows) and Windows PowerShell 5.1. This installs the NativeHTMLKit and NativeHTMLKit.UI modules too. The command returns when you close the demo window.

Each package contains the same window and the same examples. To run the examples of both languages, install both packages. The demo finds Python and PowerShell on your PATH, and when one is missing, the button for that language says what to install.

items.title: Using the window
items.text:
1. Pick an example on the left; each shows a one-line summary. The SDK examples use your own HTML and CSS with events and page updates. The NativeHTMLKit UI examples use the reactive component library.
    • All / SDK / UI narrows the list to one kind and shows how many examples match.
    • Filter examples searches titles, summaries and topics; the × button or Esc clears it.
    • Up and Down move through the list, also while you type in the filter box.
  2. Read the source in the tabs (the source panel is always dark):
    • Python and PowerShell: the code only. The page HTML and the stylesheet are replaced by a one-line pointer to their tabs. Full script shows the single file exactly as it ships.
    • HTML and CSS: the page. For SDK examples this is the page embedded in the code or loaded from index.html. For UI examples it is the HTML the library generates for the first render.
  3. Run Python or Run PowerShell starts the example in a separate process, as a normal window of its own. Start as many as you like, including the same example in both languages side by side.
  4. Running examples at the bottom lists what you started. Stop ends an example. Output opens the Output tab with everything the example printed, which shows why it stopped if it failed.

Closing the demo window also closes the examples it started.

HTML tab of an SDK example A UI example started with Run PowerShell

Examples run from a working folder under your temporary directory (nativehtmlkit-demo/<example>). Examples that save data, such as the todo list, save it where their own documentation says. The log viewer gets a sample log file that keeps growing while it runs.

items.title: Check an installation
items.text:
uvx nativehtmlkit-demo --self-test

Start-NativeHTMLKitDemo -SelfTest

The self-test runs the demo without a window. It checks every example and its source tabs, starts a few examples in each installed language, and stops them again. It prints PASS, FAIL and SKIP lines, and exits with code 0 when nothing failed. SKIP means a language is not installed.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
When an example does what you need, open its page in these docs for the explanation. Each page has the same source and a screenshot:

  • UI library examples: Python · PowerShell
  • SDK examples: Python · PowerShell
  • Install and first steps: install just the library you build with.

The demo's source is at nativehtmlkit/nativehtmlkit-demo (packages: PyPI nativehtmlkit-demo and Gallery NativeHTMLKit.Demo).

items.title: Linux and Windows
items.text: The UI library and the SDK are the same on both platforms: the same packages, API, examples and behaviour, so every page in the UI and SDK sections applies to both. This page lists the few things that really differ. (The CLI is different: shell scripts are written differently per system, so it has separate Linux and Windows sections.)

items.title: Supported systems and runtimes
items.text:
Linux Windows Desktop KDE Plasma on Wayland Interactive desktop session (also over RDP) Python SDK and UI Python 3.10+, x64, glibc 2.39 or newer (manylinux_2_39_x86_64 wheel) Python 3.10+, x64 PowerShell SDK and UI PowerShell 7.2+ PowerShell 7.2+ and Windows PowerShell 5.1 Native host bundled in the package (nativehtmlkit-host) bundled in the package (nativehtmlkit-host.exe)

If pip finds no wheel on Linux, the distribution's glibc is older than 2.39; the source distribution contains no host and cannot open windows. See Platform requirements.

items.title: What looks or behaves differently
items.text:
Topic Linux Windows Window frame KDE (KWin) decorations Windows title bar; contents render identically Native file dialogs the desktop portal (xdg-desktop-portal) the Windows common dialogs Accessibility bridge AT-SPI (Orca) UI Automation (Narrator, NVDA) Local connection between your program and the host Unix domain socket named pipe Stopping an app from outside SIGTERM to your script ends the host and backend ending your script's process ends the host and backend (job object); there are no POSIX signals Per-app folders (the desktop.paths host method; PowerShell: Invoke-NativeHTMLKitRpc -Method desktop.paths) XDG folders (~/.config, ~/.local/share, ...) AppData folders (%APPDATA%, %LOCALAPPDATA%) Live-bitmap shared files the per-user runtime directory %TEMP%\nativehtmlkit-bitmaps\ (an empty folder may remain after the app exits) File names your app creates anything but / and NUL not < > : " / \ ? *, the vertical bar, or control characters

None of these change your code, except file names (validate them on Windows) and the working-directory note below.

items.title: Windows notes
items.text:
• Working directory of the backend. On Windows the backend may start with an extended-length working directory (\\?\C:\...). Windows PowerShell 5.1's Join-Path rejects that form; resolve relative paths with [IO.Path]::GetFullPath() / [IO.Path]::Combine() (PowerShell) or pathlib (Python) instead. This is a known issue in Core 1.0.3.
  • Windows PowerShell 5.1. Supported on Windows only. Scripts must avoid PowerShell 7 syntax (?:, ??, &&, ||), should be ASCII or UTF-8 with BOM, and must unroll arrays from ConvertFrom-Json ($rows = ConvertFrom-Json $json | ForEach-Object { $_ }). $IsWindows and $IsLinux do not exist in 5.1. Loops and runspaces are slower. Every PowerShell example on this site is tested on 5.1 as well as PowerShell 7. Details: Windows PowerShell 5.1.

items.title: Linux notes
items.text:
• A plain SSH session has no desktop. Run apps inside the KDE Plasma session, or use the host's headless test mode (NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1) for automated tests; it behaves the same on both systems.
  • Python wheels need glibc 2.39+ (for example Ubuntu 24.04 and newer, Debian 13).

items.title: Screenshots on this site
items.text: The screenshots were captured on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland. On Windows the same programs look the same apart from the window frame. The CLI section has separate Windows screenshots because its scripts differ per system.

items.title: Platform requirements
items.text: The released packages documented here are Core 1.0.3, CLI 0.1.2, Python SDK 0.1.2, PowerShell SDK 0.1.2 and UI 0.1.1 (Python and PowerShell, early release). Each SDK package and the CLI archive bundle the matching Core host, so you never install Core separately.

items.title: Desktops
items.text:
Desktop Status Linux, KDE Plasma on Wayland Target desktop for all entry points Windows (x64), interactive desktop session Target desktop for all entry points Other Linux desktops, macOS Not targeted by these releases

A window needs an interactive desktop session. A plain SSH session, a service account or a CI runner can still run apps in the host's headless test mode (NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 for the SDKs, NATIVEHTMLKIT_CLI_TEST_HEADLESS=1 for the CLI): the whole protocol runs without a window, but there is no user input, no clipboard and no native file dialog. See Troubleshooting (PowerShell).

items.title: Runtimes
items.text:
Entry point Linux Windows Python SDK nativehtmlkit Python 3.10+; x64 wheel tagged manylinux_2_39_x86_64 (glibc 2.39 or newer) Python 3.10+; x64 wheel Python UI nativehtmlkit_ui as the Python SDK (pure-Python wheel) as the Python SDK PowerShell SDK NativeHTMLKit PowerShell 7.2+ PowerShell 7.2+ and Windows PowerShell 5.1 PowerShell UI NativeHTMLKit.UI PowerShell 7.2+ PowerShell 7.2+ and Windows PowerShell 5.1 CLI nativehtmlkit / nhk x64 release archive x64 release archive

If pip cannot find a compatible wheel on Linux, your distribution's glibc is probably older than 2.39. Do not fall back to the source distribution and expect a window: it contains no native host.

items.title: Check an installation

uv run nativehtmlkit-python doctor      # Python (in your uv project): the host's environment report
uv run nativehtmlkit-python version     # Python: SDK, protocol and bundled host versions as JSON
nativehtmlkit doctor             # CLI: which host it found and its version

Get-Module NativeHTMLKit -ListAvailable | Select-Object Name, Version
Get-NativeHTMLKitHostPath        # the bundled host for this platform

For per-feature availability see the capability matrix and the limitations.

items.title: Reference
items.text:
The complete API of each package is written in the repository that implements it and published here unchanged (every imported page links back to its source file).

items.title: Examples and verification
items.text:
Every example on this site is a complete program kept in the repository that owns its API, listed in that repository's examples/catalog.toml, and copied onto the site with its full source by scripts/import-docs.py. Python and PowerShell examples share catalogue ids, so each Python example page links to its PowerShell twin and back.

Section Examples Verified by CLI on Linux and Windows bash and PowerShell scripts for every command and option scripts/test-examples.sh (bash) and scripts/test-examples.ps1 (PowerShell 7 and Windows PowerShell 5.1) in nativehtmlkit-cli Python SDK 21 apps tests/integration (start-up and behaviour checks for every catalogue entry) in nativehtmlkit-python, Linux and Windows PowerShell SDK 20 apps tests/Examples.Tests.ps1 in nativehtmlkit-powershell, PowerShell 7 (Linux, Windows) and Windows PowerShell 5.1 Python UI and PowerShell UI 16 apps in each language qualification/examples/run_examples.py in nativehtmlkit_ui, Linux and Windows PowerShell 5.1

items.title: How examples are tested
items.text:
Each harness runs every example through its normal entry point against the released packages (Core 1.0.3, CLI 0.1.2, Python and PowerShell SDK 0.1.2, UI 0.1.1) with the host in headless test mode. It waits until the app is ready, drives a short scenario through public document commands (typing into fields, submitting forms, opening dialogs, reading the page back), requests an orderly quit and checks the exit status, stderr, files written and leftover processes. CLI scripts run with --timeout (exit status 124) plus their options and error paths. Every harness fails when a catalogued example is missing or an example is not catalogued.

Not covered headlessly: real pointer and keyboard input, the clipboard, native file dialogs, pixels on screen and screen readers. The screenshots on the example pages are real captures: each example was started unchanged on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland and its window captured.

items.title: Frequently asked questions
items.text:
Can I use JavaScript? No. There is no JavaScript engine. All logic runs in your Python or PowerShell program, which receives events and updates the page. See why native.

Can a page load images or CSS from the internet? No. Network URLs are always denied. Use local files under the asset root, registered ui4me-res:// bundles or inline styles. Your program itself may use the network and then display the result.

Why does my script run twice? The first run is the launcher that starts the native host; the host runs your script again as its backend. Keep side effects below Application.start() / Start-NativeHTMLKitScript or inside main(). See lifecycle.

Why does a click handler wait while a file dialog is open (Python)? Events are delivered in order on one worker thread, and open_files() waits for the user by default. Use wait=False and a done-callback. See file dialogs (PowerShell).

Why do clipboard or file-dialog calls fail in CI? In headless test mode (NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1) there is no native event loop: clipboard and native dialogs fail with RPC error -32001. Catch the error and show a message, as the examples do.

Can I simulate clicks in headless tests? There is no synthetic input. You can drive documented document operations — for example request_submit fires the form's submit event and replace_control_range fires input — and read the DOM back with get_text, get_value or get_html. Real input needs an interactive desktop.

uv add nativehtmlkit fails or installs a package without the host on Linux. The released Linux wheel is manylinux_2_39_x86_64: it needs glibc 2.39 or newer. On older systems the installer can only fall back to the source package, which has no native host. Run uv run nativehtmlkit-python doctor to check.

Does it work with Windows PowerShell 5.1? Yes, on Windows, for both the SDK and the UI module. Linux needs PowerShell 7.2 or newer.

Does it support macOS? Not in the current releases. Targets are Linux (KDE Plasma, Wayland) and Windows x64.

Which entry point should I use? See choosing an entry point. In short: a shell pipeline → CLI; quick reactive forms → UI library; everything else (dialogs, multiple windows, bitmaps, full DOM control) → the SDK, optionally mixed with the UI library.

Can I mix the UI library with SDK calls? Yes. The UI library is built on the public SDK; native dialogs, extra windows, clipboard and live bitmaps are SDK calls you make next to it.

Are the screenshots on this site real? Images marked as illustrations or placeholders are not captures. Real screenshots are added only after interactive verification on a native desktop.

How do I report a bug? Open an issue in the repository that owns the behaviour: rendering and native windows in Core, commands in the CLI, language APIs in Python or PowerShell, components in the UI library, and documentation in this site's repository. Include the versions and, if possible, a diagnostic report (see troubleshooting (PowerShell)).

items.title: Glossary
items.text:
App id : A reverse-DNS identity such as org.example.Notes (app_id= in Python, -AppId in PowerShell). It identifies the application for single-instance forwarding. Without one, a stable id is derived from the script path.

app.ready : The message a backend sends when startup is finished (at least one window exists). Python's app.run() sends it; PowerShell uses Set-NativeHTMLKitReady (or Start-NHKUi). It must arrive before the startup deadline.

app.shutdown : The host's message that the application is ending: the last window closed or a quit was accepted. It implies that every window is closed — Core 1.0.x sends no closed event for the last window — and the SDKs retire all handles.

Asset root : The folder that relative stylesheet, image and font URLs resolve against, and outside of which local resources are refused. By default the folder of a loaded HTML file; set it with asset_root= / -AssetRoot.

Backend : Your Python or PowerShell process, started and supervised by the host, holding the application logic. See lifecycle.

Before-close / before-quit policy : A callback the host asks before closing a window (on_before_close, Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeClose) or quitting (on_before_quit, Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeQuit). Returning false vetoes it.

Delegation : Registering one event handler on a container id; it fires for events whose path contains that id. See documents and handles.

Document : The HTML page shown in a window. Loading new HTML replaces it atomically and makes the previous document handle stale.

Generation : The identity of one loaded document. Handles and node references belong to one generation.

Headless / test mode : NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 (SDKs) or NATIVEHTMLKIT_CLI_TEST_HEADLESS=1 (CLI): the host runs the full protocol without showing windows. No user input, clipboard, native file dialogs or external opening.

Host : The native Core executable nativehtmlkit-host, bundled with each SDK and the CLI. It owns windows, rendering, input and desktop services.

Launcher : The first run of your script (uv run app.py, pwsh -File app.ps1). It starts the host, waits, and exits with the host's status; the host then runs the script again as the backend.

Live bitmap : A bounded RGBA8 image surface that your code fills with pixels and presents to an <img src="ui4me-bitmap://ID">. Released with its document.

Node reference : An opaque, generation-bound handle for an element that may have no id, returned by query_nodes / Get-NativeHTMLKitNodes.

Owner thread / owner runspace : The thread (Python UI) or runspace (PowerShell, PowerShell UI) that is allowed to perform UI updates. See threading.

Protocol v1 : The local JSON-RPC wire contract between backends/CLI and the host; stable since Core 1.0.3.

Pump : In PowerShell, processing of host messages on your runspace by Wait-NativeHTMLKit and by every waiting SDK call.

Stale handle : A window, document, node, bitmap or subscription whose host object no longer exists or was replaced. Using it raises StaleDocumentError (Python) or NativeHTMLKit.StaleObjectException (PowerShell).

State / computed : The UI library's observable values (state(...), New-NHKUiState) and derived values (computed(...), New-NHKUiComputed) that bound components follow automatically.

Supervisor : The host's role towards the backend: it starts it, watches it, and ends it on shutdown or failure.

Task : In PowerShell, bounded background work started with Start-NativeHTMLKitTask in an isolated runspace; its completion callback runs on the owner runspace.

ui4me-res://, ui4me-bitmap:// : URL schemes for in-memory resource bundles registered from code (register_resources, Register-NativeHTMLKitResources) and for live bitmaps. The ui4me- spellings are the stable v1 names.

items.title: Events: what the host tells your application
items.text:
Everything the user does in a NativeHTMLKit window is handled by the native host first; the host then reports what happened to the backend as notifications. This page lists every notification and event type that Core 1.0.3 sends, with their fields. It is written for both audiences:

  • App developers receive these events through an SDK's event registration API (see the Python or PowerShell SDK reference for the exact calls). The type names and fields below are what the SDK hands you.
  • Client authors receive them as raw wire-v1 frames (protocol reference §8).

Sources: the host's dispatch code and the renderer's event serializer in this repository, plus frames captured from a headless 1.0.3 host. Events that need real input (pointer, keyboard, IME, native drops) cannot be produced in headless mode and were not captured there; their field lists come from the source.

items.title: Notifications at a glance
items.text:
Method Params Sent when document.event {window_id, document_id, event} a DOM event fired in a document (user input, or a command such as focus, request_submit, show_dialog) document.error {window_id, document_id, message, fatal?} a document-level problem the backend should know about (an event too large for one frame, a failed native drop, a renderer failure — fatal: true means the document was removed) window.event {window_id, type, data} native window changes (below) app.shutdown {deadline_ms} the application is ending; exit before the deadline app.activated {args, cwd, activation_token} the user launched a single-instance app again; args is the second launch's command line desktop.preferences_changed preferences snapshot the desktop colour scheme, reduced-motion or high-contrast setting changed request.cancelled {id, reason} a pending host decision (window.before_close) was superseded, e.g. by an app-wide quit

Two host requests also need an answer ({"allow": true|false}): window.before_close {window_id, reason} and app.before_quit {reason}. SDKs expose them as close/quit handlers.

Clients must ignore notification types and members they do not know: new ones may be added within v1.

items.title: Common members
items.text:
Every DOM event object carries:

Member Meaning type Event type (tables below). element id of the nearest element with an id on the event path (the target itself if it has one); "" if none. path Ids of the identified elements on the propagation path, innermost first (only the first one for events that do not bubble, such as focus). node Generation-checked node reference of the actual target (usable with node-addressed ops). detail Click count for click/dblclick, else 0. cancelable Whether the event has a default action. default_prevented Present when cancelable: whether a set_default_action rule prevented it. shift, ctrl, alt, meta Modifier state.

Match targets on element or path. If a click lands on <span id="icon"> inside <button id="save">, element is "icon" and path is ["icon", "save", …]. Members whose names start with _ (for example _target, _element) are internal bookkeeping: ignore them; they are not part of the contract.

Depending on the target and type, these members are added:

Member When value target is a form control (text of input/textarea, value of select) checked target is a checkbox or radio selection {start, end, direction} target is a text control with a selection files target is an <input type=file> with chosen files related_element, related_node focus and mouse over/out/enter/leave events key, code, repeat, is_composing keyboard events data, input_type beforeinput, input, composition events x, y, button, buttons pointer, mouse and wheel events (viewport CSS px) pointer_id, pointer_type, is_primary, pressure pointer events delta_x, delta_y wheel old_state, new_state toggle, beforetoggle ("open"/"closed") submitter submit validity invalid (same shape as get_validity) return_value close of a <dialog> property_name, pseudo_element, elapsed_time transition events animation_name, pseudo_element, elapsed_time animation events

items.title: DOM event types
items.text: Group Types Pointer and mouse click, dblclick, auxclick, contextmenu, mousedown, mouseup, mousemove, mouseover, mouseout, mouseenter, mouseleave, pointerdown, pointerup, pointermove, pointercancel, gotpointercapture, lostpointercapture, wheel Scrolling scroll Keyboard and text editing keydown, keyup, beforeinput, input, change, select, selectionchange, copy, cut, paste IME composition compositionstart, compositionupdate, compositionend Focus focus, blur, focusin, focusout Forms submit, reset, invalid Dialogs, popovers, <details> toggle, beforetoggle, cancel (Escape on a modal dialog), close CSS transitions transitionrun, transitionstart, transitionend, transitioncancel CSS animations animationstart, animationiteration, animationend, animationcancel

items.title: Host-generated event types
items.text:
These are not DOM events; they have their own members:

Type Members Meaning link_activated element, href, url (resolved, or null), node the user activated an <a href>. The host never navigates; open it yourself (for example desktop.open_external) if you want to. dragstart element (source id), source, x, y in-page drag of an element with draggable="true" began (after 4 CSS px of movement) dragover element (target id), source, x, y the element under the pointer changed during the drag drop element (target), source released over a target dragend element, source, dropped, target always last; Escape or focus loss cancels drag_feedback phase, accepted, kind (files/text), element, node, x, y, external: true a drag from another application entered, moved over a new target or left (transitions only) drop (external) element, node, x, y, paths or text, external: true files (≤1024 local paths) or text dropped from another application onto an element that opted in with data-nativehtmlkit-drop="files text" environment_changed environment (as get_environment) the desktop preferences changed what the document's media queries see

items.title: Default actions
items.text:
Events reach the backend after the host has already acted on the input, so a handler cannot cancel anything. To stop a default action (a shortcut key, form submission, the context menu, a dialog's Escape cancel, a popover toggle), register a rule beforehand with the set_default_action op; the SDKs wrap it. The event then arrives with default_prevented: true. Example, captured from a headless host:

→ document.command {op: "set_default_action", element: "f", event: "submit"}   ← {updated: true}
→ document.command {op: "request_submit", element: "f"}
← document.event {type: "submit", element: "f", path: ["f"], cancelable: true, default_prevented: true, …}
← {submitted: true, default_prevented: true}

items.title: What a command emits
items.text:
Commands that behave like user actions emit the matching events before their response; plain state setters do not. Captured from Core 1.0.3:

Command Events (in order) focus {element: "i"} focus, focusin (and blur, focusout on the previously focused element) request_submit on a valid form submit request_submit with an empty required field invalid (with validity), then focus, focusin on that control reset_form reset check_validity with failures invalid per failing control show_dialog {modal: true} beforetoggle, focus changes, toggle close_dialog {return_value: "ok"} beforetoggle, close (with return_value), toggle show_popover / hide_popover / toggle_popover beforetoggle, toggle set_attribute {name: "open"} on <details> toggle scroll_to that moves scroll set_control_selection select, selectionchange replace_control_range beforeinput, input, selectionchange edit_command {command: "copy"} copy select_text / clear_selection selectionchange set_value, set_checked, set_selected_values, set_text, set_environment none

A typical captured frame:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"document.event","params":{"window_id":"w1","document_id":"d1",
 "event":{"type":"invalid","element":"note","path":["note"],"node":"node:1:13:1","detail":0,
  "cancelable":true,"default_prevented":false,"value":"","shift":false,"ctrl":false,"alt":false,
  "meta":false,"validity":{"valid":false,"flags":{"valueMissing":true,…},"message":"…"}}}}

items.title: Delivery guarantees
items.text:
• Events of a document are delivered in order. Events of a document that has since been replaced or unloaded are dropped, so document_id in an event always names the document that produced it.
  • A document queues at most 1024 undelivered events; an event that would not fit in one 2 MiB frame is replaced by a document.error.
  • If the backend stops reading, the host drops document.event and window.event notifications (never responses or host requests) and counts them in host.diagnostics.dropped_notifications. Keep reading while you work, or move slow work off the reading thread.

items.title: window.event
items.text:
{window_id, type, data}. Types sent by Core 1.0.3:

type data When close_requested {reason} a close was requested (title-bar button, OS, or window.request_close with reason: "backend_request"); a window.before_close decision follows after app.ready closed {} the window was destroyed (not sent for the last window when its close starts shutdown) focused {focused} the native window gained or lost keyboard focus resized {physical_width, physical_height, scale_factor} the surface size changed scale_changed {scale_factor} the display scale changed (moved to another monitor, settings) key {key, state: "pressed"/"released", repeat, physical_key} raw native key event (DOM keyboard events are sent as well when a document is loaded) dropped_files / dropped_text / text {paths} / {text} / {text, cursor, anchor} only for the built-in probe surface of a window without a document

None of these are produced in headless mode except close_requested and closed (from window.request_close).

items.title: Application lifecycle
items.text:
backend                                   host
  host.hello ────────────────────────────▶
  window.create / document.load ─────────▶
  app.ready ─────────────────────────────▶          phase: running
           ◀──────────────────────────── document.event / window.event …
  app.request_quit ──────────────────────▶          (or the user closes the last window)
           ◀──────────────────────────── app.before_quit {reason}   (request)
  {"allow": true} ───────────────────────▶
           ◀──────────────────────────── app.shutdown {deadline_ms}
  exit before deadline_ms
  • app.before_quit reasons: backend_request (from app.request_quit) and last_window (the user closed the last window). Answer {"allow": false} to keep running, e.g. to ask about unsaved work.
  • window.before_close reasons: backend_request (window.request_close) and native_close (the title-bar button or another OS close request).
  • There is no host-side deadline for these answers; always answer promptly.
  • app.shutdown makes every window and document handle stale. It is also sent when startup is cancelled (the user closed the window before app.ready).
  • app.force_quit from the backend, or Ctrl+Shift+Q pressed by the user in a document window, ends the session without asking; the backend is killed and the host exits with status 1.
  • A second launch of a single-instance app arrives as app.activated; the first instance's window is focused where the OS allows it.

Source: nativehtmlkit-core/docs/guides/events.md · edit the page there.
