  3. Check the element id and event type. Ids are case-sensitive; delegated handlers match the target's nearest id or any id on the path. submit fires on the form, not on the button, and only after native validation passed.
  4. Check that something pumps. Callbacks only run inside Wait-NativeHTMLKit or another waiting SDK command. A script blocked in Start-Sleep or a long loop on the UI runspace delays every event: use a background task.
  5. Check variable scope in callbacks created in functions or loops (closures).
path: How to troubleshoot: diagnostics levels, counters and support bundles

items.title: Turn on more detail
items.text:
$app = Start-NativeHTMLKitScript -Name 'My tool' -Diagnostics Trace

or set NATIVEHTMLKIT_DIAGNOSTICS=trace before starting (debug for less). The level applies to the SDK, the host and the backend. NATIVEHTMLKIT_VERBOSE=1 additionally relays the host's informational records to the console (nativehtmlkit-host info: ...).

At trace, the SDK records every request with its duration, every host notification and the start and end of every callback, correlated by request id and the diagnostic session id. That is how you see, for example, that a submit event arrived, which callback ran, which commands it sent and how long each took.
path: How to troubleshoot: diagnostics levels, counters and support bundles

items.title: Counters at run time
items.text:
$report = Get-NativeHTMLKitDiagnosticReport -Application $app
$report.Connection.CallbackFailures      # callbacks that threw
$report.Connection.DeferredDropped       # notifications dropped while a callback was too slow
$report.Connection.DroppedNotifications  # notifications the SDK queue dropped
$report.HostCounters.dropped_notifications

Nonzero drop counters mean the UI runspace was blocked for long stretches while events kept coming (for example pointer moves during a long callback).
path: How to troubleshoot: diagnostics levels, counters and support bundles

items.title: Support bundles
items.text:
$bundle = Export-NativeHTMLKitSupportBundle -Path (Join-Path $env:TEMP 'mytool-support.zip') -Application $app

The ZIP contains manifest.json (module, PowerShell edition and version, diagnostics level, counters, whether records were dropped) and timeline.jsonl (redacted SDK records). It never contains form values, document text, HTML, file paths, URLs, tokens, exception messages or raw host/backend output, so it is reasonable to attach to a public bug report. Nothing is uploaded. Record at trace for the most useful timeline; the history holds the last 2048 records.
path: How to troubleshoot: diagnostics levels, counters and support bundles

items.title: Document problems
items.text: Get-NativeHTMLKitDiagnostics -Document $doc lists renderer notes: unsupported CSS features, resources still pending or failed, layout notes. Get-NativeHTMLKitComputedStyle shows what a property resolved to. Images that never appear usually point to a wrong relative URL: relative URLs resolve against -AssetRoot (Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml) or the HTML file's folder (Open-NativeHTMLKitFile).
path: How to troubleshoot: diagnostics levels, counters and support bundles

items.title: Environment checks
items.text:
Get-NativeHTMLKitHostPath                         # which host binary, verified against HOST-MANIFEST.json
$caps = Get-NativeHTMLKitCapabilities -Application $app
$caps.platform; $caps.headless; $caps.file_dialogs; $caps.clipboard_text
Get-NativeHTMLKitPreferences -Application $app    # observed colour scheme / reduced motion

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/diagnostics-and-troubleshooting.md · edit the page there.
path: How to troubleshoot: diagnostics levels, counters and support bundles

items.title: How to use HTML dialogs and popovers
path: How to use HTML dialogs and popovers

items.title: How to use HTML dialogs and popovers
items.text:
Reference: Show-NativeHTMLKitHtmlDialog, Show-NativeHTMLKitPopover. Examples: 09-settings-dialog.ps1, bulk-rename (confirmation dialog), 13-keyboard-shortcuts.ps1 (help popover).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

HTML <dialog> and popover elements are drawn inside your window by the native renderer. Use them for confirmations, settings and tips; use native file dialogs for files.
path: How to use HTML dialogs and popovers

items.title: A confirmation dialog
items.text:
<dialog id="confirm" aria-labelledby="confirm-title">
  <h2 id="confirm-title">Delete 3 files?</h2>
  <button id="confirm-no">Cancel</button> <button id="confirm-yes">Delete</button>
</dialog>

Show-NativeHTMLKitHtmlDialog -Document $doc -Element confirm          # modal: the rest of the page is inert

function Close-Confirm([bool]$Yes) {
    Show-NativeHTMLKitHtmlDialog -Document $doc -Element confirm -Close -ReturnValue ''
    if ($Yes) { Remove-SelectedFiles }
}
$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element confirm-yes -Callback { Close-Confirm $true }
$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element confirm-no -Callback { Close-Confirm $false }

Show-NativeHTMLKitHtmlDialog returns immediately; it does not wait for the user. Escape closes a modal dialog (dispatching cancel, then close) without either button being clicked, which here simply means "no".
path: How to use HTML dialogs and popovers

items.title: Return values persist
items.text: A <dialog>'s return value (-ReturnValue, $evt.return_value of the close event, return_value of get_dialog) follows HTML semantics: it is kept when the dialog is shown again and when it is closed without a value, for example by Escape. A close handler that acts on return_value -eq 'yes' would therefore repeat the last "yes" after an Escape. Decide in the button handlers, as above, or clear your own "confirmed" flag every time you open the dialog. The close event is still useful for cleanup that should happen however the dialog was closed.
path: How to use HTML dialogs and popovers

items.title: A dialog with a form
items.text: Put a <form> inside the dialog and handle its submit event: native validation (min, max, required) runs first, then your handler saves and closes the dialog with a return value. 09-settings-dialog.ps1 prefills the form before opening the dialog, saves to JSON and applies the colour scheme.
path: How to use HTML dialogs and popovers

items.title: Inspect the state
items.text:
$state = Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand -Document $doc -Operation get_dialog -Parameters @{ element = 'confirm' }
$state.open; $state.modal; $state.return_value
path: How to use HTML dialogs and popovers

items.title: Popovers
items.text:
An element with the popover attribute is hidden until shown; it appears in the top layer.

<button id="help">?</button>
<div id="help-tip" popover>Paths may use * and ? wildcards.</div>

$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element help -Callback {
    $open = Show-NativeHTMLKitPopover -Document $doc -Element help-tip -Action toggle   # returns the new state
}

-Action show and -Action hide return nothing. Query the state with the get_popover document command (open). A toggle event with old_state/new_state reports changes.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/dialogs-and-popovers.md · edit the page there.
path: How to use HTML dialogs and popovers

items.title: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures
items.text:
Reference: events. Examples: 02-counter.ps1 (delegation), 04-todo-list.ps1 (dynamic lists), 08-multi-window.ps1 (closures), 13-keyboard-shortcuts.ps1 (keys).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: Register a handler
items.text:
$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element save -Callback {
    param($evt)
    Save-Report
    Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText -Document $doc -Element status -Text 'Saved.'
}
  • The callback receives one argument, the event object. Name it $evt or $e; $event is a PowerShell automatic variable.
  • There is no -Data parameter on the SDK cmdlet. Pass context by closure (below) or look it up from the event ($evt.element, $evt.value). (-Data belongs to the separate NativeHTMLKit.UI module's helpers.)
  • The callback's output is discarded; return values do not matter except for close/quit policies.
  • Errors inside a callback are caught, written to stderr and counted; the app keeps running.
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: One handler for many elements: delegation
items.text:
-Element matches when the id is the event target's nearest id or any id on the event path. Register once on a stable container and dispatch on $evt.element:

# <div id="toolbar"><button id="new">New</button><button id="open">Open</button>...</div>
$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element toolbar -Callback {
    param($evt)
    switch ($evt.element) {
        'new'  { New-Entry }
        'open' { Open-Entry }
    }
}

For lists you re-render, encode the row identity in the child ids (todo-17-delete) and parse it with a regular expression, as 04-todo-list.ps1 does. Handlers on elements that you replace with Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml keep working when they are registered on the container, because subscriptions are per document and match by id at dispatch time.
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: Read input from the event
items.text:
input and change events carry the control's current value (and checked for checkboxes), so a live filter needs no extra request:

$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type input -Element filter -Callback {
    param($evt)
    $script:filterText = ([string]$evt.value).Trim()
    Update-Table
}
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: Closures and scope
items.text:
Variable lookup in a callback happens when it runs. Three rules cover almost every case:

1. At script level, read script variables directly and write them with $script:.

$count = 0
$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element inc -Callback {
    $script:count++                                   # $count++ would change a local copy only
    Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText -Document $doc -Element value -Text ([string]$script:count)
}

2. A callback created inside a function or a loop needs .GetNewClosure(). Without it, a function's locals are gone when the callback runs, and a loop variable has its final value:

foreach ($name in 'alpha', 'beta') {
    # Without .GetNewClosure() both buttons would report 'beta'.
    $null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element "btn-$name" -Callback {
        Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText -Document $doc -Element status -Text "Clicked $name"
    }.GetNewClosure()
}

3. Inside a .GetNewClosure() scriptblock, $script: is a different scope. The closure runs in its own dynamic module, so $script:count++ there does not change the script's $count. Share mutable state through a reference type captured by the closure, typically a hashtable:

$state = @{ Count = 0 }
function Add-Counter([string]$Id) {
    $null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element $Id -Callback {
        $state.Count++                                # the same hashtable everywhere
    }.GetNewClosure()
}

Functions defined in your script remain callable from closures, and $doc/$app captured by the closure stay valid as long as the document and application are alive. 08-multi-window.ps1 uses this pattern for per-window state.
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: When callbacks run, and re-entrancy
items.text:
Callbacks run during Wait-NativeHTMLKit and during any command that waits for a host reply. If your top-level code calls Submit-NativeHTMLKitForm, the submit handler may run before Submit-NativeHTMLKitForm returns. While one callback runs, the SDK does not start another notification callback (they are queued), but SDK commands inside the callback still work and still answer close/quit decisions.

Two consequences:

  • Keep callbacks short. Long work blocks every other event: move it to a background task.
  • A callback that closes the application (Close-NativeHTMLKit) while your top-level code is waiting in another command makes that command throw NativeHTMLKit.DisconnectedException (... did not complete: the application connection was closed). Quit with Request-NativeHTMLKitQuit instead.
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: Default actions happen first
items.text:
The native default action (typing, focus movement, toggling a checkbox, submitting) has already happened when the callback runs, so $evt.default_prevented is informational. To stop a default action, register a rule before the input arrives:

# Enter in the search box must not submit the surrounding form.
Set-NativeHTMLKitPreventDefault -Document $doc -Element search -EventType keydown -Key Enter
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: Keyboard shortcuts
items.text: Register keydown without -Element to see every key in the document, then build a chord string from the modifier flags and $evt.key (DOM key names: s, Enter, Escape, F1, ArrowDown). 13-keyboard-shortcuts.ps1 maps chords such as ctrl+shift+u to scriptblocks. The keyboard and focus guide covers shortcuts, default-action rules, focus and the caret in detail.
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: Window and host notifications
items.text:
Window state changes and desktop preference changes are notifications, not document events:

Register-NativeHTMLKitNotification -Application $app -Method 'desktop.preferences_changed' -Callback {
    param($params)
    Update-ThemeLabel
}

One callback per method; register again to replace it, -Callback $null to remove it.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/events-and-callbacks.md · edit the page there.
path: How to handle events: callbacks, delegation, scope and closures

items.title: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs
path: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs

items.title: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs
items.text:
Reference: Show-NativeHTMLKitFileDialog. Examples: 07-file-preview.ps1, bulk-rename (folder picker).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

The dialogs are the desktop's own file dialogs, attached to one of your windows (modal for it).
path: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs

items.title: Open one or several files
items.text:
try {
    $pick = Show-NativeHTMLKitFileDialog -Window $window -Kind OpenFiles -Title 'Import CSV' -Multiple $true -Filters @(
        @{ name = 'CSV files'; extensions = @('csv') }
        @{ name = 'Text files'; extensions = @('txt', 'log') })
} catch [NativeHTMLKit.RpcException] {
    Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText -Document $doc -Element status -Text ('No file dialog: ' + $_.Exception.RpcMessage)
    return
}
if ($pick.cancelled) { return }
foreach ($path in $pick.paths) { Import-Csv -LiteralPath $path | Add-Rows }

The call waits without a deadline while the user decides, and keeps pumping events, so the app stays responsive. The result is @{ cancelled; paths }; paths are full paths.
path: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs

items.title: Save a file
items.text:
$target = Show-NativeHTMLKitFileDialog -Window $window -Kind SaveFile -Title 'Export report' -FileName 'report.csv' -Directory ([Environment]::GetFolderPath('MyDocuments')) -Filters @(@{ name = 'CSV'; extensions = @('csv') })
if (-not $target.cancelled) { $rows | Export-Csv -LiteralPath $target.paths[0] -NoTypeInformation }

-FileName is only valid with -Kind SaveFile. Whether the dialog asks before overwriting, and whether it appends the filter's extension, is decided by the operating system's dialog.
path: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs

items.title: Choose a folder
items.text:
$folder = Show-NativeHTMLKitFileDialog -Window $window -Kind ChooseFolder -Title 'Folder to scan'
if (-not $folder.cancelled) { Open-Folder $folder.paths[0] }
path: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs

items.title: Not waiting
items.text: -NoWait returns a NativeHTMLKit.Request immediately. Await it with Wait-NativeHTMLKitRpc (same result) or close the dialog from code with Stop-NativeHTMLKitRpc. One native dialog per window can be open at a time; a second request fails with code -32005 (busy).
path: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs

items.title: When dialogs are unavailable
items.text:
Headless test mode and some sessions have no native dialogs: the call throws NativeHTMLKit.RpcException (code -32001, Native file dialogs are unavailable in headless mode). Check first and offer a fallback, for example a path text box or a script parameter:

$caps = Get-NativeHTMLKitCapabilities -Application $app
if (-not $caps.file_dialogs) { Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentAttribute -Document $doc -Element browse -Name disabled }
path: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs

items.title: After the dialog
items.text:
Treat the returned paths as untrusted input: show them with Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText or encode them, read files with -LiteralPath, and handle access errors. To show a file in the file manager, use Open-NativeHTMLKitExternal -Target $path -Reveal -Window $window.

Native dialogs cannot be exercised by the headless example harness; the examples verify the fallback path. Verify dialog journeys in a desktop session.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/file-dialogs.md · edit the page there.
path: How to open, save and choose folders with native dialogs

items.title: How to build forms with validation
path: How to build forms with validation

items.title: How to build forms with validation
items.text:
Reference: forms. Examples: 03-form-validation.ps1, 09-settings-dialog.ps1.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.
path: How to build forms with validation

items.title: Let the native form validate first
items.text:
Write the HTML constraints you can (required, type="email", min/max, minlength, maxlength, pattern) and handle the submit event. The host validates before it dispatches submit; for an invalid form it dispatches one invalid event per failing control, in document order, and your submit handler does not run. Pressing Enter in a field or clicking a type="submit" button submits; there is no page navigation.

invalid does not bubble (its path holds only the control), so subscribe document-wide and collect the messages into an error summary. The event's validity.message is the native message:

$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type invalid -Callback {
    param($evt)
    # One event per invalid control, in document order, before (instead of) 'submit'.
    $element = [string]$evt.element
    if (-not $script:labels.ContainsKey($element)) { return }
    $message = 'Invalid value'
    if ($null -ne $evt.validity -and $evt.validity.message) { $message = [string]$evt.validity.message }
    $script:errors.Add($script:labels[$element] + ': ' + $message)
    Show-Errors
    Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText -Document $doc -Element result -Text ''
}

Show-Errors renders the list with every message encoded by [Net.WebUtility]::HtmlEncode.
path: How to build forms with validation

items.title: Read all values at once
items.text:
$values = @{}
foreach ($entry in @((Get-NativeHTMLKitFormData -Document $doc -Form signup).entries)) {
    # Ordered; checkboxes may repeat a name.
    if (-not $values.ContainsKey($entry.name)) { $values[$entry.name] = New-Object System.Collections.Generic.List[string] }
    $values[$entry.name].Add([string]$entry.value)
}

Entries follow the HTML rules: unchecked checkboxes are absent, a checked checkbox without a value attribute reports on, and repeated names (multi-select, several checkboxes with one name) appear several times, which is why each name collects a list.
path: How to build forms with validation

items.title: Add your own rules
items.text:
For a rule HTML cannot express, such as two passwords that must match, set a custom validity message. It makes the control invalid, so the native validation blocks the submit and reports the message in the control's invalid event, until an empty message clears it:

function Update-PasswordMatch {
    # A custom validity message makes the control invalid until it is cleared again.
    $same = (Get-NativeHTMLKitValue -Document $doc -Element password) -ceq (Get-NativeHTMLKitValue -Document $doc -Element confirm)
    $message = ''
    if (-not $same) { $message = $mismatch }
    $null = Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand -Document $doc -Operation set_custom_validity -Parameters @{ element = 'confirm'; message = $message }
}

Run it from the input events of both fields and once more before a programmatic submit. Callbacks run after native dispatch, so a fast typist can submit before the last input event updated the custom validity: check the rule again in the submit handler. Rules that need lookups (reserved names, a directory query) belong in the submit handler too; show their messages next to the fields (aria-invalid="true" marks them for assistive technology) and move focus to the first invalid field with Set-NativeHTMLKitFocus.
path: How to build forms with validation

items.title: Fill, reset and drive a form
items.text:
• Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentValue, Set-NativeHTMLKitChecked, Set-NativeHTMLKitSelectedValues prefill controls. They do not dispatch input/change events.
  • Reset-NativeHTMLKitForm restores the initial values; clear your own error texts as well.
  • Submit-NativeHTMLKitForm submits programmatically with validation, returning submitted = $false when blocked. Scripted checks use it to exercise the real submit path without input devices.
path: How to build forms with validation

items.title: Long-running submit
items.text:
Do not block the submit handler with slow work (a REST call, a directory query). Disable the button, start a background task, and re-enable it in -OnCompleted:

$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type submit -Element request -Callback {
    $user = @((Get-NativeHTMLKitFormData -Document $doc -Form request).entries | Where-Object { $_.name -eq 'user' })[0].value
    Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentAttribute -Document $doc -Element send -Name disabled
    $null = Start-NativeHTMLKitTask -Application $app -ArgumentList @($user) -ScriptBlock {
        param($user) Start-Sleep -Seconds 2; "Ticket created for $user"
    } -OnCompleted {
        param($result)
        Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText -Document $doc -Element status -Text $result[0]
        Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentAttribute -Document $doc -Element send -Name disabled -Remove
    }
}

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/forms-and-validation.md · edit the page there.
path: How to build forms with validation

items.title: How to handle the keyboard and focus
path: How to handle the keyboard and focus

items.title: How to handle the keyboard and focus
items.text:
Reference: events, focus and selection, Set-NativeHTMLKitPreventDefault. Examples: 13-keyboard-shortcuts.ps1 (shortcut table, Tab in an editor), 04-todo-list.ps1 (Enter submits, Escape cancels, focus moves into the edit field).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

The host handles the keyboard natively: typing, caret movement, Tab navigation, Enter in forms and Escape in dialogs all work without any PowerShell code. Your script observes keys through keydown/keyup events and moves the focus with Set-NativeHTMLKitFocus.
path: How to handle the keyboard and focus

items.title: Shortcuts with keydown
items.text:
A keydown event carries key (the DOM key name: a, S, Enter, Escape, Tab, F1, ArrowDown, ...), code (the physical key), repeat and the modifier flags ctrl, shift, alt, meta. Build a chord string and look it up in a table of scriptblocks:

$shortcuts = @{
    'ctrl+s'       = { Save-Snippet }
    'ctrl+shift+u' = { Convert-SelectionToUpper }
    'f1'           = { $null = Show-NativeHTMLKitPopover -Document $doc -Element help -Action toggle }
}

function ConvertTo-Chord($KeyEvent) {
    $parts = @()
    if ($KeyEvent.ctrl) { $parts += 'ctrl' }
    if ($KeyEvent.alt) { $parts += 'alt' }
    if ($KeyEvent.shift) { $parts += 'shift' }
    if ($KeyEvent.meta) { $parts += 'meta' }
    $parts += ([string]$KeyEvent.key).ToLowerInvariant()
    return ($parts -join '+')
}

# Without -Element the handler sees every keydown in the document.
$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type keydown -Callback {
    param($evt)
    $chord = ConvertTo-Chord $evt
    if ($shortcuts.ContainsKey($chord)) { & $shortcuts[$chord] }
}

With -Element, only keys pressed while the focus is inside that element arrive, which is how a list reacts to Escape only while one of its rows is being edited:

$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type keydown -Element todos -Callback {
    param($evt)
    if ($evt.key -eq 'Escape' -and $null -ne $state.Editing) { Stop-TodoEdit }
}

With Shift held, key is the shifted character (U, not u), so the chord helper lower-cases it. Use $evt.code (KeyU) when you care about the physical key rather than the character.
path: How to handle the keyboard and focus

items.title: Stop a default action: register it before the key arrives
items.text:
Callbacks run after the host has already performed the default action, so a callback cannot stop Tab from moving the focus or Enter from submitting a form. Register a rule up front instead:

# Tab (without Shift) indents in the editor instead of moving focus; the keydown handler inserts spaces.
Set-NativeHTMLKitPreventDefault -Document $doc -Element editor -EventType keydown -Key Tab -Shift $false

# Enter in the search box must not submit the surrounding form.
Set-NativeHTMLKitPreventDefault -Document $doc -Element search -EventType keydown -Key Enter

-Key is case-sensitive and matches the DOM key name. A modifier you do not pass matches either state. The rule applies to the element and everything inside it; at most 256 rules per document.
path: How to handle the keyboard and focus

items.title: Enter and Escape for free
items.text:
• Enter in a form submits it (HTML implicit submission): the submit event arrives, and a required field that is empty blocks the submission and gets invalid instead. This is why the examples handle submit on a <form> rather than click on its button.
  • Escape in a modal <dialog> sends cancel and then close. Escape on an auto popover closes it. See dialogs and popovers.
path: How to handle the keyboard and focus

items.title: Move the focus
items.text:
Set-NativeHTMLKitFocus -Document $doc -Element edit-title        # focus an element (or -Node)
$focused = Get-NativeHTMLKitFocusedElement -Document $doc        # .element (id or $null), .node
Set-NativeHTMLKitFocus -Document $doc -Blur                      # nobody has the focus afterwards

Behaviour checked with Core 1.0.3 in headless mode:

  • Focusing an element that cannot take the focus (a heading without tabindex, a disabled control, an element made inert by a modal dialog) throws NativeHTMLKit.RpcException code -32602 FOCUS_MOVE_REJECTED: not a focusable area. Wrap the call in try/catch when the target may be hidden or disabled.
  • A successful focus change sends focus and focusin events for the new element, like a click.
  • Opening a modal dialog with Show-NativeHTMLKitHtmlDialog focuses its first focusable control.
  • After a document loads, no element had the focus in headless mode, even with an autofocus attribute. When the first field should have the focus, call Set-NativeHTMLKitFocus after loading the page.

After re-rendering a region with Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml, the old elements are gone and so is their focus. Focus the new element explicitly, as the todo list does after switching a row into edit mode:

$state.Editing = $id
Update-Todos                                              # renders <input id="edit-title">
Set-NativeHTMLKitFocus -Document $doc -Element edit-title
path: How to handle the keyboard and focus

items.title: Tab order
items.text:
Sequential Tab navigation follows the document order of focusable elements: links, buttons and form controls, plus any element with tabindex="0". tabindex="-1" makes an element focusable from PowerShell but skips it with Tab. Positive tabindex values reorder navigation, but they make forms hard to follow; prefer arranging the markup in the order you want. Disabled controls and everything behind an open modal dialog are skipped.

Style the focus ring with :focus-visible (keyboard focus) rather than :focus, and use :focus-within to highlight the row or card that contains the focused control:

button:focus-visible, input:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #3a6ff7; outline-offset: 2px; }
li:focus-within { background: #eef3ff; }
path: How to handle the keyboard and focus

items.title: Caret and selection in text controls
items.text:
$sel = Get-NativeHTMLKitSelection -Document $doc -Element editor        # start, end (UTF-16 offsets), direction
$null = Set-NativeHTMLKitSelection -Document $doc -Element editor -Start 0 -End 5
# Replace the selection (or insert at the caret) and put the caret after the new text:
$null = Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand -Document $doc -Operation replace_control_range -Parameters @{
    element = 'editor'; replacement = '    '; selection_mode = 'end' }

length in the selection result is the length of the whole value, not of the selection: use end - start. Invoke-NativeHTMLKitEditCommand runs undo, redo, cut, copy, paste, select_all and delete through the native editor.
path: How to handle the keyboard and focus

items.title: Testing keyboard code without a keyboard
items.text:
Headless mode (NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1) has no synthetic key presses. Keep the action behind each shortcut in a function or scriptblock and call it from the test, or pass an object with the same fields as a real event to your dispatcher, as the -SelfTest of 13-keyboard-shortcuts.ps1 does. Check real key handling, focus rings and screen-reader announcements once on each desktop you support.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/keyboard-and-focus.md · edit the page there.
path: How to handle the keyboard and focus

items.title: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close
items.text:
Every NativeHTMLKit PowerShell app follows the same lifecycle. This guide explains each step and the mistakes that break it. Reference: lifecycle. Examples: 01-hello.ps1 (the skeleton), 17-focus-timer.ps1 (quit confirmation, saving after shutdown).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: The skeleton
items.text:
param([string]$Folder)                 # 1. parameters: parsed in both runs
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
Import-Module NativeHTMLKit

$app = Start-NativeHTMLKitScript -Name 'Folder report'   # 2. the dividing line
try {
    $window = New-NativeHTMLKitWindow -Application $app -Title 'Folder report'
    $doc = Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml -Window $window -Html $html
    $null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element refresh -Callback { Update-Report }
    Update-Report                       # 3. initial content
    Set-NativeHTMLKitReady -Application $app
    Wait-NativeHTMLKit -Application $app -UntilShutdown  # 4. run until the user quits
} finally {
    Close-NativeHTMLKit -Application $app                # 5. always
}
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: 1. Start-NativeHTMLKitScript runs your script twice
items.text:
When you run pwsh -File ./report.ps1 -Folder C:\Data, the first process becomes the launcher: Start-NativeHTMLKitScript writes a private temporary manifest, starts the native host, and waits. The host starts pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ./report.ps1 -Folder C:\Data again, the backend. In the backend, the same call connects to the host and returns the application object. When the host exits, the launcher exits with the host's exit code, so the launcher never executes the lines after the call.

Consequences:

  • Everything above the call runs twice. Put only param(), Import-Module and pure definitions there. Side effects (writing files, prompting, starting services) go below.
  • Script parameters reach the backend because the launcher reuses the command-line arguments. If you dot-source or call the script from an interactive prompt, pass them explicitly with -ArgumentList.
  • The backend runs with -NoProfile -NonInteractive: Read-Host, Get-Credential prompts and profile functions are not available. Collect input in the window.
  • Standard output and errors of the backend are relayed by the host to the launcher's console, so Write-Host and errors still appear where you started the app.
  • $PSScriptRoot and $PSCommandPath refer to the script in both runs; the backend's working folder is the launcher's current folder.
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: 2. Build the first screen, then Set-NativeHTMLKitReady
items.text:
Create at least one window, load its document, register handlers and fill initial content, then call Set-NativeHTMLKitReady. The host enforces a startup deadline (-StartupTimeoutMilliseconds, default 30 s) for reaching ready. Before ready, closing the only window cancels startup.

Set-NativeHTMLKitReady without any window fails (RpcException -32008, invalid state).
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: 3. Wait-NativeHTMLKit -UntilShutdown is the event loop
items.text:
All callbacks run inside Wait-NativeHTMLKit (and inside any command that waits for the host). -UntilShutdown returns when the host shuts the app down, after the user closed the last window or a quit was accepted. For periodic work, prefer a background task timer (06-log-tail.ps1, 12-live-chart.ps1) over a hand-written loop; if you need a loop, use the pump form:

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

while ($true) {
    $null = Wait-NativeHTMLKit -Application $app -TimeoutMilliseconds 200
    if ((Get-NativeHTMLKitDiagnosticReport -Application $app).Connection.ShutdownRequested) { break }
    Update-Clock
}
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: 4. Quitting: use Request-NativeHTMLKitQuit
items.text:
A Quit button or menu item should call Request-NativeHTMLKitQuit. The host asks the quit policy (Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeQuit), then shuts down every window, and Wait-NativeHTMLKit -UntilShutdown returns. The host exits with code 0.

$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element quit -Callback {
    $null = Request-NativeHTMLKitQuit -Application $app
}
Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeQuit -Application $app -Callback { -not $script:busy }   # last output decides

Do not end the app by calling Close-NativeHTMLKit from a callback: it does stop the event loop, but the host was never asked to quit, so it reports nativehtmlkit-host error: application failed (reason=Backend connection lost: peer disconnected) and exits with code 1 (observed with Core 1.0.3).
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: 5. Close-NativeHTMLKit in finally
items.text: Close-NativeHTMLKit retires every handle, removes callbacks and requests cancellation of background tasks. It accepts $null and is idempotent, so a finally block is always safe. If an exception escapes your script, PowerShell reports it, the backend exits, and the host exits with code 1 and application failed on stderr: the error is visible in the launcher's console.
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: Ask before quitting, save after shutdown
items.text:
A quit policy can veto a quit and ask the user instead. The host calls it for every quit request, including the one that follows closing the last window. Show an HTML <dialog> and return $false; the dialog's button sets a flag and asks again:

Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeQuit -Application $app -Callback {
    if ($timer.Running -and -not $timer.AllowQuit) {
        Show-NativeHTMLKitHtmlDialog -Document $doc -Element confirm-quit
        $false
        return
    }
    $true
}
$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $doc -Type click -Element quit-anyway -Callback {
    $timer.AllowQuit = $true
    Show-NativeHTMLKitHtmlDialog -Document $doc -Element confirm-quit -Close -ReturnValue quit
    $null = Request-NativeHTMLKitQuit -Application $app      # the policy runs again and now allows it
}

The policy only runs after Set-NativeHTMLKitReady; a quit requested earlier is not offered to it.

Code after Wait-NativeHTMLKit -UntilShutdown runs once the host has shut down. It is the place to save state, with plain PowerShell only: the windows are gone and commands that talk to the host fail.

Wait-NativeHTMLKit -Application $app -UntilShutdown
# The host has shut down: plain PowerShell only from here on.
Set-Content -LiteralPath $statsPath -Value (ConvertTo-Json @{ completed = $timer.Completed } -Compress) -Encoding UTF8

Per-application folders for such files come from the host: (Invoke-NativeHTMLKitRpc -Application $app -Method 'desktop.paths') returns config, data, cache, state and runtime (XDG folders on Linux, AppData folders on Windows), named after the -AppId. The host does not create them; create the folder before writing. 17-focus-timer.ps1 and 04-todo-list.ps1 use them.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: Running a manifest instead
items.text: Deployments that start the host themselves use an app.toml (see project scaffolding): Start-NativeHTMLKitHost -Manifest ./app.toml or nativehtmlkit-host run --app app.toml. The backend script then calls Start-NativeHTMLKitScript (which only connects in that case) or Connect-NativeHTMLKit.
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: Single instance
items.text: By default (-Instance single) a second launch of the same script (same AppId) is forwarded to the running instance instead of starting a second app. Use -Instance multiple for tools that may run several times, and set a fixed -AppId such as org.example.Inventory when the script may be moved (the default AppId is derived from the script path).
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: Testing without a desktop
items.text:
NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 makes the launcher start the host with --headless: the whole protocol runs without windows on screen, so scripted checks can create windows, load documents, submit forms, read back text and quit. There is no native input, clipboard or file dialog. All examples in this repository accept -SelfTest and are run this way by tests/Examples.Tests.ps1.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/lifecycle.md · edit the page there.
path: How to structure an app script: start, ready, wait, quit, close

items.title: How to draw live images: charts and previews with RGBA bitmaps
path: How to draw live images: charts and previews with RGBA bitmaps

items.title: How to draw live images: charts and previews with RGBA bitmaps
items.text:
Reference: live bitmaps. Example: 12-live-chart.ps1 (a live memory chart).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

A live bitmap is a pixel buffer you fill in PowerShell and the document shows through <img src="nativehtmlkit-bitmap://ID">. Frames go through shared memory created by the host, so a 360x120 frame (about 170 KB) does not travel through the message channel.
path: How to draw live images: charts and previews with RGBA bitmaps

items.title: Create, draw, present
items.text:
$doc = Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml -Window $window -Html '<img id="chart" src="nativehtmlkit-bitmap://cpu" style="width:360px;height:120px">'
$bitmap = New-NativeHTMLKitLiveBitmap -Document $doc -Id cpu -Width 360 -Height 120
$frame = New-Object byte[] (360 * 120 * 4)      # R, G, B, A per pixel, rows from the top
# ... set pixels ...
$null = Send-NativeHTMLKitLiveBitmap -Bitmap $bitmap -Pixels $frame
  • Pixel format: RGBA8 with straight alpha (not premultiplied). Pixel (x, y) starts at byte (y * Width + x) * 4. Use alpha 255 for opaque pixels.
  • Send-NativeHTMLKitLiveBitmap returns after the host copied the frame, so you can reuse the same byte[] for the next frame.
  • Size the <img> with CSS to the bitmap size (or a multiple) for crisp pixels.
path: How to draw live images: charts and previews with RGBA bitmaps

items.title: Draw fast in PowerShell
items.text:
Per-pixel loops are slow in PowerShell, especially in Windows PowerShell 5.1. Keep frames small and:

  • prepare a background once (fill, grid lines) and start each frame with [Buffer]::BlockCopy($background, 0, $frame, 0, $background.Length);
  • draw only what changes: a line chart is a few pixels per column (vertical spans between consecutive points);
  • pass a real byte[]; an object[] of numbers is converted, which costs extra time.
path: How to draw live images: charts and previews with RGBA bitmaps

items.title: Animate with a timer
items.text:
Present new frames from a periodic tick. A background task that only sleeps is a simple timer whose completion runs on the UI runspace:

function Start-Tick {
    $null = Start-NativeHTMLKitTask -Application $app -ScriptBlock { Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 500 } -OnCompleted {
        Add-Sample; $null = Write-Frame
        Start-Tick
    }
}

The tick stops by itself when the application closes. If a callback may run while a present of the same bitmap is in progress, use Send-NativeHTMLKitLiveBitmap -Try, which returns $null instead of throwing.
path: How to draw live images: charts and previews with RGBA bitmaps

items.title: Lifetime
items.text:
The bitmap belongs to its document. Loading a new document, closing the window or closing the application releases it; Remove-NativeHTMLKitLiveBitmap releases it earlier and is idempotent.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/live-bitmaps.md · edit the page there.
path: How to draw live images: charts and previews with RGBA bitmaps

items.title: How to package and distribute an app
path: How to package and distribute an app

items.title: How to package and distribute an app
items.text:
Reference: lifecycle (Start-NativeHTMLKitScript, Start-NativeHTMLKitHost), tooling. Related: project scaffolding.

A NativeHTMLKit PowerShell app is a folder of scripts and page files plus the NativeHTMLKit module, which bundles the native host for Linux x64 and Windows x64 and verifies its hash on every launch. Users need PowerShell 7.2+ (Linux or Windows) or Windows PowerShell 5.1 (Windows).
path: How to package and distribute an app

items.title: Project layout
items.text:
InventoryTool/
  app.ps1         entry point: Start-NativeHTMLKitScript, windows, handlers
  index.html      the page, loaded with Open-NativeHTMLKitFile (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'index.html')
  style.css       referenced from index.html with a relative URL
  lib/*.ps1       optional helpers, dot-sourced below Start-NativeHTMLKitScript
  app.toml        optional manifest for launchers that start the host themselves

New-NativeHTMLKitProject -Path ./InventoryTool -Name 'Inventory tool' -AppId 'org.example.InventoryTool' creates the first four files. Always locate files from $PSScriptRoot, never from the current directory: users start apps from shortcuts and other folders. Save scripts as ASCII or UTF-8 with BOM so Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads them correctly (details).
path: How to package and distribute an app

items.title: Identity, name and version
items.text:
$app = Start-NativeHTMLKitScript -Name 'Inventory tool' -AppId 'org.example.InventoryTool' -Version '1.0.0' -Icon (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'icon.png')
  • -AppId is how the desktop and the host recognise the app. Keep it stable across versions. With the default -Instance single, starting the app a second time hands over to the running copy; -Instance multiple allows several copies.
  • The per-user folders reported by Invoke-NativeHTMLKitRpc -Application $app -Method 'desktop.paths' (config, data, cache, state) are named after the -AppId. Create the folder before writing to it and write files atomically (write name.tmp, then [IO.File]::Replace), as 04-todo-list.ps1 does.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.
path: How to package and distribute an app

items.title: Option 1: depend on the module from the PowerShell Gallery
items.text:
The simplest distribution is your folder plus a setup line:

Install-Module NativeHTMLKit -RequiredVersion 0.1.2 -Scope CurrentUser
pwsh -NoProfile -File ./InventoryTool/app.ps1            # Windows PowerShell: powershell.exe -NoProfile -File .\InventoryTool\app.ps1

Pin the version you tested. If you publish your app as a PowerShell module itself, declare the dependency in its manifest so Install-Module brings the SDK along:

# InventoryTool.psd1
@{
    ModuleVersion   = '1.0.0'
    RootModule      = 'InventoryTool.psm1'
    RequiredModules = @(@{ ModuleName = 'NativeHTMLKit'; RequiredVersion = '0.1.2' })
}
path: How to package and distribute an app

items.title: Option 2: ship the module next to the app
items.text:
For machines without Gallery access, save the module once and ship it inside your folder:

Save-Module -Name NativeHTMLKit -RequiredVersion 0.1.2 -Path ./InventoryTool/Modules

A tiny launcher puts that folder first on PSModulePath and starts the app. The host and the backend inherit the environment, so the backend run loads the same copy:

# InventoryTool/run.ps1
$env:PSModulePath = (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'Modules') + [IO.Path]::PathSeparator + $env:PSModulePath
& (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'app.ps1') @args

Users start pwsh -NoProfile -File run.ps1. The saved module contains the hosts for both platforms, so the same folder works on Linux and Windows. The release zip NativeHTMLKit-0.1.2-linux-x64+win-x64.zip from the GitHub releases has the same module folder if you prefer to unpack it yourself.
path: How to package and distribute an app

items.title: Starting the app
items.text:
• From a terminal or a script: pwsh -NoProfile -File <folder>/app.ps1 or powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File <folder>\app.ps1. Script arguments after the path reach both runs of the script.
  • From a shortcut: use the same command as the shortcut target (Windows) or the Exec= line of a .desktop file (Linux). PowerShell itself starts in a console or terminal; check on the target desktop how your shortcut behaves before you hand it out.
  • From your own launcher that starts the host directly: write an app.toml (see project scaffolding) and run Start-NativeHTMLKitHost -Manifest <folder>/app.toml. The backend's Start-NativeHTMLKitScript call then only connects. Note that Start-NativeHTMLKitHost always starts a desktop session: unlike Start-NativeHTMLKitScript, it does not switch the host to headless mode when NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 is set (observed with 0.1.2).

Execution policy: pwsh -File and powershell.exe -File honour the machine's execution policy. Signed scripts, -ExecutionPolicy Bypass on the command line, or an organisation policy are the usual answers; choose what your environment allows.
path: How to package and distribute an app

items.title: Before you ship
items.text:
• Give every window a -SelfTest path (or a Pester test) that drives it through the SDK, and run it in CI with NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1: the host runs the whole protocol without a desktop.
  • Test once on each real desktop and PowerShell edition you support: native dialogs, clipboard, focus and window placement depend on the platform.
  • Do not set NATIVEHTMLKIT_HOST_BINARY in production. It replaces the bundled, hash-verified host and exists for SDK development.
  • Keep secrets out of HTML and out of command lines; see security.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/packaging-and-distribution.md · edit the page there.
path: How to package and distribute an app

items.title: How to start a new app project
path: How to start a new app project

items.title: How to start a new app project
items.text: Reference: New-NativeHTMLKitProject. A complete multi-file app: examples/bulk-rename.
path: How to start a new app project

items.title: Generate a project
items.text:
Install-Module NativeHTMLKit -Scope CurrentUser
New-NativeHTMLKitProject -Path ./InventoryTool -Name 'Inventory tool' -AppId 'org.example.InventoryTool'
pwsh -File ./InventoryTool/app.ps1            # or: powershell.exe -NoProfile -File .\InventoryTool\app.ps1

The folder contains:

File Purpose app.ps1 The backend script: Start-NativeHTMLKitScript, window, Open-NativeHTMLKitFile index.html, one click handler, ready, wait, close. Saved as UTF-8 with BOM for Windows PowerShell 5.1. index.html The page: a name field, a Greet button and a result line. style.css Light/dark styles using prefers-color-scheme. app.toml Optional manifest for deployments that start the host themselves.

The generated app runs unchanged; tests/Examples.Tests.ps1 starts one in headless mode.
path: How to start a new app project

items.title: Grow it
items.text:
• Keep markup in index.html and styles in style.css; reference images and fonts with relative URLs, which resolve against the HTML file's folder.
  • Keep logic in functions in app.ps1 (or dot-source helper .ps1 files from $PSScriptRoot below Start-NativeHTMLKitScript). Make the logic that does not touch the UI pure, so it can be tested with Pester without a host, like Get-RenamePlan in bulk-rename/app.ps1.
  • Add a -SelfTest switch that drives the app through the SDK and quits, and run it in CI with NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 (see the examples).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.
path: How to start a new app project

items.title: The manifest (app.toml)
items.text:
[app]
id = "org.example.InventoryTool"
name = "Inventory tool"
version = "1.0.0"

[backend]
program = "pwsh"                 # "powershell.exe" with -WindowsPowerShell
args = ["-NoLogo", "-NoProfile", "-NonInteractive", "-ExecutionPolicy", "Bypass", "-File", "{app_dir}/app.ps1"]
cwd = "{app_dir}"

[host]
startup_timeout_ms = 30000
shutdown_timeout_ms = 5000
max_windows = 8
instance = "single"

Start it with Start-NativeHTMLKitHost -Manifest ./app.toml (waits) or -NoWait (returns the host process). {app_dir} is the manifest's folder. For everyday development you do not need the manifest: Start-NativeHTMLKitScript writes an equivalent one for each run.
path: How to start a new app project

items.title: Identity and instances
items.text: The AppId identifies the app to the desktop and decides single-instance forwarding. Use your own reverse-DNS name and keep it stable across versions. -Instance multiple (or instance = "multiple") allows several copies at once.
path: How to start a new app project

items.title: Distributing
items.text:
Users need the NativeHTMLKit module (which bundles the native host for Linux x64 and Windows x64) and your project folder. Declare the dependency in your own module manifest (RequiredModules = @(@{ ModuleName = 'NativeHTMLKit'; ModuleVersion = '0.1.2' })) or install it in your setup script with Install-Module NativeHTMLKit -Scope CurrentUser.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/project-scaffolding.md · edit the page there.
path: How to start a new app project

items.title: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets
path: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets

items.title: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets
items.text: NativeHTMLKit has no JavaScript engine and no network server, so classic browser attacks such as script injection or cross-site requests do not apply. Markup injection still does: untrusted text inserted as HTML can change your UI, add misleading controls or load local resources. These rules keep an app safe.
path: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets

items.title: 1. Show text as text
items.text:
Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText never parses its input. Use it for anything that did not come from your own source code: user input, file content, log lines, process names, error messages, data from web services.

Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText -Document $doc -Element preview -Text (Get-Content -LiteralPath $path -Raw)
path: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets

items.title: 2. Encode every value you put into HTML
items.text:
When you build HTML (tables, lists), encode each untrusted value with [System.Net.WebUtility]::HtmlEncode(); it is available in both PowerShell editions and encodes <, >, &, " and ', so it is also correct inside double- or single-quoted attribute values.

$row = '<tr data-name="' + [Net.WebUtility]::HtmlEncode($file.Name) + '"><td>' +
       [Net.WebUtility]::HtmlEncode($file.Name) + '</td></tr>'

Never put untrusted values into tag names, attribute names, style attributes, CSS text or URLs without validating them against a strict pattern (for example ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$ for an id, a ^#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$ colour). Generate element ids from your own counters, not from data.
path: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets

items.title: 3. Treat event data as input
items.text: $evt.value, $evt.element and form entries come from the document, which the user controls. Validate them before using them in file paths, command lines or queries. Parse ids you generated with an anchored regular expression ('^todo-(\d+)-delete$') instead of trusting their content.
path: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets

items.title: 4. Files and paths
items.text:
• Use -LiteralPath with paths from dialogs or users, so [ and * are not wildcards.
  • Check that a path chosen in a dialog is what you expect (extension, folder) before writing.
  • Open-NativeHTMLKitExternal refuses executables, scripts and shortcuts, and only accepts http, https, mailto, file and absolute paths; still validate URLs you build from data.
path: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets

items.title: 5. Background tasks get data, not objects
items.text: Start-NativeHTMLKitTask refuses SDK objects in -ArgumentList. Pass the minimum data the worker needs; do not pass credentials unless the work needs them, and prefer PSCredential objects over plain-text passwords.
path: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets

items.title: 6. Secrets and logs
items.text:
• The host's launch token (UI4ME_TOKEN) is removed from the process environment when the backend connects, so programs your app starts do not inherit it. Do not log it.
  • SDK diagnostics and support bundles are redacted (no values, text, paths or tokens). Your own Write-Host output is not: avoid printing passwords, tokens or personal data.
  • The launcher's temporary manifest folder is private to your user (mode 0700 on Linux, per-user %TEMP% on Windows) and removed after the run.
path: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets

items.title: 7. Integrity of the host
items.text:
The module verifies the bundled host binary against the SHA-256 in HOST-MANIFEST.json before running it, and refuses to run a mismatching file. NATIVEHTMLKIT_HOST_BINARY bypasses this check by design: set it only to binaries you trust.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/security.md · edit the page there.
path: Security: untrusted text, HTML, files and secrets

items.title: How to style and lay out the page
path: How to style and lay out the page

items.title: How to style and lay out the page
items.text:
Reference: documents (stylesheets, computed style, environment). What HTML and CSS the host supports, in detail: HTML and CSS support in Core. Examples: 04-todo-list.ps1 (light and dark palette), 09-settings-dialog.ps1 (theme switch, replaceable stylesheet), 15-data-table.ps1 (app shell with a sticky table header), bulk-rename/ (separate index.html and style.css).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

The page is rendered by the NativeHTMLKit Core host with its own native engine, not by a browser. It understands modern HTML and CSS (flexbox, grid, custom properties, media queries, transitions) but runs no JavaScript and loads nothing from the network. Everything interactive is a PowerShell callback.
path: How to style and lay out the page

items.title: Where the CSS lives
items.text:
Approach Use it for <style> inside the HTML here-string Small single-file apps, like most examples. index.html + style.css loaded with Open-NativeHTMLKitFile Larger apps. Relative URLs (style.css, images, fonts) resolve against the HTML file's folder. Add-NativeHTMLKitStylesheet / Set-NativeHTMLKitStylesheet CSS that changes at run time: user font size, themes, generated rules. 
$doc = Open-NativeHTMLKitFile -Window $window -Path (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'index.html')

# A placeholder sheet that the app replaces later.
$userSheet = (Add-NativeHTMLKitStylesheet -Document $doc -Css '').sheet
$null = Set-NativeHTMLKitStylesheet -Document $doc -Sheet $userSheet -Css 'body { font-size: 18px; }'

Use single-quoted here-strings (@' ... '@) for HTML and CSS so PowerShell leaves $ and backticks alone. If you need to insert values, use .Replace('%TOKEN%', $value) or the -f operator on a here-string whose literal braces are doubled.
path: How to style and lay out the page

items.title: An application layout
items.text:
Desktop windows are usually an app shell: fixed toolbars, one scrolling region, maybe a side panel. Flexbox on a full-height body does that:

body { margin:0; height:100vh; display:flex; font:13px sans-serif; }
.main { flex:1; display:flex; flex-direction:column; min-width:0; padding:14px 16px; }
.tools { display:flex; gap:10px; align-items:center; margin-bottom:10px; }
.scroll { flex:1; overflow:auto; }                 /* only this region scrolls */
th { position:sticky; top:0; background:#e9ecf2; } /* the header row stays visible */
aside { width:240px; border-left:1px solid #dde1e8; }

That is the layout of 15-data-table.ps1. Grid works too (grid-template-columns, named areas, gap), as do tables, position: sticky/fixed, multi-column text and container queries. Give windows a minimum size that fits the layout: New-NativeHTMLKitWindow ... -MinWidth 420 -MinHeight 360.
path: How to style and lay out the page

items.title: State as classes
items.text:
Keep presentation in CSS and let PowerShell switch classes:

Set-NativeHTMLKitClass -Document $doc -Element body -Name running            # add
Set-NativeHTMLKitClass -Document $doc -Element body -Name running -Remove    # remove

.running #clock { color: #8ef0b6; }
tr.low td { color: #b03a2e; }
li.done .text { text-decoration: line-through; }

Class and attribute changes for many elements belong in one Invoke-NativeHTMLKitBatch (updating the page). Attribute selectors and ARIA attributes work well together: th[aria-sort=ascending]::after { content: " \25B2"; }.
path: How to style and lay out the page

items.title: Light and dark
items.text:
prefers-color-scheme follows the desktop setting. Define colours once as custom properties and switch the palette in a media query:

:root { --bg:#f6f7fb; --card:#fff; --text:#1d2433; --accent:#3a6ff7; }
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root { --bg:#141923; --card:#1d2433; --text:#e8ecf5; --accent:#7aa2ff; }
}
body { background:var(--bg); color:var(--text); }

To offer a Light / Dark / System choice in the app, override the media query per document:

$null = Set-NativeHTMLKitEnvironment -Document $doc -ColorScheme dark      # light, dark or system
$null = Set-NativeHTMLKitEnvironment -Document $doc -ReducedMotion reduce  # reduce, no-preference or system

system removes the override. prefers-reduced-motion works the same way; honour it in your transitions and animations.
path: How to style and lay out the page

items.title: Images, fonts and icons
items.text:
Resources load only from the document's asset root (the HTML file's folder, or -AssetRoot), from data: URLs (up to 4 MiB) and from in-memory bundles. http: and https: URLs are refused.

# An inline page that references files next to the script:
$doc = Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml -Window $window -Html $page -AssetRoot $PSScriptRoot

# Generated or embedded bytes, without temporary files:
$png = [IO.File]::ReadAllBytes((Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'logo.png'))
$null = Register-NativeHTMLKitResources -Document $doc -Name brand -Entries @{ 'logo.png' = @{ Bytes = $png; Mime = 'image/png' } }
# <img src="nativehtmlkit-res://brand/logo.png" alt="Logo">

PNG, JPEG, GIF (first frame), WebP, BMP and static SVG are supported. @font-face loads TTF, OTF and WOFF/WOFF2 from the same places; the generic families (sans-serif, monospace, system-ui) use the desktop's fonts. For pixels you compute (charts, previews) use a live bitmap.
path: How to style and lay out the page

items.title: What is not there
items.text: Markup with <script>, <iframe>, on... attributes or contenteditable is refused: loading it, or inserting it with Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml, throws NativeHTMLKit.RpcException -32602 (for example INVALID_ARGUMENT: Unsupported active element: script) and the document stays as it was. Date, time and colour inputs are refused too (no native picker); use text inputs with a pattern. <canvas>, <video> and <audio> show empty boxes. Links never navigate; the host sends a link_activated event and your script decides (for example Open-NativeHTMLKitExternal). The Core guide lists the CSS features and selectors that are off in Core 1.0.3.
path: How to style and lay out the page

items.title: When something looks wrong
items.text:
# What did the engine compute?
(Get-NativeHTMLKitComputedStyle -Document $doc -Element title -Properties @('color', 'font-size')).properties.'font-size'.value

# Why does a declaration have no effect?
Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand -Document $doc -Operation explain -Parameters @{ element = 'title'; property = 'top' }
# -> status 'not_applicable', reason 'position is static: offsets only apply to positioned elements'

# What did the engine drop or refuse in this document?
(Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand -Document $doc -Operation get_diagnostics).diagnostics

# CSS you add at run time is checked on the spot:
(Add-NativeHTMLKitStylesheet -Document $doc -Css 'h1 { colr: red }').diagnostics
# -> category 'unknown-property', excerpt 'colr', line 1, column 6

These calls work in headless mode, so a -SelfTest can assert on computed styles. Fonts, colours and the final look still need one check on each real desktop.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/styling-and-layout.md · edit the page there.
path: How to style and lay out the page

items.title: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands
items.text:
Reference: documents, nodes. Examples: 02-counter.ps1, 04-todo-list.ps1, 05-process-viewer.ps1, 06-log-tail.ps1, 15-data-table.ps1 (one batch per render), 16-dom-explorer.ps1 (nodes without ids).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

The document lives in the native host; PowerShell changes it with commands addressed by element id. Each command is one request to the host, so prefer a few large updates over many small ones.
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: Choose the right command
items.text: You want to Use Show a value, message or any untrusted text Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText (never parsed as HTML) Render a list or table from data Build HTML with encoded values, then Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml Append a row or log line Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml -Position beforeend Toggle state styling Set-NativeHTMLKitClass -Name selected [-Remove] Enable/disable, aria-*, value attributes Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentAttribute [-Remove] Change a control's current value Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentValue, Set-NativeHTMLKitChecked, Set-NativeHTMLKitSelectedValues Change several things at once, consistently Invoke-NativeHTMLKitBatch Count matching elements (Find-NativeHTMLKitElement -Selector ...).matched_nodes Work with elements that have no id Get-NativeHTMLKitNodes + Invoke-NativeHTMLKitNodeBatch Anything else in the Core protocol Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand -Operation <op>
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: Render data as HTML safely
items.text:
$rows = New-Object System.Text.StringBuilder
foreach ($svc in Get-Service | Sort-Object DisplayName) {
    $state = 'stopped'; if ($svc.Status -eq 'Running') { $state = 'running' }
    [void]$rows.Append("<tr class=`"$state`"><td>" + [Net.WebUtility]::HtmlEncode($svc.DisplayName) +
        '</td><td>' + [Net.WebUtility]::HtmlEncode([string]$svc.Status) + '</td></tr>')
}
Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml -Document $doc -Element services -Html $rows.ToString()

Encode every value that did not come from your own source code, including file names, process names, log lines and user input. The class names above come from a fixed set, so they need no encoding. See security.
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: Atomic updates with a batch
items.text:
A batch applies all operations or none, so the user never sees a half-updated view:

Invoke-NativeHTMLKitBatch -Document $doc -Operations @(
    @{ op = 'set_text'; element = 'total'; text = '1,204' }
    @{ op = 'remove_class'; element = 'total'; name = 'loading' }
    @{ op = 'insert_html'; element = 'history'; position = 'afterbegin'; html = '<li>' + [Net.WebUtility]::HtmlEncode($entry) + '</li>' }
    @{ op = 'trim_children'; element = 'history'; keep = 20; from = 'end' }
)

trim_children keeps a bounded list: from = 'start' (default) removes the oldest children when you append at the end, from = 'end' removes the last ones when you insert at the beginning.
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: Long or growing views
items.text:
• Append with -Position beforeend and cap the length with trim_children, as 06-log-tail.ps1 does for a log of 500 lines.
  • Keep a scroll container at its end while lines arrive: Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand -Document $doc -Operation set_scroll_follow -Parameters @{ element = 'log'; follow = $true }.
  • Re-render big tables in one Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml call rather than one command per row, and keep a frame under 2 MiB of JSON (limit 200 rows or page through data).
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: Stylesheets at run time
items.text:
Load your CSS with the document (<style> or <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">). For values chosen at run time, add one stylesheet and replace its text:

$sheet = (Add-NativeHTMLKitStylesheet -Document $doc -Css '').sheet
$null = Set-NativeHTMLKitStylesheet -Document $doc -Sheet $sheet -Css ":root { --accent: $accent; }"

$accent must be a value you validated (for example ^#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$): CSS text is code.
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: Elements without ids: nodes
items.text:
Generated markup often has no ids. Node references reach those elements:

$sample = Get-NativeHTMLKitNode -Document $doc -Element sample          # id -> node
$children = (Get-NativeHTMLKitNodeChildren -Node $sample -Limit 256).children
foreach ($child in $children) {
    $node = Get-NativeHTMLKitNode -Document $doc -Reference $child.node   # wrap a reference string
    $info = Get-NativeHTMLKitNodeInfo -Node $node                         # type, name, attributes, text, previous, next
    if ($info.type -eq 'element') { Invoke-NativeHTMLKitNodeOperation -Node $node -Operation add_class -Parameters @{ name = 'seen' } }
}
$items = (Get-NativeHTMLKitNodes -Document $doc -Selector '#sample li').nodes   # CSS query: node + id (or $null)

Host replies are objects: an element's attributes are properties ($info.attributes.PSObject.Properties), and a text node reports its text, including the whitespace between tags. A reference belongs to one document generation; after the element is removed or replaced (for example by Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml on its parent), using it throws. 16-dom-explorer.ps1 walks, moves (move_element with target_node), edits and deletes nodes this way.
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: Read state back
items.text: Get-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText, Get-NativeHTMLKitValue, Get-NativeHTMLKitChecked, Get-NativeHTMLKitComputedStyle and commands such as get_attribute and get_html read the live document. They are also how automated checks verify a UI without a screen (the examples' -SelfTest blocks).
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: Replacing the whole document
items.text:
Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml/Open-NativeHTMLKitFile on the same window replaces the document atomically. The old $doc and all its subscriptions, nodes and bitmaps become stale: register handlers again on the new document object.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/updating-the-page.md · edit the page there.
path: How to update the document: text, HTML, classes, batches and commands

items.title: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7: writing scripts that run on both
path: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7: writing scripts that run on both

items.title: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7: writing scripts that run on both
items.text: The module supports PowerShell 7.2+ on Linux x64 and Windows x64, and Windows PowerShell 5.1 on Windows (manifest: PowerShellVersion = '5.1', CompatiblePSEditions = Desktop, Core, .NET Framework 4.7.2). The cmdlets, parameters and results are the same on both editions. All examples in this repository are checked on both by tests/Examples.Tests.ps1.
path: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7: writing scripts that run on both

items.title: Which edition runs your backend
items.text: Start-NativeHTMLKitScript relaunches the script with the same edition that started it: powershell.exe -File app.ps1 gives a Windows PowerShell 5.1 backend, pwsh -File app.ps1 a PowerShell 7 backend. A manifest names its program explicitly (pwsh or powershell.exe).
path: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7: writing scripts that run on both

items.title: Language features to avoid for 5.1
items.text:
PowerShell 7 only Write instead $a ? $b : $c if ($a) { $b } else { $c } $x ?? 'default', $x ??= 1 if ($null -eq $x) { 'default' } else { $x } cmd1 && cmd2, cmd1 \|\| cmd2 separate statements, if ($?) { ... } $obj?.Prop, $arr?[0] explicit $null checks $IsWindows, $IsLinux [Environment]::OSVersion.Platform -eq [PlatformID]::Win32NT ForEach-Object -Parallel Start-NativeHTMLKitTask for background work ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable read PSCustomObject properties, or copy into a hashtable Join-Path a b c (several children) Join-Path (Join-Path a b) c Get-Content -Raw default UTF-8 5.1 defaults to the ANSI code page for BOM-less files; pass -Encoding UTF8

The example harness rejects the ternary, null-coalescing, pipeline-chain and null-conditional operators and the $Is* variables by parsing every example.
path: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7: writing scripts that run on both

items.title: File encoding
items.text: Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads a .ps1 without a byte-order mark in the system ANSI code page. Non-ASCII characters in string literals ('Prüfung', '–') then turn into other characters. Save scripts that contain non-ASCII text as UTF-8 with BOM (New-NativeHTMLKitProject does), or keep them ASCII and put text in index.html (which is read as UTF-8). When writing files yourself on 5.1, pass an explicit encoding: [IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, $text, (New-Object Text.UTF8Encoding($false))).
path: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7: writing scripts that run on both

items.title: Console output
items.text: In a backend started by Start-NativeHTMLKitScript on Windows, the SDK sets [Console]::OutputEncoding to UTF-8, so [Console]::Out.WriteLine() relays Unicode exactly. Windows PowerShell's own formatting (Write-Output of objects) may still use a legacy code page; prefer showing text in the window.
path: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7: writing scripts that run on both

items.title: Other differences you may meet
items.text:
• Execution policy. The relaunch uses -ExecutionPolicy Bypass for the backend process only. The first run (powershell.exe -File app.ps1) still follows your machine's policy; downloaded scripts may need Unblock-File.
  • Performance. Windows PowerShell 5.1 is slower at loops and runspace creation. Keep live bitmap frames small and polling periods at a few hundred milliseconds or more.
  • Linux. Only PowerShell 7 exists; the bundled host is runtimes/linux-x64/nativehtmlkit-host and needs a graphical session (KDE Plasma on Wayland is the qualified desktop).
  • Paths. Use Join-Path and [IO.Path] instead of hard-coded \ or /; file names are case-sensitive on Linux.

Source: nativehtmlkit-powershell/docs/guides/windows-powershell-51.md · edit the page there.
path: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7: writing scripts that run on both

items.title: How to use several windows
items.text:
Reference: windows. Example: 08-multi-window.ps1 (a window manager: note windows listed, renamed, resized and closed from a main window).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Each window has its own document
items.text:
$main = New-NativeHTMLKitWindow -Application $app -Title 'Inventory'
$mainDoc = Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml -Window $main -Html $mainHtml

$details = New-NativeHTMLKitWindow -Application $app -Title 'Details' -Width 480 -Height 360
$detailsDoc = Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml -Window $details -Html $detailsHtml

Event subscriptions, element ids and stylesheets are per document: the same id in two windows is two different elements. The host limits the number of windows to Start-NativeHTMLKitScript -MaxWindows (default 16, at most 64).

items.title: Keep per-window state in a table
items.text:
Create windows from a function and keep their state in a hashtable keyed by $window.Id. Because the callbacks are created inside the function, capture its locals with .GetNewClosure() and share mutable state through the captured hashtable ($script: does not work inside a closure; see closures and scope):

$state = @{ Notes = @{} }
function New-NoteWindow($State) {
    $window = New-NativeHTMLKitWindow -Application $app -Title 'Note'
    $document = Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml -Window $window -Html $noteHtml
    $note = @{ Window = $window; Document = $document; Dirty = $false }
    $State.Notes[$window.Id] = $note
    $null = Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Document $document -Type input -Callback { $note.Dirty = $true }.GetNewClosure()
    Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeClose -Window $window -Callback { -not $note.Dirty }.GetNewClosure()
    return $note
}

items.title: Closing windows
items.text:
• Close-NativeHTMLKitWindow asks the window's close policy (after Set-NativeHTMLKitReady), the same path as the title-bar close button. The policy's last output decides.
  • The handle's Closed property becomes $true once the host confirms; listen to the window.event notification with type = 'closed' to update your own lists, because the user can close secondary windows at any time:
Register-NativeHTMLKitNotification -Application $app -Method 'window.event' -Callback {
    param($params)
    if ($params.type -eq 'closed' -and $state.Notes.ContainsKey($params.window_id)) {
        $state.Notes.Remove($params.window_id)
        Update-WindowTable $state
    }
}
  • When the user closes the last window, the host shuts the app down. To make one window the "main" window whose close quits the app even while other windows are open, request a quit when its closed event arrives (the quit closes every remaining window). There is one callback per notification method, so this goes into the same window.event callback:
Register-NativeHTMLKitNotification -Application $app -Method 'window.event' -Callback {
    param($params)
    if ($params.type -eq 'closed' -and $params.window_id -eq $main.Id) {
        $null = Request-NativeHTMLKitQuit -Application $app
        return
    }
    if ($params.type -eq 'closed' -and $state.Notes.ContainsKey($params.window_id)) {
        $state.Notes.Remove($params.window_id)
        Update-WindowTable $state
    }
}

items.title: Listing windows
items.text:
Get-NativeHTMLKitWindowList returns one array object: assign it first.

$windows = Get-NativeHTMLKitWindowList -Application $app
"$($windows.Count) window(s): " + (($windows | ForEach-Object { $_.title }) -join ', ')

items.title: Window state
items.text:
Set-NativeHTMLKitWindow changes title, size, constraints, minimized/maximized/fullscreen state and focus; Get-NativeHTMLKitWindow reports what was requested and what the desktop observed. Positioning with -X/-Y works only where the platform allows it (window_positioning in Get-NativeHTMLKitCapabilities; not on Wayland). Request-NativeHTMLKitAttention flags a window that needs the user (for example when a background job finished).
