items.title: Clipboard and desktop services
items.text: All of these talk to the native desktop. They raise RpcError -32001 in headless mode and where the platform lacks the service, so handle that error.

items.title: Clipboard (text)
items.text:
from nativehtmlkit import RpcError

def copy_result(_event):
    try:
        app.set_clipboard_text(document.get_value("output"))     # at most 1 MiB
        document.set_text("status", "Copied")
    except RpcError as error:
        document.set_text("status", "Clipboard unavailable" if error.code == -32001 else f"Failed ({error.code})")

def paste(_event):
    try:
        document.set_value("input", app.clipboard_text())
    except RpcError:
        document.set_text("status", "Clipboard unavailable")

Inside text controls the native editor handles Ctrl+C/Ctrl+V itself. To trigger it from a button, use document.edit("copy", "editor") / edit("paste", "editor"); the transfer completes asynchronously and accepted does not guarantee that the OS accepted it.

items.title: Open links and files
items.text:
Links in a document never navigate. Activating one sends link_activated:

def on_link(event):
    url = event.get("url") or ""
    if url.startswith("https://"):
        app.open_external(url, window=window)      # default browser

document.on("link_activated", on_link)

open_external(target) accepts http, https, mailto and file URIs or an absolute path and opens it with the default application; other schemes are refused (-32003), as are executable file types on Windows. reveal_file(path) shows a file in the file manager. Both return {"accepted", "cancelled", "parent_forwarded", "presented"}; accepted means the desktop took the request, not that an application window appeared.

items.title: Follow the desktop theme
items.text:
prefs = app.desktop_preferences()
# {"color_scheme": "dark" | "light" | None, "reduced_motion": ..., "high_contrast": ..., "available": bool, "source": ...}
app.on_desktop_preferences(lambda prefs: document.set_text("scheme", prefs["color_scheme"] or "unknown"))

You rarely need this for styling: CSS @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) and (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) follow the desktop automatically. Override per document with document.set_environment(color_scheme="dark") and return to the desktop value with set_environment(color_scheme="system").

items.title: Per-application directories
items.text:
paths = app.rpc.call("desktop.paths")      # {"config", "data", "cache", "state", "runtime"}
store = Path(paths["data"]) / "todos.json"
store.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

The directories are derived from the application id (pass a stable app_id to Application.start), using the XDG directories on Linux and AppData on Windows. They are not created automatically.

items.title: Attention
items.text: window.request_attention("informational") (or "critical") asks the window manager to flag the window, e.g. when a long job finished in the background. Unsupported in headless mode and limited on Wayland.

items.title: Check before offering a feature
items.text:
features = app.capabilities()["features"]
if features["clipboard_text"]["available"] is False:
    document.set_attribute("copy", "disabled", "")

available is None when the host has not observed the service yet; treat that as "try it".

Example: text_toolbox.py.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/clipboard-and-desktop.md · edit the page there.

items.title: First checks
items.text:
uv run nativehtmlkit-python version      # SDK, protocol and host provenance (exit 1 if the host is missing/mismatched)
uv run nativehtmlkit-python doctor       # the host's own environment report

items.title: Turn on tracing
items.text:
NATIVEHTMLKIT_DIAGNOSTICS=trace uv run app.py
# or: uv run nativehtmlkit-python --diagnostics trace run app:setup

Records go to ~/.local/state/nativehtmlkit/diagnostics/ (Linux) or %LOCALAPPDATA%\NativeHTMLKit\diagnostics\ (Windows), or NATIVEHTMLKIT_DIAGNOSTICS_DIR. They contain names, ids, counts and timings, never your data. Export one session as a ZIP for a bug report with uv run nativehtmlkit-python support bundle.zip. Details: diagnostics reference.

items.title: Symptoms
items.text:
"My handler never runs." Look for document.dispatch records with your event_type: matched: 0 means the event arrived but no subscription matched. Usual causes: - element= names an element that is not the target or an identified ancestor of it. Print event["element"] and event["path"] from a document-wide handler. - The event does not bubble (invalid, focus, blur, toggle, close, mouseenter): subscribe on the target or without element. - You subscribed on an old document. load_html/load_file create a new window.document. - You expected an event from a programmatic change: set_value and friends fire no events.

StaleDocumentError. The window closed or the document was replaced. Use window.document (not a saved reference), check window.closed, and catch NativeHTMLKitError in background threads.

RpcError -32602 "Unknown element ID". The id is not in the current document (typo, element removed by a re-render, or the action runs against the wrong window).

RpcError -32001. Not available in this session: headless mode (NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1), no desktop service (e.g. no file-dialog portal), or platform policy (Wayland placement/focus). See app.capabilities()["features"].

RpcError -32005. A limit: window count, 1 MiB inline HTML, bitmap budget, one native dialog per window, too many pending requests.

The window freezes / events arrive late. A callback is busy (slow work, wait=True dialog). Look at callback.completed duration_ms in a trace. Move work to a thread or use wait=False. Dropped events show up as rpc.notification_dropped and in app.rpc.dropped_notifications.

My print() output is missing. Backend output is relayed by the launcher on every diagnostics level. When you started the host yourself (nativehtmlkit-python-host run --app), look at the host's standard error.

The application exits with status 1 right after start. Read the relayed traceback. Typical: an exception in main()/setup(), a window closed before app.ready, start-up took longer than startup_timeout_ms, or app.close() was called.

StartupError / HostVerificationError. No usable host: use a platform wheel (Linux x64 glibc 2.39+, Windows x64), not the source distribution; reinstall if the bundled host fails its SHA-256 check. NATIVEHTMLKIT_HOST_BINARY overrides the host for development.

CSS does not apply. document.diagnostics() lists unsupported CSS and pending resources; document.computed_style([...], "id") shows the effective values and document.command("explain", element="id", property="color") explains one.

items.title: An About / Support window
items.text:
diagnostics.py puts the useful facts in one window: platform, renderer and headless state from app.capabilities(), which native services the host offers and whether it has observed them (see below), the desktop preferences, loss counters from app.host_diagnostics() and the SDK recorder, and a Save support bundle button:

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

from nativehtmlkit import diagnostics, export_support_bundle

caps = app.capabilities()
offered = caps["file_dialogs"]                     # top-level flag: the API is enabled in this session
observed = caps["features"]["file_dialogs"]["available"]   # True/False once observed, None before
host = app.host_diagnostics()                      # dropped_notifications, pending_jobs, ...
failures = sum(r["event"] == "callback.failed" for r in diagnostics.recorder().history())
path = export_support_bundle(folder / "support.zip", overwrite=True)   # manifest.json + timeline.jsonl

Treat None as "not observed", never as "unavailable": on a native desktop, Core 1.0.3 reports available: None for these services (availability is established by the native request itself) while the top-level flag is True; headless it reports False for both. The example's feature_state() turns the pair into one of "available", "enabled (not observed)", "unavailable" or "not available". The top-level flags are clipboard_text, file_dialogs, external_open, drag_drop, ime and accessibility; the matching feature entries have the same names except drag_drop, which is incoming_drop.

The bundle is written locally and contains no document text, form values or paths.

items.title: Testing without a desktop
items.text:
NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 runs the real host headless. Everything except native services works, and you can drive forms with request_submit and read state back with get_text, query_nodes, computed_style, validity and so on. This repository's tests/integration/example_checks.py tests every example that way.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/diagnostics-and-troubleshooting.md · edit the page there.

items.title: HTML dialogs and popovers
items.text: These are in-document elements rendered by the host, not native OS dialogs (for those see file dialogs).

items.title: A modal <dialog>
items.text:
<dialog id="confirm">
  <p>Delete this item?</p>
  <button id="confirm-yes">Delete</button> <button id="confirm-no">Cancel</button>
</dialog>

def ask(_event):
    document.show_dialog("confirm")            # modal=True by default

def answered(event):
    if event["element"] == "confirm-yes":
        delete_selected()
    document.close_dialog("confirm", "yes" if event["element"] == "confirm-yes" else "no")

document.on("click", ask, element="delete")
document.on("click", answered, element="confirm")

close_dialog(id, return_value) closes it and fires close with event["return_value"]. document.command("get_dialog", element="confirm") returns {"open", "modal", "return_value"}. Pressing Escape on a modal dialog is a native close request: the host fires cancel and close. As in HTML, that does not reset the return value, so track the outcome of the current opening in your own state when it matters. cancel is cancelable: document.prevent_default("confirm", "cancel") keeps the dialog open on Escape.

items.title: A form inside a dialog
items.text:
Put a <form> in the dialog and handle its submit; close the dialog from the handler. This gives you validation and Enter-to-submit for free:

def on_save(_event):
    entries = {e["name"]: e.get("value", "") for e in document.form_data("settings-form")["entries"]}
    apply(entries)
    document.close_dialog("settings", "saved")

document.on("submit", on_save, element="settings-form")
document.on("close", lambda e: document.set_text("status", "Dialog closed"), element="settings")

Fill the form before show_dialog with set_value, set_checked and set_selected_values, and move focus with document.focus(...). Native validation (required, min, max) runs before submit, so an out-of-range value keeps the dialog open.

Report the outcome from the button and submit handlers rather than from close: after Escape the dialog still carries the return value of its previous closing. settings_dialog.py does this: Save writes the JSON file, applies the settings and calls close_dialog("settings", "saved"); Cancel calls close_dialog("settings", "cancelled").

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Popovers
items.text:
<button id="help-button">?</button>
<div id="help" popover>Shortcuts: Ctrl+S saves, Escape cancels.</div>

document.on("click", lambda e: document.toggle_popover("help"), element="help-button")

show_popover, hide_popover and toggle_popover (returns the new open state) work on elements with the popover attribute. document.command("get_popover", element="help") returns {"open", "kind"}. Popovers and dialogs fire beforetoggle and toggle with old_state / new_state; these do not bubble, so subscribe on the element itself.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/dialogs-and-popovers.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Subscribe to an event
items.text:
def on_save(event: dict) -> None:
    document.set_text("status", "Saved")

unsubscribe = document.on("click", on_save, element="save")
# later: unsubscribe()

document.on(type, callback, element=None) calls callback(event) for each event of that type. event is a dict; the event reference lists every member and type.

items.title: Delegate: one handler for many elements
items.text:
element= matches the target and everything inside it. The event's element member names the nearest element with an id, and path lists every identified ancestor. Render ids that encode what you need and parse them in one handler:

# <ul id="todos"> <li id="todo-7"> ... <button id="todo-7-delete">Delete</button> </li> </ul>
def on_list_click(event):
    kind, number, action = (event["element"].split("-") + ["", "", ""])[:3]
    if kind == "todo" and action == "delete":
        delete_todo(int(number))

document.on("click", on_list_click, element="todos")

A click on a cell without an id reports its nearest identified ancestor, e.g. the <tr id="row-…">. Delegated handlers survive replace_html of the list's children, so re-rendering never needs re-subscribing. (todo.py, data_table.py)

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Non-bubbling events (focus, blur, invalid, toggle, close, mouseenter, ...) have a path with only their target: subscribe on the target itself or without element.

items.title: Typing and keys
items.text:
• input fires for each edit and carries the control's current value: document.on("input", lambda e: search(e["value"]), element="search").
  • change fires when a checkbox, radio or select changes (checked / value in the event) and when a text field is committed.
  • keydown/keyup carry key ("a", "Enter", "Escape", "ArrowDown"…), code and the shift/ctrl/alt/meta flags.
  • Enter in a text field submits its form (HTML implicit submission), so a submit handler covers both the button and the keyboard.
def on_key(event):
    if event["key"] == "Escape":
        cancel_edit()
    elif event["key"] == "s" and event["ctrl"]:
        save()
document.on("keydown", on_key)

Shortcut tables, prevent_default for keys, focus and the text selection are covered in keyboard and focus.

items.title: See which events arrive
items.text:
When you are unsure which element, path or value an interaction produces, log the events. This complete program delegates five event types from one container and keeps the newest 50 lines:

import html
import time

from nativehtmlkit import Application

PAGE = """<!doctype html><html><head><meta charset="utf-8"><style>
  body { font: 14px sans-serif; margin: 16px; } ol { font: 12px monospace; }
</style></head><body>
  <section id="controls">
    <button id="hello">Click me</button>
    <input id="name" placeholder="Type here">
    <select id="color"><option>red</option><option>green</option></select>
    <label><input id="agree" type="checkbox"> Checkbox</label>
  </section>
  <ol id="log"></ol>
</body></html>"""
FIELDS = ("element", "path", "value", "checked", "key", "related_element")


def main() -> None:
    with Application.start(name="Event inspector") as app:
        document = app.open_html(PAGE, title="Event inspector", width=760, height=520).document
        log = document.node("log")

        def record(event: dict) -> None:
            details = ", ".join(f"{name}={event[name]!r}" for name in FIELDS if event.get(name) not in (None, "", []))
            line = f"{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')} {event['type']}: {details}"
            document.insert_html("log", f"<li>{html.escape(line)}</li>", position="afterbegin")
            log.trim_children(50, from_start=False)      # keep the newest 50 (the first children)

        # focus/blur do not bubble; their bubbling twins focusin/focusout work with delegation.
        for kind in ("click", "input", "change", "focusin", "focusout"):
            document.on(kind, record, element="controls")
        app.run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items.title: Stop a native default action
items.text:
Callbacks run after the host handled the event, so returning a value cannot cancel anything. Register a rule up front instead:

document.prevent_default("editor", "keydown", key="Tab")    # Tab stays in the editor
document.prevent_default("search-form", "submit")           # handled only in Python

Activating a link never navigates: you receive link_activated with href and the resolved url, and decide yourself (for example app.open_external(url)).

items.title: Which thread runs my callback?
items.text:
Callback Thread document.on, app.on_window_event, app.on_desktop_preferences one application event thread, strictly in event order window.on_before_close, app.on_before_quit an SDK worker thread, so they are answered even while an event callback is busy done-callbacks of wait=False dialogs and rpc.call_async a fresh completion thread per result app.on_shutdown the thread that called app.run() asyncio callbacks (adapter.on_document_event) your event loop

Consequences:

  • Callbacks may call any SDK method (they never run on the transport's reader thread).
  • One slow callback delays every later event. Keep callbacks short; move slow work to a thread or an asyncio task.
  • The SDK queues at most 128 pending notifications. If callbacks fall that far behind, further events are dropped (app.rpc.dropped_notifications, diagnostics record rpc.notification_dropped).
  • An exception in a callback prints its traceback to standard error; other callbacks still run and the application keeps going.

items.title: Programmatic changes do not fire events
items.text: set_value, set_checked and other mutations do not emit input/change. If a computed field depends on an input you set from Python, call the update function yourself. request_submit, reset_form, show_dialog/close_dialog and the popover methods do fire their events, which makes them useful in tests.

items.title: Window events
items.text:
def on_window(params):
    if params["type"] == "resized":
        print("now", params["data"]["physical_width"], "px wide")
app.on_window_event(on_window)

Types: close_requested, closed, resized, scale_changed, focused, key. See on_window_event.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/events-and-callbacks.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Native file dialogs
items.text: Window.open_files, save_file and choose_folder show the platform's own dialog, parented to the window (on Linux through the desktop portal).

items.title: Non-blocking (recommended inside callbacks)
items.text:
from nativehtmlkit import RpcError

FILTERS = [{"name": "Text files", "extensions": ["txt", "md", "csv"]}]   # no dots

def open_clicked(_event):
    future = window.open_files(title="Open a text file", filters=FILTERS, wait=False)
    future.add_done_callback(opened)

def opened(future):
    try:
        result = future.result()           # {"cancelled": bool, "paths": [...]}
    except RpcError as error:
        status(f"No file dialog here (code {error.code})")
        return
    if result["cancelled"]:
        status("Cancelled")
        return
    load(Path(result["paths"][0]))

document.on("click", open_clicked, element="open")

With wait=False the event callback returns at once, so other events keep flowing while the dialog is open. The done-callback runs on an SDK completion thread and may call any SDK method. future.cancel() asks the host to close the dialog.

items.title: Blocking
items.text:
result = window.save_file(title="Export", file_name="report.csv", filters=[{"name": "CSV", "extensions": ["csv"]}])
if not result["cancelled"]:
    Path(result["paths"][0]).write_text(csv_text, encoding="utf-8")

wait=True (the default) has no timeout. Inside an event callback it holds up all later document and window events until the user answers (close/quit decisions are still handled). That is fine for scripts, less so for interactive windows.

items.title: Options and results
items.text:
Method Options paths open_files multiple=False, title, directory, filters one or more paths save_file file_name, title, directory, filters one path (the file is not created for you) choose_folder title, directory one directory

paths is empty and cancelled is True when the user cancelled.

items.title: When dialogs are unavailable
items.text:
Headless runs (NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1) and sessions without a dialog service raise RpcError -32001; a second dialog on the same window raises -32005. Check app.capabilities()["file_dialogs"] up front (the top-level flag: does the host offer dialogs in this session?) or handle the error as above. capabilities()["features"]["file_dialogs"]["available"] is None ("not observed") on a native desktop with Core 1.0.3, so do not treat None as "no dialogs". Either way, and keep a fallback (a path input field) where it matters. (checksum.py combines both.)

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Reading the chosen file
items.text:
Paths are plain strings: use pathlib.Path. Check the size before reading, decode explicitly and show content with set_value/set_text (never as markup). The file_viewer.py example does this, lists a chosen folder and saves with "Save As…".

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

<input type="file"> in a form is an alternative: the host shows the picker on click and document.files("upload") or form_data return the chosen paths.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/file-dialogs.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Forms and validation
items.text: The host implements HTML forms natively: controls, constraint validation, implicit submission (Enter), reset, <select multiple>, checkbox groups and file inputs. Python listens for submit and reads the values.

items.title: Handle a submission
items.text:
def on_submit(event):
    entries = document.form_data("contact")["entries"]
    values = {}
    for entry in entries:                        # in document order
        values.setdefault(entry["name"], []).append(entry.get("value", ""))
    save_contact(name=values["name"][0], topics=values.get("topic", []))
    document.reset_form("contact")

document.on("submit", on_submit, element="contact")
  • form_data(form, submitter=None) returns ordered entries {"kind": "text", "name", "value"}; file inputs give {"kind": "file", "name", "filename", "path"}. Repeated names appear once per value; unchecked checkboxes are absent.
  • event["submitter"] is the id of the button that submitted (use several submit buttons for "Save" / "Save as draft").
  • There is no navigation: the form stays as it is until you change or reset it.

items.title: Built-in validation
items.text:
Use HTML attributes: required, minlength/maxlength, min/max/step, pattern, type="email"/"number"/"url". On submit the host validates first. If anything is invalid it fires one invalid event per failing control and no submit.

errors = []
def on_invalid(event):
    errors.append(f'{event["element"]}: {event["validity"]["message"]}')
document.on("invalid", on_invalid)     # "invalid" does not bubble: subscribe document-wide

Inspect a control any time:

document.validity("email")
# {"valid": False, "will_validate": True, "message": "Please enter an email address.",
#  "flags": {"typeMismatch": True, "valueMissing": False, ...}}
document.check_validity("signup")       # {"valid": False, "count": 2, "invalid": ["name", "email"]}

items.title: Custom rules
items.text:
set_custom_validity(element, message) marks a control invalid with your message until you clear it with "". Re-check on input, and again in the submit handler, because events reach Python after native dispatch (a quick user can submit before the last input was handled):

def check_passwords(_event=None):
    same = document.get_value("password") == document.get_value("confirm")
    document.set_custom_validity("confirm", "" if same else "The passwords do not match.")

document.on("input", check_passwords, element="password")
document.on("input", check_passwords, element="confirm")

items.title: Submit, reset and fill from Python
items.text:
document.request_submit("signup", submitter="create")   # {"submitted": bool, "default_prevented": bool}
document.reset_form("signup")                           # back to the HTML defaults; fires "reset"
document.set_value("name", "Ada")                       # no input/change events
document.set_selected_values("country", ["fr"])
document.set_checked("terms", True)
document.options("country")     # [{"value", "label", "selected", "disabled"}, ...]

request_submit runs validation exactly like a click, which makes forms easy to test headless (NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1). See tests/integration/example_checks.py.

items.title: Show results safely
items.text:
Values typed by the user are untrusted. Put them into the page with set_text/set_value, or html.escape() them before replace_html/insert_html (see security).

Example: signup_form.py (required fields, email, number range, select, checkbox group, password confirmation, error summary, welcome message).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/forms-and-validation.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Keyboard and focus
items.text:
How to add keyboard shortcuts, keep keys such as Tab inside an editor, move focus and work with the text selection of a control, using the NativeHTMLKit Python SDK 0.1.2. The complete application is keyboard_shortcuts.py, a snippet editor with Tab indentation, Ctrl+S, Ctrl+L, Ctrl+Shift+U and an F1 help popover.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Read keys
items.text:
keydown and keyup events carry the logical key ("a", "A", "Enter", "Escape", "Tab", "ArrowDown", "F1"...), the physical code ("KeyA"), repeat and the modifier flags ctrl, shift, alt and meta (see the event reference).

def on_key(event: dict) -> None:
    if event["key"] == "Escape":
        cancel_edit()

document.on("keydown", on_key)                    # every key in the document
document.on("keydown", on_key, element="todos")   # only while focus is inside #todos

Keyboard events bubble, so element= matches keys pressed while focus is on that element or on anything inside it.

items.title: A shortcut table
items.text:
Turn each event into a normalised chord string and look it up in a dictionary. This keeps every shortcut in one place and makes the actions easy to call from tests:

def chord(event: dict) -> str:
    """{'key': 'U', 'ctrl': True, 'shift': True} -> 'ctrl+shift+u'."""
    parts = [name for name in ("ctrl", "alt", "shift", "meta") if event.get(name)]
    return "+".join(parts + [str(event.get("key", "")).lower()])

shortcuts = {
    "ctrl+s": save,
    "ctrl+l": insert_timestamp,
    "ctrl+shift+u": upper_case_selection,
    "f1": lambda: document.toggle_popover("help"),
    "escape": lambda: document.hide_popover("help"),
}

def on_key(event: dict) -> None:
    action = shortcuts.get(chord(event))
    if action:
        action()

document.on("keydown", on_key)

key reports the character the key produced, so with Shift held a letter arrives in upper case; lower-casing it in chord makes "ctrl+shift+u" match either way.

items.title: Stop the default action of a key
items.text:
Callbacks run after the host has handled the key, so a callback cannot stop Tab from moving focus or Enter from submitting a form. Register a rule up front with prevent_default; the host then cancels the default action before it happens and your callback still receives the event:

# Tab (without Shift) in the editor no longer moves focus; Shift+Tab still does.
document.prevent_default("editor", "keydown", key="Tab", shift=False)

def on_key(event):
    if chord(event) == "tab":
        document.replace_control_range("editor", "    ", selection_mode="end")   # indent
document.on("keydown", on_key, element="editor")

Rules can be narrowed with key=, shift=, ctrl=, alt= and meta=, and removed again with prevent=False. Matching events report default_prevented: True. Other preventable events include submit, paste, contextmenu and wheel.

Enter in a single-line field submits its form (HTML implicit submission). Usually that is what you want: handle submit and both the button and the keyboard are covered.

items.title: Move focus
items.text:
document.focus("edit-title")              # an id or a Node
document.blur()                           # whatever has focus
info = document.focused_element()         # {"element": "edit-title", "node": "..."} or None

Use focus() after you render something the user should type into next, for example an inline edit field (see todo.py). The HTML autofocus attribute focuses a control when the page loads.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

focus() from Python fires the same focus/blur/focusin/focusout events as a click or Tab. focus and blur do not bubble: subscribe on the element itself, or without element and filter on event["element"]. focusin/focusout bubble, so a handler on a form sees focus moving between its fields; all four report the element on the other side of the move in related_element.

document.on("focusin", lambda e: document.add_class(e["element"], "active"), element="form")
document.on("focusout", lambda e: document.remove_class(e["element"], "active"), element="form")

items.title: Work with the selection of a text field
items.text:
control_selection(element) returns {"start", "end", "direction", "length", "node"} for an <input> or <textarea>. Offsets are UTF-16 code units, not Python string indices: an emoji counts as two. Convert through UTF-16 when you slice the value:

selection = document.control_selection("editor")
start, end = selection["start"], selection["end"]
units = document.get_value("editor").encode("utf-16-le")
selected = units[start * 2:end * 2].decode("utf-16-le")
document.replace_control_range("editor", selected.upper(), selection_mode="end")
  • set_control_selection(element, start, end, direction="none") selects a range (or places the caret when start == end).
  • replace_control_range(element, text, start=None, end=None, selection_mode="preserve") replaces the selection (or the given range) and can place the caret after the new text with selection_mode="end". It goes through the editor, so the user can undo it.
  • edit("undo" | "redo" | "cut" | "copy" | "paste" | "select_all" | "delete", element) runs a native editing command.

items.title: Test keyboard logic without a keyboard
items.text:
Headless mode has no synthetic key presses. Keep the logic in plain methods and feed them event dictionaries of the same shape, as the repository's checks do for the snippet editor:

editor.on_key({"type": "keydown", "key": "U", "ctrl": True, "shift": True, "alt": False, "meta": False})
assert document.get_value("editor") == "A    b"

Try the real keys once on each desktop you support: keyboard layouts, input methods and window managers can reserve some combinations.

items.title: Window-level keys
items.text:
app.on_window_event(callback) also receives window key events with key, state ("pressed"/"released"), repeat and physical_key (see on_window_event). For shortcuts inside a page, the document keydown handler above is simpler: it carries the modifier flags and respects prevent_default rules.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/keyboard-and-focus.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Three ways to start
items.text: Entry point Use it when Your code Application.start() in a script Normal applications: uv run app.py, uv run -m pkg.app with Application.start(...) as app: ...; app.run() uv run -m nativehtmlkit run module:func Module-level code must run once; quick experiments def func(app): ... (the runner calls app.run()) Application.from_environment() with a manifest You ship your own app.toml (pinned interpreter, fixed app id) and launch it with nativehtmlkit-python-host run --app app.toml Application.from_environment(), or Application.start(), which only connects in that case

items.title: Application.start() and the second run
items.text:
The native host must own the windows and supervise the Python process. When you run uv run app.py, Application.start() starts the host, and the host runs the same Python command again (the interpreter uv started, with the same script and arguments) as its backend. In that second run start() connects and returns the Application. The first process waits, relays output, and exits with the host's status.

So code before start() runs twice, and code after it runs once (in the backend):

import json
from nativehtmlkit import Application

CONFIG = {"title": "Notes"}            # fine: no side effects at import time

def main() -> None:
    with Application.start(name="Notes", app_id="org.example.Notes") as app:
        settings = json.loads(open("settings.json").read())   # runs once, in the backend
        app.open_html(render(settings), title=CONFIG["title"])
        app.run()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

start() refuses to run from an interactive interpreter, python -c or standard input (StartupError), because the host could not run it again. Arguments (sys.argv) and the working directory are passed to the second run unchanged.

items.title: uv run -m nativehtmlkit run
items.text:
uv run -m nativehtmlkit run notes:setup --name "Notes"

The launcher process never imports your module; only the backend does, once. setup(app) creates windows and registers callbacks, then returns; the runner calls app.run(). An async def entry point is awaited first. See the command reference.

A module can support both styles:

def setup(app):                       # uv run -m nativehtmlkit run focus_timer:setup
    build(app)

def main():                           # uv run focus_timer.py
    with Application.start(name="Focus timer") as app:
        setup(app)
        app.run()

(focus_timer.py)

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Start-up phase
items.text:
Between connecting and app.run() (which sends app.ready) the application is starting:

  • create at least one window first: app.ready without a window fails (RpcError -32008);
  • if the user closes a window, or Python closes the last window, before app.ready, the host cancels start-up and stops;
  • the host allows startup_timeout_ms (default 30 s) for reaching ready.

Do slow initialisation after run() started (in a thread) or show a "Loading…" page first.

items.title: Quitting
items.text:
Trigger What happens User closes the last window on_before_close of that window, then on_before_quit (reason last_window), then shutdown window.request_close() on the last window the same app.request_quit() on_before_quit (reason backend_request), then shutdown on_before_quit returns False the application keeps running Ctrl+Shift+Q in a window forced quit without asking; the backend is killed

Shutdown: the host sends app.shutdown with a deadline (shutdown_timeout_ms, default 5 s). The SDK delivers events that arrived before it, retires all handles, runs on_shutdown callbacks in the thread of app.run(), and run() returns. Your process must exit before the deadline.

app.on_before_quit(lambda: not editor.dirty or confirm_in_dialog())
app.on_shutdown(lambda: save_state(state_file))       # no window/document calls here

app.close() (or leaving the with block early) disconnects at once: run() returns, but the host treats the lost connection as an application failure (exit status 1). Use request_quit() to end deliberately.

items.title: Errors
items.text: An exception that escapes main() inside the with block is printed (with traceback, before the connection closes) and the host exits with status 1. Exceptions in callbacks are printed and the application continues. If the host disappears, run() raises DisconnectedError.

items.title: Single instance
items.text:
Application.start(instance="single") (the default) hands a second launch of the same app id to the running application instead of starting another one. instance="multiple" allows independent copies.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/lifecycle.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Live bitmaps
items.text: Use a live bitmap when Python produces pixels: charts, plots, camera or emulator frames, image previews, generated art.

items.title: Set up
items.text:
<img id="plot" src="ui4me-bitmap://plot" width="480" height="200" alt="Signal plot">

WIDTH, HEIGHT = 480, 200
bitmap = document.create_bitmap("plot", WIDTH, HEIGHT)     # id must match the img URL

items.title: Draw a frame
items.text:
A frame is WIDTH * HEIGHT * 4 bytes of straight-alpha RGBA, row by row from the top:

frame = bytearray(bytes((16, 22, 34, 255)) * (WIDTH * HEIGHT))   # fill the background
def put(x, y, rgba):
    i = (y * WIDTH + x) * 4
    frame[i:i + 4] = bytes(rgba)
for x in range(WIDTH):
    put(x, HEIGHT // 2, (94, 196, 255, 255))                       # a horizontal line
bitmap.present(frame)

present returns once the host copied the frame ({"sequence", "presented_to_engine", "slot_released"}), so you may reuse the buffer afterwards.

items.title: Animate from a thread
items.text:
import threading, time
from nativehtmlkit import NativeHTMLKitError

stop = threading.Event()
app.on_shutdown(stop.set)

def producer():
    background = draw_grid()                       # bytes, drawn once
    while not stop.is_set():
        frame = bytearray(background)              # fast copy
        draw_line(frame, next_samples())           # only the pixels that change
        try:
            if bitmap.try_present(frame) is None:
                pass                               # previous frame still being presented: skip
        except (NativeHTMLKitError, RuntimeError):
            return                                 # document gone or bitmap closed
        time.sleep(1 / 30)

threading.Thread(target=producer, daemon=True).start()

try_present never queues: it returns None if another present of this bitmap is in progress. Update text such as counters at a lower rate, in one batch.

items.title: Performance tips
items.text:
• Per-pixel Python loops cost roughly microseconds per pixel: redraw only what changes, copy a pre-rendered background, use slice assignment for rows.
  • Larger work (NumPy, Pillow) works too: pass anything that exposes the buffer protocol with exactly slot_bytes bytes, e.g. numpy_array.tobytes() or a memoryview.
  • Keep the <img> width/height equal to the bitmap size for 1:1 pixels; CSS may scale it.

items.title: Lifetime and limits
items.text:
The bitmap is released by bitmap.close() and automatically when its document is replaced, unloaded or closed; afterwards present raises. Limits: 1–4096 pixels per side, 8 bitmaps and 64 MiB per document, 256 MiB per host (RpcError -32005 beyond that).

Example: live_chart.py (this process's working set sampled twice per second, drawn from a background thread, with Pause/Resume). Reference: LiveBitmap.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/live-bitmaps.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Packaging and distribution
items.text: A NativeHTMLKit application is an ordinary Python program that depends on the nativehtmlkit wheel; the wheel bundles the native host for its platform.

items.title: Project layout
items.text:
Start from nativehtmlkit-new myapp --name "My App" (app.py, index.html, style.css, pyproject.toml, optional app.toml); project scaffolding explains each file and how to grow and test the project.

Locate assets relative to your code, never the current directory:

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
window = app.open_file(HERE / "index.html")

For an installed package, keep HTML/CSS/images as package data and resolve them with importlib.resources.files("mypackage") / "ui" / "index.html" (a real file path when installed normally), or load the markup as a string with load_html(..., asset_root=...).

items.title: Distribute as a Python package
items.text:
[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "1.0.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = ["nativehtmlkit==0.1.2"]

[project.gui-scripts]
myapp = "myapp.app:main"

Users install with uv tool install myapp and start myapp; during development, uv run -m myapp (with a myapp/__main__.py that calls main()) or uv run myapp work in the project. Application.start() re-runs the same Python command as the backend. On Linux this was checked for installed script launchers and -m; on Windows, -m uses the same mechanism as uv run app.py, while generated .exe script launchers were not part of the 0.1.2 checks, so try yours before relying on it.

Platform support follows the nativehtmlkit wheels: Linux x64 (glibc 2.39+) and Windows x64, Python 3.10+. The source distribution of nativehtmlkit has no host.

items.title: Identity and data
items.text:
• Give the application a stable app_id (Application.start(app_id="com.example.MyApp")). It controls single-instance hand-off and names the per-app directories from desktop.paths.
  • Store user data under app.rpc.call("desktop.paths")["data"] (or config/state), create the directory yourself and write files atomically (write a temporary file, then os.replace).
  • Set name, version and icon in Application.start(...).

items.title: Explicit manifests
items.text: For launchers, desktop entries or installers that should start a fixed interpreter, use a manifest and nativehtmlkit-python-host run --app /path/to/app.toml (format). {app_dir} in manifest strings is replaced by the manifest's directory. The backend then connects with Application.start() or Application.from_environment().

items.title: Before you ship
items.text:
• Run your UI headless in CI (NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1) and assert on DOM state.
  • Test once on each real desktop you support: native dialogs, clipboard, focus and window placement depend on the platform.
  • Do not set NATIVEHTMLKIT_HOST_BINARY in production; the bundled host is hash-verified on every launch.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/packaging-and-distribution.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Project scaffolding
items.text: How to start a new NativeHTMLKit application project with the nativehtmlkit-new command, what the generated files do, and how to grow the project into a real tool. Reference: nativehtmlkit-new. A complete multi-file app in this shape: examples/bulk_rename (see the bulk rename tutorial).

items.title: Generate a project
items.text:
uvx --from nativehtmlkit nativehtmlkit-new InventoryTool --name "Inventory tool"
cd InventoryTool
uv run app.py                      # creates .venv and installs nativehtmlkit on first run

uvx runs the generator without installing anything; the generated pyproject.toml makes the folder a uv project. The generator's own closing message still says python app.py; use uv run app.py.

A window with a name field and an Add item button opens. The command prints the files it created and refuses to write into a directory that is not empty (exit status 2). Options:

Option Meaning DIRECTORY New or empty project directory. --name NAME Display name; defaults to the directory name. It also forms the application id. --python INTERPRETER Interpreter written into the optional app.toml (default: the one running the command; under uvx a temporary one in uv's cache, so set program in app.toml to .venv's interpreter if you use the manifest).

The folder contains:

File Purpose app.py The backend: Application.start(name=..., app_id=...), app.open_file(HERE / "index.html"), a click handler that uses set_text, an error handler, app.run(). index.html The page: a heading, a name field, an Add item button and a status line. style.css Styles for the page, referenced from index.html with a relative URL. pyproject.toml Project metadata; depends on nativehtmlkit>=0.1.1, so uv run app.py installs it. app.toml Optional manifest for launchers and deployments that start the host themselves.

The application id is org.nativehtmlkit.examples.<slug> (for "Inventory tool": org.nativehtmlkit.examples.inventory_tool). Change APP_ID in app.py and id in app.toml to your own reverse-DNS name before you ship.

items.title: How the generated app starts
items.text:
uv run app.py starts the native host, and the host runs app.py a second time as its backend (see lifecycle). That is why the generated code keeps all work inside main():

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

def main() -> None:
    with Application.start(name=APP_NAME, app_id=APP_ID) as app:
        window = app.open_file(HERE / "index.html", title=APP_NAME, width=860, height=560)
        ...
        app.run()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Resolve files relative to __file__, never the current directory: users start the app from anywhere.

items.title: Grow it
items.text:
• Markup and styles stay in files. Edit index.html and style.css; images and fonts next to them load through relative URLs. See styling and layout.
  • Give every element you touch from Python an id, and use one delegated handler for lists (see events and callbacks).
  • Split logic from the UI. Put decisions in plain functions that take data and return data, like plan_renames() in bulk_rename/app.py. They can be unit-tested with pytest without a host.
  • Wrap the window in a class whose methods are the user's actions (add, rename, undo). Event handlers call those methods, and so can tests.
  • Expose a build(app, ...) function that opens the window and returns that object; main() calls it, and a test can call it inside a headless host.
  • Helper modules next to app.py are importable (from processes import list_processes), because the script's folder is on sys.path in the backend as well.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Test it headless
items.text:
Move the generated handler out of main() into a build() function, so a test can create the same window:

# app.py
from pathlib import Path

from nativehtmlkit import Application, Document

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
APP_NAME = "Inventory tool"
APP_ID = "org.example.InventoryTool"


def add_item(document: Document) -> None:
    title = document.get_value("item-name").strip() or "Untitled"
    document.set_text("status", "Added: " + title)     # set_text never interprets HTML
    document.set_value("item-name", "")


def build(app: Application) -> Document:
    window = app.open_file(HERE / "index.html", title=APP_NAME, width=860, height=560)
    window.document.on("click", lambda _event: add_item(window.document), element="add-item")
    return window.document


def main() -> None:
    with Application.start(name=APP_NAME, app_id=APP_ID) as app:
        build(app)
        app.run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Then run the real host without a window and drive the document through the SDK:

# check_app.py, next to app.py
import threading

import app as inventory


def check(application):
    document = inventory.build(application)
    document.set_value("item-name", "<b>Widget</b>")
    inventory.add_item(document)                      # what the click handler calls
    assert document.get_text("status") == "Added: <b>Widget</b>"
    assert document.get_value("item-name") == ""
    print("check passed")
    threading.Timer(0.5, application.request_quit).start()

NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 uv run -m nativehtmlkit run check_app:check     # prints: check passed

A failed assert ends the run with exit status 1 and the traceback. Headless mode has no pointer or keyboard input, so call the same functions the handlers call. The repository's tests/integration/example_checks.py tests every example this way.

items.title: The manifest (app.toml)
items.text:
You do not need the manifest during development. Launchers, desktop entries and installers that should start a fixed interpreter use it:

[app]
id = "org.nativehtmlkit.examples.inventory_tool"
name = "Inventory tool"
version = "1.0.0"

[backend]
program = "/path/to/venv/bin/python"     # the interpreter given with --python
args = ["{app_dir}/app.py"]              # {app_dir} is the manifest's folder
cwd = "{app_dir}"

[host]
startup_timeout_ms = 30000
shutdown_timeout_ms = 5000
max_windows = 4
instance = "single"

Start it with nativehtmlkit-python-host run --app app.toml. The backend's Application.start() connects to the host that started it. instance = "single" forwards a second launch to the running copy; "multiple" allows several copies. The complete format is in the command-line reference.

items.title: Ship it
items.text:
Packaging and distribution explains how to publish the project as a Python package with a gui-scripts entry point, where to store user data and what to test before a release.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/project-scaffolding.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Security
items.text: NativeHTMLKit runs no JavaScript and loads no remote content over HTTP, so classic web XSS cannot execute code. Markup injection still matters: untrusted text interpreted as HTML can rearrange your UI, spoof controls or hide information. Treat the page like any other UI that shows untrusted data.

items.title: Text is safe, markup is trusted
items.text:
Safe for any string Parses HTML: trusted input only set_text, set_value, Node.set_text, append_text, batch set_text, set_attribute values replace_html, insert_html, Node.insert_html/replace_html, batch insert_html/replace_children_html, load_html

Escape every untrusted value you put into markup, including attribute values:

import html
row = (f'<li id="file-{index}" title="{html.escape(path_text)}">'
       f'{html.escape(file_name)}</li>')
document.insert_html("files", row)

html.escape escapes &, <, >, " and ' (with the default quote=True), which covers text and quoted attribute values. Never put untrusted data into element ids, tag names, unquoted attributes, style or CSS: build those from your own values (numbers, known keys) and map them back in Python, as the examples do with id="todo-7-delete".

Untrusted text includes user input, file names and contents, clipboard text, network data, command-line arguments and anything read back from the document.

items.title: Trusted HTML and CSS
items.text:
Markup and styles you ship with the application are trusted. Load them from your package (load_file) or constants. Do not load HTML files chosen by the user as documents; show their text with set_value/set_text instead.

add_stylesheet and register_resources take trusted content too; never build CSS from untrusted strings.

items.title: Links and external targets
items.text:
Documents never navigate; a link activation only sends link_activated to Python. Decide explicitly what to open, and check the scheme yourself before calling open_external:

def on_link(event):
    url = event.get("url") or ""
    if url.startswith(("https://", "mailto:")):
        app.open_external(url, window=window)

The host itself refuses schemes other than http, https, mailto and file (and executable files on Windows).

items.title: Files
items.text:
• Paths from dialogs and forms are chosen by the user, but their content is still untrusted: limit sizes, decode explicitly, handle errors.
  • Write application data atomically into the per-application directories (desktop.paths).

items.title: Process and credentials
items.text:
• The host connection is a private local endpoint (a Unix socket in a 0700 runtime directory, or a named pipe restricted to the current logon session) and requires a single-use launch token. The SDK removes the token from os.environ when it connects, so child processes you start do not inherit it.
  • Diagnostics never record payloads or form values. --host-log/NATIVEHTMLKIT_HOST_LOG writes raw host records that include your application's output: treat those files as sensitive.
  • NATIVEHTMLKIT_HOST_BINARY runs an unverified host; use it only for development. The bundled host is checked against its pinned SHA-256 on every launch.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/security.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Styling and layout
items.text: How to style NativeHTMLKit windows with CSS from Python: what the renderer supports, how to lay out an application window, how to follow or override light and dark mode, and how to change styles at run time. Applies to the NativeHTMLKit Python SDK 0.1.2 with Core 1.0.3.

items.title: Which HTML and CSS work
items.text:
The host renders HTML and CSS natively with a documented desktop profile, ui4me-desktop-1.0 in Core 1.0.3, not with a browser engine. Everyday CSS works: flexbox and grid (including subgrid), calc(), custom properties (var()), color-mix(), light-dark(), @media (including prefers-color-scheme), @container, @layer, @supports, @font-face, transitions and animations. Pages have no JavaScript: behaviour lives in Python.

The authoritative list is Core's HTML and CSS support guide. You can also ask the running host. The css_profile document command returns every feature id with a state (on, off, filtered or unavailable):

profile = document.command("css_profile")
print(profile["version"])                                    # ui4me-desktop-1.0
states = {f["id"]: f["state"] for f in profile["features"]}
states["css.display.grid"]                                   # 'on'
states["css.function.color-mix"]                             # 'on'
[name for name, state in states.items() if state != "on"]    # what to avoid

A small explorer that renders this list with a live filter:

import html
from nativehtmlkit import Application

PAGE = """<!doctype html><html><head><meta charset="utf-8"><style>
  body { font: 14px sans-serif; margin: 0; padding: 16px; }
  input { width: 100%; box-sizing: border-box; padding: 8px; margin: 8px 0; }
  table { border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; }
  td { padding: 4px 8px; border-bottom: 1px solid #dde3ee; }
  tr.on td:last-child { color: #1d6b34; } tr.off td:last-child { color: #8a1f1f; }
</style></head><body>
  <input id="filter" type="search" placeholder="Filter, for example grid or color-mix" aria-label="Filter features">
  <table><tbody id="rows"></tbody></table>
</body></html>"""


def main() -> None:
    with Application.start(name="CSS support") as app:
        document = app.open_html(PAGE, title="CSS support", width=640, height=720).document
        features = sorted(document.command("css_profile")["features"], key=lambda f: f["id"])

        def render(event=None):
            needle = (event or {}).get("value", "").strip().lower()
            document.replace_html("rows", "".join(
                f'<tr class="{html.escape(f["state"])}"><td>{html.escape(f["id"])}</td>'
                f'<td>{html.escape(f["state"])}</td></tr>' for f in features if needle in f["id"].lower()))

        document.on("input", render, element="filter")
        render()
        app.run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

When a rule does not apply, ask why:

document.computed_style(["color", "display"], "title")
# {"properties": {"color": {"value": "rgb(31, 138, 76)", "status": "supported", ...}, ...}}
document.command("explain", element="title", property="color")
# {"status": "applied", "reason": "the declaration takes effect on this element", "value": ...}
document.diagnostics()["diagnostics"]          # unsupported CSS, pending or denied resources

computed_style reports an unknown property as "status": "invalid" with a reason.

items.title: Lay out an application window
items.text:
A window is a viewport, not a page that scrolls as a whole. Most tools want fixed bars and one scrolling region. Make body a flex column of the window's height and let the middle part scroll; the bulk rename and keyboard shortcuts examples use this shell:

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

body   { margin: 0; display: flex; flex-direction: column; height: 100vh; }
header { padding: 10px 14px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line); }
main   { flex: 1; overflow: auto; padding: 0 14px; }      /* only this part scrolls */
footer { display: flex; gap: 8px; align-items: center; padding: 8px 14px; }
#summary { flex: 1; }                                       /* pushes the buttons to the right */

Other patterns used by the examples:

  • Toolbars and form rows: display: flex; gap: 8px; align-items: center; with flex: 1 on the field that should grow.
  • Label/field forms: display: grid; grid-template-columns: auto 1fr; gap: 8px 12px;.
  • Sidebars: a flex row with a fixed-width aside and min-width: 0 on the flexible part (data_table.py).
  • Sticky table headers: th { position: sticky; top: 0; } inside the scrolling container.
  • Numbers: text-align: right; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; for aligned columns.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Set a minimum window size so the layout never collapses: app.open_html(page, width=900, height=620, min_width=640, min_height=400).

items.title: Light and dark mode
items.text:
Define colours as custom properties and override them for dark mode. The host evaluates prefers-color-scheme from the desktop's preference (where the platform reports it):

:root { color-scheme: light dark; --bg: #f5f6fa; --panel: #fff; --text: #1b2333; --accent: #2f62d0; }
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root { --bg: #161a22; --panel: #1f2430; --text: #e5e9f2; --accent: #7aa2ff; }
}
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }

Override the scheme for one document, for example from a settings dialog (settings_dialog.py):

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

document.set_environment(color_scheme="dark")       # "light", "dark" or "system" (follow the desktop again)
document.set_environment(reduced_motion="reduce")   # "reduce", "no-preference" or "system"
document.environment()                              # {"color_scheme": "dark", "color_scheme_source": "app", ...}

app.desktop_preferences() returns what the desktop reported (color_scheme, reduced_motion, high_contrast; None where unknown) and app.on_desktop_preferences(callback) tells you when it changes.

items.title: Change styles at run time
items.text:
Prefer toggling classes (add_class/remove_class) and letting CSS do the rest. For values chosen at run time, such as an accent colour, keep one small stylesheet and replace it:

sheet = document.add_stylesheet(":root { --accent: #2f6fd0; }")["sheet"]   # a handle

def set_accent(colour: str) -> None:
    if colour in ("#2f6fd0", "#1f8a4c", "#b4451f"):        # only values you control
        document.replace_stylesheet(sheet, f":root {{ --accent: {colour}; }}")

document.stylesheets()          # every sheet: <style>, <link> and attached ones
document.remove_stylesheet(sheet)

Never build CSS from untrusted text; treat it like markup (see security). For a single element, set_attribute(id, "style", "width:40%") sets an inline style (progress bars in checksum.py).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Files, fonts and images
items.text:
• Keep markup and styles in files and load them with app.open_file(HERE / "index.html") or window.load_file(path). Relative URLs in the HTML (style.css, images, fonts) resolve against the HTML file's folder. For an HTML string, pass asset_root= to name that folder.
  • Remote URLs are never loaded. An <img src="https://..."> is reported as RESOURCE_DENIED by document.diagnostics(). Ship assets with your application, or register in-memory files with document.register_resources(name, {...}) and reference them as ui4me-res:// URLs (see the document reference).
  • Fonts: declare your own with @font-face and a relative URL. The host ships a default sans-serif font, so text renders even if you bring none.

items.title: Related
items.text:
• Updating the page: classes, attributes and re-rendering.
  • Project scaffolding: the index.html + style.css project layout.
  • Live bitmaps: pixels drawn from Python, for charts and images.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/styling-and-layout.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Text, values, attributes, classes
items.text:
document.set_text("title", f"Hello, {name}")              # plain text, safe for any string
document.set_value("email", "ada@example.org")            # input/textarea/select value
document.set_checked("remember", True)
document.set_attribute("save", "disabled", "")            # boolean attribute on
document.remove_attribute("save", "disabled")
document.set_attribute("bar", "style", "width:40%")       # inline style
document.add_class("row-4", "selected")
document.remove_class("row-4", "selected")

Read back with get_text, get_value, get_checked, and for attributes document.command("get_attribute", element="bar", name="style")["value"].

Prefer toggling classes and letting CSS do the work. For example, to filter a log by level, give each row its level as a class and switch one class on the container instead of re-rendering rows:

#log.min-WARN .DEBUG, #log.min-WARN .INFO { display: none; }

document.remove_class("log", "min-INFO"); document.add_class("log", "min-WARN")

The hidden attribute works too: set_attribute(id, "hidden", "") / remove_attribute(id, "hidden").

items.title: Render a list or table from data
items.text:
Build markup with escaped values and replace the container's children:

import html

def render(items):
    rows = "".join(
        f'<li id="item-{item.id}"><span class="name">{html.escape(item.name)}</span>'
        f'<button id="item-{item.id}-delete">Delete</button></li>' for item in items)
    document.replace_html("items", rows or '<li class="empty">Nothing here</li>')

Re-rendering a list of a few hundred rows this way is simple and fast. Handlers delegated to the container (element="items") keep working. Table rows (<tr>) can be rendered into a <tbody id>. (data_table.py, process_viewer.py)

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Keep accessibility attributes in step with the view, for example the sort state of a column header: {"op": "set_attribute", "element": "col-Name", "name": "aria-sort", "value": "ascending"}.

items.title: Append without re-rendering
items.text:
document.insert_html("log", f'<div class="line">{html.escape(text)}</div>')   # position="beforeend"
document.insert_html("log", "<div>first</div>", position="afterbegin")

position is beforebegin, afterbegin, beforeend or afterend.

items.title: Batch several changes
items.text:
document.batch([...]) applies up to 1024 operations in one round trip and one transaction: all are applied or none.

document.batch([
    {"op": "insert_html", "element": "log", "position": "beforeend", "html": rows},
    {"op": "trim_children", "element": "log", "keep": 500, "from": "start"},   # drop oldest rows
    {"op": "set_text", "element": "count", "text": f"{total} records"},
])

Batch ops: set_text, set_attribute, remove_attribute, add_class, remove_class, insert_html, replace_children_html, remove_element, move_element, append_text, trim_children. If one fails (say, an unknown id), the error names it and nothing changed.

A batch is also the way to keep related changes consistent. The counter example updates the number, two state classes and a bounded history in one transaction (counter.py):

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

document.batch([
    {"op": "set_text", "element": "value", "text": str(value)},
    {"op": "add_class" if value < 0 else "remove_class", "element": "value", "name": "negative"},
    {"op": "insert_html", "element": "history", "position": "afterbegin",
     "html": f"<li>{html.escape(f'{reason} -> {value}')}</li>"},
    {"op": "trim_children", "element": "history", "keep": 8, "from": "end"},   # drop the oldest
])

trim_children keeps keep children and removes the rest from the start or the end.

items.title: Elements without ids
items.text:
Use nodes:

first_item = document.node(reference=document.query_nodes("#menu li")["nodes"][0]["node"])
first_item.add_class("active")
document.node("menu").trim_children(10)          # keep the 10 newest children

(dom_explorer.py)

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Counting and finding
items.text:
document.query_nodes(".line.ERROR")["total"]     # number of matches
document.query("#todos li")["ids"]                # ids of matching elements that have one
document.command("has_element", element="todo-3")["exists"]

items.title: Styles at run time
items.text:
sheet = document.add_stylesheet(":root { --accent: #c2410c; }")["sheet"]
document.replace_stylesheet(sheet, ":root { --accent: #2563eb; }")
document.computed_style(["color", "display"], "status")["properties"]["display"]["value"]
document.set_environment(color_scheme="dark")      # drives @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)

items.title: Scrolling
items.text:
document.scroll_into_view("row-120", block="center")
document.command("set_scroll_follow", element="log", follow=True)   # stay at the end as rows arrive
document.scroll_to(y=0)

items.title: Loading a whole new page
items.text:
window.load_html(html) / window.load_file(path) replaces the document. The previous Document, its nodes and subscriptions become stale: register handlers again on the new window.document. Inline HTML is limited to 1 MiB; keep large content in files or render it in pages.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/updating-the-page.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Open more windows
items.text:
main = app.open_html(MAIN_PAGE, title="Library", width=900, height=600)
detail = app.open_html(DETAIL_PAGE, title="Book", width=420, height=520, min_width=320, min_height=300)

Each window has its own document and its own subscriptions. Windows are limited by Application.start(max_windows=...) (default 16, host maximum 64); the host admits 16 live documents. Creating more fails with RpcError -32005.

items.title: Read and change state
items.text:
state = window.state()
state["title"], state["width"], state["height"]            # as requested, logical pixels
state["observed"]["maximized"]                              # what the platform reports, or None
window.set(title="Book — edited", width=640, height=480)
window.set(maximized=True)
window.set(resizable=False)
window.set(min_width=320, min_height=240)                   # constraints come in pairs

set returns the new state. Platform policy is reported as RpcError -32001: on Linux the Wayland compositor decides placement and focus, so x/y, focus=True, visible= on an existing window and minimized=False are refused there. Catch the error where you use them:

from nativehtmlkit import RpcError
try:
    window.set(x=100, y=80)
except RpcError as error:
    if error.code != -32001:
        raise

app.rpc.call("window.list") returns the state of every open window.

items.title: React to window changes
items.text:
def on_window(params):
    kind, window_id = params["type"], params["window_id"]
    if kind == "closed":
        forget(window_id)              # the Window object is already marked closed
    elif kind == "resized":
        relayout(params["data"]["physical_width"])

app.on_window_event(on_window)

items.title: Ask before closing a window
items.text:
def allow_close() -> bool:
    if note.dirty:
        note.document.add_class("unsaved-warning", "shown")   # tell the user why
        return False                                          # keep the window open
    return True

note_window.on_before_close(allow_close)

The policy runs for the user's close button and for window.request_close(). Return quickly: the host waits for the answer. To close after the user confirmed, clear the flag and call request_close() again.

items.title: Close a window from Python
items.text:
detail.request_close()

Closing the last window quits the application (after on_before_quit). To make one window the "main" window whose closing quits everything, quit when its closed event arrives:

def on_window(params):
    if params["type"] == "closed" and params["window_id"] == main.id:
        app.request_quit()
app.on_window_event(on_window)

items.title: Stale windows
items.text:
After a window closed, window.closed is True and every call on it, its document or nodes raises StaleDocumentError without contacting the host. Code that keeps windows in a dict should drop them on closed.

Example: window_manager.py (note windows with unsaved-change guards, a live window table with rename/resize/maximize/close, quit when the main window closes).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Source: nativehtmlkit-python/docs/guides/windows.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Python SDK API reference
items.text:
Reference for nativehtmlkit 0.1.2 (bundles NativeHTMLKit Core 1.0.3, public wire protocol v1; Python 3.10+). Everything listed here is importable from nativehtmlkit unless noted.

from nativehtmlkit import Application

def main() -> None:
    with Application.start(name="Hello") as app:
        window = app.open_html('<button id="go">Go</button><p id="out">Ready</p>')
        window.document.on("click", lambda event: window.document.set_text("out", "Clicked"), element="go")
        app.run()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The object model is Application → Window → Document → Node. The Rust host owns windows, rendering and input; Python owns logic and talks to the host over a local, authenticated connection.

items.title: Rules that apply everywhere
items.text:
• Two processes. Application.start() re-runs your script as the host's backend. Keep side effects inside main(), after start(). See lifecycle.
  • Thread-safe. Any method may be called from any thread. Callbacks run on SDK threads (threading summary).
  • Generation-bound handles. A replaced, unloaded or closed document, its nodes and its window raise StaleDocumentError locally.
  • Text vs markup. set_text/set_value never parse HTML. replace_html/insert_html parse trusted markup only; escape user data with html.escape. See security.
  • Headless. With NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 everything except native services works without a desktop; those raise RpcError -32001.
