"""Task list with per-row Done/Remove buttons and an All/Open/Done filter.

Teaches: the "slot pool" pattern. The UI tree is fixed once mounted, so the app creates
MAX_TASKS rows up front and shows, hides and relabels them from state (ui.when + bound text +
bound button labels). Also: computed counts, a disabled Add button and "Clear done".

Run:  uv run todo.py      (uv add nativehtmlkit_ui)
"""
from itertools import count

from nativehtmlkit_ui import UI, computed, state

MAX_TASKS = 8


def main(app):
    next_id = count(1)
    tasks = state([])          # [{"id": 1, "title": "...", "done": False}, ...]
    title = state("")
    show = state("all")

    visible = computed(lambda: [t for t in tasks.value
                                if show.value == "all" or t["done"] == (show.value == "done")])
    open_count = computed(lambda: sum(not t["done"] for t in tasks.value))
    full = computed(lambda: len(tasks.value) >= MAX_TASKS)

    def task_at(row):
        rows = visible.value
        return rows[row] if row < len(rows) else None

    def add(_event):
        text = title.value.strip()
        if text and not full.value:
            tasks.set([*tasks.value, {"id": next(next_id), "title": text, "done": False}])
            title.set("")

    def toggle(row):
        task = task_at(row)
        if task:
            tasks.set([dict(t, done=not t["done"]) if t["id"] == task["id"] else t for t in tasks.value])

    def remove(row):
        task = task_at(row)
        if task:
            tasks.set([t for t in tasks.value if t["id"] != task["id"]])

    ui = UI(title="Tasks", width=640, height=620)
    with ui.column():
        ui.heading("Tasks", level=1)
        with ui.row():
            ui.input(title, label="New task", placeholder="Water the plants")
            ui.button("Add", on_click=add, disabled=lambda: full.value or not title.value.strip())
        with ui.when(full):
            ui.alert(f"The list is full ({MAX_TASKS} tasks). Remove or clear some first.")
        with ui.row():
            ui.select(show, [("all", "All"), ("open", "Open"), ("done", "Done")], label="Show")
            ui.badge(lambda: f"{open_count.value} open, {len(tasks.value) - open_count.value} done")
        with ui.card():
            with ui.when(lambda: not visible.value):
                ui.text("Nothing here.", muted=True)
            for row in range(MAX_TASKS):
                with ui.when(lambda row=row: task_at(row) is not None):
                    with ui.row():
                        ui.text(lambda row=row: ("[x] " if task_at(row)["done"] else "[ ] ") + task_at(row)["title"]
                                if task_at(row) else "")
                        ui.button(lambda row=row: "Reopen" if task_at(row) and task_at(row)["done"] else "Done",
                                  variant="secondary", on_click=lambda _e, row=row: toggle(row))
                        ui.button("Remove", variant="quiet", on_click=lambda _e, row=row: remove(row))
        ui.button("Clear done", variant="danger", disabled=lambda: open_count.value == len(tasks.value),
                  on_click=lambda _e: tasks.set([t for t in tasks.value if not t["done"]]))
    ui.mount(app)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    from nativehtmlkit import Application
    with Application.start(name="Tasks") as application:
        main(application)
        application.run()

items.title: Source: python/word_counter.py
items.text:
View on GitHub

"""Word counter: count words in a text file in a worker thread, with progress and Cancel.

Teaches: starting background work from a button, handing progress and results back to the UI
owner with ui.post(), throttled progress (at most five updates per second), a Cancel button
driven by a threading.Event, and a busy state that disables Count while the worker runs.
Run:     uv run word_counter.py [FILE]   (without FILE it counts 20,000 lines of generated text)
Guide:   docs/python/guides/background-work.md
"""
import re
import sys
import threading
import time
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

from nativehtmlkit import Application
from nativehtmlkit_ui import UI, state

WORD = re.compile(r"[^\W\d_]+(?:'[^\W\d_]+)?")
SAMPLE_WORDS = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog while native windows render html".split()
SAMPLE_LINES = 20_000


def sample_lines():
    return [" ".join(SAMPLE_WORDS[(i + j) % len(SAMPLE_WORDS)] for j in range(9)) for i in range(SAMPLE_LINES)]


def main():
    with Application.start(name="Word counter") as app:
        source = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else None
        progress = state("Press Count to start.")
        top_words = state([])
        running = state(False)
        cancel = threading.Event()

        def finish(message, words):          # runs on the UI owner thread
            progress.set(message)
            top_words.set(words)
            running.set(False)

        def work():                          # runs on the worker thread; touches no state
            try:
                lines = source.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines() if source else sample_lines()
            except OSError as error:
                ui.post(finish, f"Cannot read the file: {error.strerror or error}", [])
                return
            counts, last = Counter(), 0.0
            for number, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
                if cancel.is_set():
                    ui.post(finish, "Cancelled.", [])
                    return
                counts.update(word.lower() for word in WORD.findall(line))
                if time.monotonic() - last > 0.2:
                    last = time.monotonic()
                    ui.post(progress.set, f"{number / max(1, len(lines)):.0%} - {number:,} lines")
            ui.post(finish, f"Done: {sum(counts.values()):,} words, {len(counts):,} different, {len(lines):,} lines.",
                    [f"{word}: {count:,}" for word, count in sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:10]])

        def start(_event):
            if running.value:
                return
            cancel.clear()
            running.set(True)
            top_words.set([])
            progress.set("Starting...")
            threading.Thread(target=work, name="word-count", daemon=True).start()

        ui = UI(title="Word counter", theme="daylight", density="regular", width=560, height=560)
        with ui.column():
            ui.heading("Word counter", level=1)
            ui.text(f"Source: {source.name if source else 'generated sample text'}", muted=True)
            with ui.row():
                ui.button("Count", on_click=start, disabled=running)
                ui.button("Cancel", variant="secondary", on_click=lambda _e: cancel.set(),
                          disabled=lambda: not running.value)
            ui.alert(progress)
            with ui.card():
                ui.heading("Most frequent words", level=2)
                ui.text_list(top_words)
        try:
            ui.mount(app)
            app.on_shutdown(cancel.set)
            app.run()
        finally:
            cancel.set()
            ui.dispose()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items.title: Background work
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: background work.

Goal: run slow or periodic work without freezing the window, report progress, cancel it, and get the results into the UI safely.

items.title: The rule
items.text:
Event handlers run on the UI owner thread. While one runs, no other event, posted function or DOM update of that UI is processed, so handlers must return quickly. Run slow work elsewhere (a thread or an executor) and hand every result back with ui.post(fn, *args), which runs fn on the UI owner.

Why post() and not state.set() directly from the worker? Setting a state from another thread is allowed and the window write still happens on the owner, but:

  • the open defect B-0002 can corrupt a Computed whose dependencies are set from several threads at once, and
  • doing all writes on the owner keeps your handlers and posted functions free of races.

items.title: Run one job and report the result
items.text:
From the background example:

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2)
cancel = threading.Event()

def calculate(n):                    # runs on an executor thread; touches no state
    total = 0
    for start in range(0, n, 10_000):
        if cancel.is_set():
            raise InterruptedError("cancelled")
        total += sum(range(start, min(n, start + 10_000)))
    return total

def finished(text):                  # runs on the UI owner
    status.set(text)
    busy.set(False)

def run(_event):
    cancel.clear()
    busy.set(True)
    status.set("Running")
    future = executor.submit(calculate, 500_000)

    def completed(f):                # runs on an executor thread
        try:
            ui.post(finished, f"Done: {f.result()}")
        except InterruptedError:
            ui.post(finished, "Cancelled")
        except Exception as exc:
            ui.post(finished, f"Failed: {type(exc).__name__}")
    future.add_done_callback(completed)

ui.button("Calculate", on_click=run, disabled=busy)
ui.button("Cancel", variant="secondary", on_click=lambda _e: cancel.set(), disabled=lambda: not busy.value)
ui.mount(app)
app.on_shutdown(cancel.set)
app.on_shutdown(lambda: executor.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True))

items.title: Report progress and cancel
items.text:
A worker that reports progress posts small updates, at most a few per second. From the word_counter example:

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

def work():                                  # worker thread; touches no state
    counts, last = Counter(), 0.0
    for number, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
        if cancel.is_set():
            ui.post(finish, "Cancelled.", [])
            return
        counts.update(word.lower() for word in WORD.findall(line))
        if time.monotonic() - last > 0.2:    # at most five updates per second
            last = time.monotonic()
            ui.post(progress.set, f"{number / len(lines):.0%} - {number:,} lines")
    ui.post(finish, f"Done: {sum(counts.values()):,} words ...", top_ten(counts))

ui.post(progress.set, text) is the shortest way to set one state on the owner. Several posts before the owner catches up are coalesced into one window update.

items.title: Streams and timers
items.text:
A producer thread that posts many items (the log_viewer example):

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

stop = threading.Event()

def produce():
    n = 0
    while not stop.wait(0.2):
        n += 1
        try:
            ui.post(receive, make_line(n))
        except RuntimeError:            # owner queue full (4096): drop instead of blocking
            pass

threading.Thread(target=produce, daemon=True).start()
app.on_shutdown(stop.set)

The same structure gives a one-second clock (the dashboard example): a thread that waits one second and posts the new time.

items.title: SDK futures
items.text: SDK calls with wait=False return a concurrent.futures.Future; hand their result over the same way: future.add_done_callback(lambda f: ui.post(chosen, f)) (the SDK calls guide).

items.title: Forms, inputs and validation
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: forms and inputs.

Goal: bind inputs, checkboxes and selects to state, validate as the user types, and only allow submitting a valid form.

items.title: Two-way binding
items.text:
Control Python State holds Text input ui.input(name, label="Name", kind="text") str Checkbox ui.checkbox(terms, label="I accept") bool Select ui.select(plan, [("free", "Free"), ("team", "Team")], label="Plan") the option value as str
  • Input kinds: text, password, search, email, number. A number input still gives a string; convert and validate it yourself.
  • Each keystroke updates the state; there is no "on blur" mode.
  • Setting the state from code updates the control (description.set("") clears the field after "Add"). Typing never triggers a write-back, so the caret and IME stay intact.
  • The control must be bound to a real State (a Computed raises TypeError).
  • choices accepts any iterable of (value, text) pairs, for example CATEGORIES.items().

items.title: Validation as derived state
items.text:
Do not read values from the DOM. Compute the problems from the states (the signup_form example):

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

def problems():
    found = []
    if email.value and not EMAIL.match(email.value.strip()):
        found.append("Enter a valid email address.")
    if confirm.value and confirm.value != password.value:
        found.append("Passwords do not match.")
    if age.value and not (age.value.isdigit() and 16 <= int(age.value) <= 120):
        found.append("Age must be a whole number from 16 to 120.")
    return found

errors = computed(problems)
complete = computed(lambda: all(s.value for s in (name, email, password, confirm, age)) and terms.value)
can_submit = computed(lambda: complete.value and not errors.value)

with ui.when(errors):
    ui.text_list(errors)
ui.button("Create account", on_click=submit, disabled=lambda: not can_submit.value)

A single message works the same way (the settings editor): problem = computed(lambda: find_problem(snapshot.value)) returns "" when everything is valid, and with ui.when(problem): ui.text(problem) shows it only when there is one.

items.title: Patterns that make forms pleasant
items.text:
• Only complain about fields the user touched. Each rule starts with "if the field is not empty"; a separate muted hint says "Fill in every field" until the form is complete.
  • Disable, then re-check. The submit handler checks can_submit.value again before acting.
  • Parse at the boundary. The expense tracker keeps the amount as text in state and converts it with Decimal only when adding; an invalid amount sets an error state shown in an alert inside when.
  • Reset by setting states. "Start over" sets every state back to its initial value; the controls follow.
  • Show results instead of the form. Two when regions (form / confirmation) switch on a welcome state.

items.title: Loading and saving form data
items.text:
Create the states from the loaded data, keep a snapshot of the last saved values and compare (the settings-editor tutorial builds this step by step):

loaded = read_settings(path)
name = state(str(loaded["DisplayName"]))
...
snapshot = computed(lambda: {"DisplayName": name.value.strip(), ...})
saved = state(snapshot.value)
changes = computed(lambda: "All changes saved" if snapshot.value == saved.value else "Unsaved changes")

Write files atomically (a temporary file in the same folder, then os.replace), so a crash never leaves half a settings file.

items.title: Keyboard events
items.text: ui.on(element, kind, callback) registers other event kinds, for example keydown on an input to submit with Enter. Do not register input or change on a bound control: it would replace the binding's own handler. Keyboard handling beyond button activation was not part of the 0.1.1 GUI qualification, so verify it in your target environment.

items.title: Native form features
items.text: The UI does not wrap <form>, HTML constraint validation (required, pattern) or form data. They are SDK document features (Document.form_data, validity) for apps that build their own markup.

items.title: Related
items.text:
Python reference: controls · lists and conditional content · expense-tracker tutorial

Source: nativehtmlkit_ui/docs/python/guides/forms-and-inputs.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Layouts and the responsive grid
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: layouts.

Goal: arrange components with rows, columns, cards and a grid that adapts to the window.

items.title: Containers
items.text:
Python Element Use for with ui.column(): div.nhk-col The main vertical flow of a window. with ui.row(): div.nhk-row Toolbars, a field next to its button, badges next to a heading. Wraps when narrow. with ui.card(): div.nhk-card Grouping related content on a panel. with ui.grid(): div.nhk-grid Dashboards and settings pages: equal-width cells. with ui.stack(): div.nhk-stack Tight vertical groups (6 px gap). Python only. with ui.container("section", css_class="x"): any allowed tag Your own structure and classes. Python only.

Containers are context managers; components created inside the with block become children.

items.title: A typical window
items.text:
with ui.column():
    with ui.row():
        ui.heading("Settings", level=1)
        ui.badge(lambda: "Unsaved changes" if dirty.value else "All changes saved")
    with ui.grid():
        with ui.card():
            ui.heading("Profile", level=3)
            ui.input(name, label="Display name")
        with ui.card():
            ui.heading("Editor", level=3)
            ui.select(font_size, FONT_SIZES, label="Font size")
    with ui.row():
        ui.button("Save", on_click=save)
        ui.button("Revert", variant="secondary", on_click=revert)

The full version is the settings example.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: How the grid responds
items.text:
nhk-grid uses three equal columns. When the window's viewport is at most 1000 px wide it switches to two columns, at most 620 px to one column (and the app padding shrinks to 14 px). Cells keep min-width: 0, so long text wraps instead of widening the grid. There is no column-span API; for a wide cell put the content outside the grid, or wrap it in ui.container(css_class="wide") with extra CSS .wide { grid-column: 1 / -1; }.

Rows wrap: a labelled input or select is a flex item of at least 150 px that grows (flex: 1 1 200px), so a row of three fields becomes two lines in a narrow window. The dashboard example shows six cards that reflow as you resize.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Fields directly in a column (known defect B-0014)
items.text:
The 0.1.1 stylesheet applies the row rule flex: 1 1 200px to fields placed directly in a column too, where the 200 px basis becomes the field's height: a labelled input followed by more content leaves a large gap. Fields inside a row or a card are not affected. Until it is fixed, add this extra CSS when you put labelled inputs directly in ui.column() or ui.stack():

FIELD_FIX = ".nhk-col > .nhk-field, .nhk-stack > .nhk-field { flex: 0 0 auto; }"
ui = UI(title="Create account", extra_css=FIELD_FIX)

The signup_form and multi_window examples do this (with the .nhk-col selector).

items.title: Density and window size
items.text:
UI(density=...) changes control height, font size, gaps and padding for the whole window (compact 30 px controls / 13 px font, regular 36 / 14, comfortable 42 / 15). width and height are the requested initial window size in CSS pixels (the host may clamp it to the screen). Use comfortable for touch screens and forms that are read more than written, compact for tool windows. The theme_preview example shows every density.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Rules of thumb
items.text:
• Exactly one outer column() per window keeps spacing consistent.
  • Put a label on every input and select (label=); placeholders disappear.
  • Headings: one level=1 per window, level=2 or level=3 inside cards.
  • The tree is fixed after mount. Plan every region you need up front and toggle it with when.

items.title: Related
items.text:
Python reference: layout containers · CSS reference · theming

Source: nativehtmlkit_ui/docs/python/guides/layouts.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Lists and conditional content
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: lists and conditional content.

Goal: show collections and optional parts of a window, given that the component tree is fixed once the window opens.

items.title: Conditional regions
items.text:
with ui.when(error):                       # str state: shown when non-empty
    ui.alert(error)
with ui.when(lambda: not visible.value):   # any truthy/falsy expression
    ui.text("No expenses to show yet.", muted=True)

A region is always in the document and only toggles display: none (class nhk-hidden). Hidden inputs keep their values; showing the region again is instant. Regions nest (the settings example hides the "autosave interval" field, and inside it an error alert). Typical uses: empty states, validation messages, "paused" banners, swapping a form for a confirmation (two regions with opposite conditions). The condition uses Python truthiness: "", 0, None, [] and False hide the region.

items.title: Text lists
items.text:
ui.text_list(visible, formatter=lambda e: f"{e['description']} ({e['category']}): {e['amount']:.2f}")
  • Items are always escaped text; markup in data is shown literally.
  • A change replaces all <li> children at once. Show a bounded window of data (the log viewer shows the newest 14 of up to 500 lines) rather than thousands of rows.
  • Filtering and sorting belong in a computed value, not in the list.

items.title: Interactive rows: the slot pool
items.text:
A text list cannot hold buttons. When each row needs actions, create a fixed number of row "slots" at build time and bind each slot to "the item at position i of the visible list" (the todo example):

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

MAX_TASKS = 8

def task_at(row):
    rows = visible.value
    return rows[row] if row < len(rows) else None

for row in range(MAX_TASKS):
    with ui.when(lambda row=row: task_at(row) is not None):
        with ui.row():
            ui.text(lambda row=row: task_at(row)["title"] if task_at(row) else "")
            ui.button(lambda row=row: "Reopen" if task_at(row) and task_at(row)["done"] else "Done",
                      variant="secondary", on_click=lambda _e, row=row: toggle(row))
            ui.button("Remove", variant="quiet", on_click=lambda _e, row=row: remove(row))
  • Bind row=row as a default argument, or every lambda sees the last loop value.
  • Handlers look the item up at click time (task_at(row)) and act on its id, so they stay correct when the filter or order changes.
  • Cap the model at the number of slots and say so in the UI (Add is disabled and an alert appears when the list is full).

items.title: When you outgrow this
items.text: For large tables, rich per-row markup or virtual scrolling, render that part yourself with the SDK's document API (for example ui.document.insert_html(element_id, html), with your own escaping via html.escape) inside a container you created with ui.container() and own completely. The UI library deliberately has no data grid.

items.title: Related
items.text:
Python reference: dynamic regions · forms and inputs · log_viewer example

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Mixing the UI with direct SDK calls
path: Mixing the UI with direct SDK calls

items.title: Mixing the UI with direct SDK calls
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: mixing the UI with SDK calls.

Goal: use SDK services (dialogs, clipboard, window control, DOM queries) from a UI app.
path: Mixing the UI with direct SDK calls

items.title: The handles
items.text:
The UI library covers components and state. Everything else belongs to the Python SDK, and a UI app calls it directly. The handles you need are on the UI object after mounting:

Python Use ui.app (or the app you passed) Clipboard, quit, preferences, window events ui.window Dialogs, request_close, window state ui.document Reading DOM state, focus, scrolling, stylesheets element.id Target id for document calls (every component returns its Element)
path: Mixing the UI with direct SDK calls

items.title: Clipboard
items.text:
from nativehtmlkit import RpcError

def copy(_event):
    try:
        app.set_clipboard_text(result.value)
        status.set(f"Copied {len(result.value)} characters to the clipboard.")
    except RpcError as error:
        status.set(f"Clipboard unavailable: {error}")

Always handle the error: the clipboard is not available everywhere. In the host's headless test mode it fails with code -32001 ("Clipboard requires a native event loop"), which is the path the example harness verifies (the clipboard_tool example).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.
path: Mixing the UI with direct SDK calls

items.title: File dialogs
items.text:
Start the dialog without blocking the owner thread and post the result back (the file_picker example):

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

def choose(_event):
    busy.set(True)
    future = ui.window.open_files(multiple=True, title="Choose files to inspect", wait=False)
    future.add_done_callback(lambda f: ui.post(chosen, f))

def chosen(future):                         # on the UI owner
    busy.set(False)
    try:
        result = future.result()            # {"cancelled": bool, "paths": [...]}
    except RpcError as error:
        status.set(f"File dialogs are unavailable here: {error}")
        return
    ...

Dialogs are unavailable in headless mode (-32001), so the harness verifies the error path; the interactive dialog path was not part of the automated run.
path: Mixing the UI with direct SDK calls

items.title: Reading the DOM
items.text:
The UI's states are the source of truth, but SDK reads are useful for focus management and tests:

el = ui.input(name, label="Name")
...
ui.document.focus(el.id)                     # after mount
ui.document.get_value(el.id)                 # what the native control holds
path: Mixing the UI with direct SDK calls

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Do not change bound properties behind the UI's back (set_text on an element whose text is bound): the next flush may overwrite it, and the UI cannot know. Change the state.
  • Do not add elements into managed containers with raw document calls; the UI's tree would no longer describe the document. Use a raw_html container you own, or a separate window.
  • SDK calls from a handler run on the owner thread and block it while they wait. Prefer wait=False futures for anything user-operated (dialogs).
  • Window and application lifecycle (request_close, request_quit) always belongs to your code.

items.title: Multiple windows and multiple UIs
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: multiple windows.

Goal: open more than one window, share state between them, and handle closing.

items.title: One UI per window
items.text:
Each UI object is one window. Create as many as you need from one SDK application; they may bind the same states, and every window updates when a shared state changes (the multi_window example). Each UI has its own owner thread; updates of different windows are independent.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Open a window from a handler
items.text:
def open_inspector(_event):
    inspector = UI(title="Inspector 1", width=420, height=320, theme="graphite")
    with inspector.column():
        inspector.text(lambda: f"Note: {note.value}")            # same state as the main window
        inspector.button("Close inspector", variant="secondary",
                         on_click=lambda _e: inspector.window.request_close())
    inspector.mount(app)                                         # allowed from a handler

Mounting from an event handler of another UI is allowed. Build the new UI completely before mount().

items.title: Notice closed windows
items.text:
window_id = inspector.window.id

    def on_window(event):                                        # SDK event thread
        if event.get("window_id") == window_id and event.get("type") == "closed":
            unsubscribe()
            main_ui.post(lambda: open_inspectors.set(open_inspectors.value - 1))
    unsubscribe = app.on_window_event(on_window)
  • A UI disposes itself when its window closes (by the user or window.request_close()).
  • app.on_window_event callbacks run on an SDK thread; hand work to a UI with post().
  • Closing the last window ends the application (Core asks for quit with reason last_window).

items.title: Limits (known defect B-0003)
items.text: Every mount() registers an application shutdown callback that cannot be removed (open defect B-0003). Cap the number of windows a long-running app creates, or reuse them; the example allows three inspectors at a time.

items.title: Clean up
items.text: Dispose every UI you created in finally (ui.dispose() is idempotent). Window and application lifecycle (request_close, request_quit) always belongs to your code.

items.title: Related
items.text:
Python reference: mounting and the UI owner · SDK calls

Source: nativehtmlkit_ui/docs/python/guides/multiple-windows.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Reactive state and computed values
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: reactive state.

Goal: keep application data in states, derive everything else, and let the window follow.

Every example in this library follows one rule: the window shows state; event handlers change state; nothing writes to the window directly.

items.title: Model data as state
items.text:
from nativehtmlkit_ui import UI, computed, state

expenses = state([])        # source data
show = state("all")         # a choice the user makes

state(value) returns a State. Read it with .value, change it with .set(new). Components bound to it (ui.text(expenses), ui.input(show)) update themselves.

items.title: Derive values with computed
items.text:
visible = computed(lambda: [e for e in expenses.value if show.value in ("all", e["category"])])
total = computed(lambda: sum(e["amount"] for e in visible.value))

ui.heading(lambda: f"Total: {total.value:.2f}")              # bound expression
ui.badge(lambda: f"{len(visible.value)} of {len(expenses.value)} expenses")
  • computed() records which states its function reads, on every run. You never list dependencies.
  • A bound lambda (lambda: ...) works like an anonymous computed for one element.
  • Prefer a named computed when several places use the same derived value or when it is expensive: it is evaluated once per change, not once per element. Handlers can read it too (cannot_add.value).
  • Computed values can depend on computed values (total reads visible).

items.title: Change data by replacing it
items.text:
Change detection compares values with ==. Mutating in place is invisible:

expenses.value.append(item)                     # WRONG: nobody is notified
expenses.set([*expenses.value, item])           # right: a new list
tasks.set([dict(t, done=not t["done"]) if t["id"] == task_id else t for t in tasks.value])

Store records as dicts or tuples that you replace instead of edit, and give list items an id when rows can be toggled or removed (the todo example).

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Side effects: subscribe
items.text:
When a change should trigger something that is not display (a counter, saving, logging), use subscribe. It runs synchronously on the thread that set the state:

note.subscribe(lambda: edits.set(edits.value + 1))     # examples/python/multi_window.py

Keep subscribers short. Never block in them, and never touch ui.document from a subscriber that may run on a worker thread; set another state or use ui.post().

items.title: Dirty tracking and snapshots
items.text:
A computed snapshot of several fields makes "unsaved changes" trivial (the settings example and the settings-editor tutorial):

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

current = computed(lambda: {key: s.value for key, s in fields.items()})
saved = state(current.value)
dirty = computed(lambda: current.value != saved.value)
ui.button("Save", on_click=save, disabled=lambda: not dirty.value)

Dicts compare by content in Python, so the snapshot can be compared directly.

items.title: Where states may be changed
items.text: States may be set from any thread; the window update always happens on the UI owner thread. However, a Computed whose dependencies are set from several threads at once is affected by the open defect B-0002 (a false "circular dependency" error and a stale value). Make all writes that feed one computed on the UI owner: ui.post(state.set, value). See background work.

items.title: Related
items.text:
Python reference: reactive values · architecture · expenses example

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Source: nativehtmlkit_ui/docs/python/guides/reactive-state.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Testing your UI
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: testing.

Goal: test application logic quickly, then prove it against the real native host.

items.title: 1. Logic without a host
items.text:
Most UI logic is plain state. Test it without any window:

from nativehtmlkit_ui import computed, state

def test_total_follows_filter():
    expenses = state([{"category": "food", "amount": 3}, {"category": "home", "amount": 5}])
    show = state("all")
    visible = computed(lambda: [e for e in expenses.value if show.value in ("all", e["category"])])
    total = computed(lambda: sum(e["amount"] for e in visible.value))
    assert total.value == 8
    show.set("home")
    assert total.value == 5

UI.html() renders the full document without a host, which is enough to check structure, labels and escaping:

from nativehtmlkit_ui import UI

def test_text_is_escaped():
    ui = UI(title="t")
    ui.text("<b>x</b>")
    assert "<b>x</b>" in ui.html()

The library's own unit tests do the same with a fake SDK (python/tests).

items.title: 2. The real host, headless
items.text:
Set NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 and start the app normally. The SDK launches the real Core host in headless mode: the whole protocol runs (documents load, commands apply, events can be delivered) but no window is shown. Native input does not exist there, and services that need a desktop (clipboard, file dialogs, opening URLs) fail with error -32001, so code paths for those errors get exercised.

In a test you can then:

  • read DOM state through the SDK: ui.document.get_text(el.id), get_value, get_checked, command("get_attribute", element=..., name="disabled");
  • wait for pending window updates with ui.sync();
  • assert health: ui.diagnostics has no errors, event_queue_dropped == 0 and dom_uncertain is False;
  • end with app.request_quit() and check the process exits 0.

items.title: 3. The example harness
items.text:
qualification/examples/run_examples.py runs every example and tutorial step listed in examples/catalog.toml this way, in Python and PowerShell, each through its own normal entry point (python example.py [args]), unchanged. A small probe records the mounted UIs, replays the scenario from qualification/examples/scenarios.json, reads the DOM back, and quits:

"expenses": {"steps": [
  {"op": "type", "label": "Description", "value": "Coffee"},
  {"op": "type", "label": "Amount", "value": "3.50"},
  {"op": "click", "label": "Add expense"},
  {"op": "expect_text", "contains": ["Coffee (Food): 3.50", "Total: 3.50"]},
  {"op": "expect_value", "label": "Description", "value": ""}
]}

Steps: click, type, check, choose (simulated events), expect_text / wait_text (visible text, skipping hidden regions), expect_value, expect_disabled, expect_uis, close_window, sleep. Each step may target another window with "ui": 1 and the n-th matching control with "nth". A scenario may give "args" for the command line (the settings editor gets a file name in a fresh temporary folder) and separate "py"/"ps" step lists.

# an environment with the nativehtmlkit SDK and nativehtmlkit_ui installed
python qualification/examples/run_examples.py --lang py --python /path/to/venv/bin/python

Per example it requires: ready reached, all steps passed, clean UI diagnostics, exit code 0, no traceback on stderr, and no leftover host/backend process. It also fails when a catalogue entry lacks a file in either language, a file has no scenario, or a script under examples/ is not in the catalogue.

What this proves and what not. Events are injected at the UI library's SDK callback entry point after writing the control value with the public SDK, so the app's handlers, state, computed values and document writes run against the real host exactly as after native input. It does not prove native input, focus, IME, rendering or accessibility.

items.title: 4. On a desktop
items.text: Run the example normally and use it. For repeatable GUI checks, drive real input with your platform's tooling and read state back through the SDK, as the repository's qualification/gui driver does on KDE Plasma Wayland and Windows.

items.title: Theming and custom CSS
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: theming and custom CSS.

Goal: pick a theme and density, adjust colours, and style your own elements.

items.title: Themes and densities
items.text:
ui = UI(title="Dashboard", theme="graphite", density="regular", extra_css=CSS)
  • Themes: cobalt (dark blue, default), graphite (dark grey), daylight (light).
  • Densities: compact (default), regular, comfortable.
  • The CSS reference lists every token and class.

To see them all, run the theme_preview example with different arguments. It uses Application.start(instance="multiple"), so several previews can run side by side:

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

uv run theme_preview.py cobalt compact
uv run theme_preview.py daylight comfortable "#0f7b6c"

items.title: Override design tokens
items.text:
Extra CSS is appended after the built-in stylesheet, so the same selector wins. Override tokens on body.nhk-theme-<name>; every component follows. From theme_preview.py:

extra = (f"body.nhk-theme-{theme} {{ --nhk-accent: {accent}; --nhk-accent-strong: {accent}; "
         f"--nhk-focus: {accent}; }}") if accent else ""
ui = UI(title=f"Theme preview: {theme}/{density}", theme=theme, density=density, extra_css=extra)

Change --nhk-accent, --nhk-accent-strong and --nhk-focus together and check contrast against --nhk-accent-text.

items.title: Style your own elements
items.text:
ui.element() creates an allowed tag with your own class (from the dashboard example):

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

CSS = """
.metric { font-size: 30px; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: -0.02em; margin: 4px 0; }
.nhk-card { border-top: 3px solid var(--nhk-accent); }
body.nhk-theme-daylight { --nhk-accent: #0f7b6c; --nhk-accent-strong: #0b6458; --nhk-focus: #0f7b6c; }
"""
...
ui.element("div", css_class="metric", text=clock)

Guidelines:

  • Use var(--nhk-*) in your own rules so they work in every theme.
  • Target classes, never generated ids (they are random per run).
  • Extra CSS is trusted developer input. Do not build it from user input (the preview only accepts an accent that matches #RRGGBB).
  • Core renders a defined CSS subset natively (no browser engine); test layouts on your target desktops. See Core's HTML/CSS support.

items.title: Choose the theme at start
items.text: Theme and density are fixed when the window opens. Take them from the command line (the dashboard and theme preview), from a saved setting (the settings-editor tutorial starts in the saved theme), or from the desktop: read app.desktop_preferences() before building the UI and pick daylight or a dark theme. Inspect the returned dictionary on your systems first; the UI library does not interpret it.

items.title: Related
items.text:
CSS reference · layouts · Python reference: UI

Source: nativehtmlkit_ui/docs/python/guides/theming-and-custom-css.md · edit the page there.

items.title: Trusted and untrusted content
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same guide for PowerShell: trusted and untrusted content.

Goal: show user, file and network data safely, and know when raw HTML is acceptable.

items.title: The rule
items.text:
Content Use Escaped? Anything a user typed, a file contained, a process printed or a server returned text, heading, badge, alert, text_list, button labels Yes, always Attribute values passed to ui.element(attrs=...) ui.element, ui.container Yes (" and < encoded) Static markup you wrote and ship with the app ui.raw_html(markup) No, inserted verbatim Extra CSS UI(extra_css=...) No (trusted)

Text components never interpret markup. In the message_preview example, typing <b>bold</b> & <i>x</i> into the message field shows exactly those characters in the preview and in the sent list; the harness reads the element text back through the SDK and checks it.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

ui.text(lambda: message.value or "Nothing typed yet.")     # safe for any input
ui.raw_html(HELP)                                          # HELP is a constant in the source

items.title: Why raw HTML is dangerous even without JavaScript
items.text:
NativeHTMLKit runs no JavaScript, but injected markup can still restyle or hide your interface, fake buttons and labels, add elements whose ids clash with managed ones, or reference images and other resources. Treat raw_html like code: only constants, reviewed like code.

If you must display structured untrusted data (a table of records), build it from text components or escape every value yourself with html.escape before composing markup, and render it into a container you own.

items.title: Other built-in guards
items.text:
• Element ids are generated; passing id in attrs raises ValueError.
  • Attribute names must be plain names and may not start with on (no inline handlers).
  • ui.element only accepts an allow-list of tags; anything else must go through raw_html, which makes trusted markup explicit in review.
  • Logs: the examples never log typed values. Keep secrets (passwords) out of print, logs and diagnostics you export.

items.title: Tutorial (Python): build an expense tracker
items.text:
In about 30 minutes you build a small native desktop app with nativehtmlkit_ui: enter expenses, validate amounts, remove the last entry, filter by category and see totals that update by themselves. Along the way you learn the library's whole model: state, components bound to state, event handlers that change state, and computed values.

Every step is a complete program in examples/tutorials/python/ and the finished app is examples/python/expenses.py. All of them are run by the repository's example harness against the real NativeHTMLKit host.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

The PowerShell version of this tutorial is here.

items.title: Step 0: install and check
items.text:
You need uv on Linux (KDE Plasma Wayland is the primary desktop) or Windows.

uv init --app expenses && cd expenses
uv add nativehtmlkit_ui         # also installs the nativehtmlkit SDK with its native host
uv run python -c "import nativehtmlkit_ui; print(nativehtmlkit_ui.__version__)"    # 0.1.1

items.title: Step 1: a window with bound inputs
items.text:
Create expenses.py:

from nativehtmlkit_ui import UI, state


def main(app):
    description = state("")
    amount = state("")

    ui = UI(title="Expenses", width=760, height=640)
    with ui.column():
        ui.heading("Expenses", level=1)
        with ui.card():
            with ui.row():
                ui.input(description, label="Description", placeholder="Coffee with Sam")
                ui.input(amount, label="Amount", placeholder="0.00")
            ui.text(lambda: f"New expense: {description.value or '...'}, {amount.value or '0.00'}", muted=True)
    ui.mount(app)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    from nativehtmlkit import Application
    with Application.start(name="Expenses") as application:
        main(application)
        application.run()

Run it with uv run expenses.py and type into both fields: the preview line follows every keystroke.

What happened:

  • state("") creates an observable value. ui.input(description, ...) binds it two ways: typing sets the state, and setting the state changes the field.
  • ui.text(lambda: ...) is bound to an expression. The library records which states the lambda read (description, amount) and re-evaluates it when one of them changes.
  • with ui.column():, ui.card() and ui.row() arrange components; the layout guide explains them.
  • ui.mount(app) opens the window. You build the whole tree before mounting; afterwards you only change state.
  • Application.start() starts the native host, which runs this same script again as its backend. That is why all work happens inside main() behind if __name__ == "__main__":; code at module level would run twice.

(Complete file: examples/tutorials/python/expenses_step1.py.)

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Step 2: a list of expenses
items.text:
Add a list state, an Add expense button and a list. Replace the body of main with:

    expenses = state([])
    description = state("")
    amount = state("")

    def add(_event):
        expenses.set([*expenses.value, {"description": description.value.strip(), "amount": amount.value.strip()}])
        description.set("")
        amount.set("")

    def remove_last(_event):
        expenses.set(expenses.value[:-1])

    ui = UI(title="Expenses", width=760, height=640)
    with ui.column():
        ui.heading("Expenses", level=1)
        with ui.card():
            with ui.row():
                ui.input(description, label="Description", placeholder="Coffee with Sam")
                ui.input(amount, label="Amount", placeholder="0.00")
            with ui.row():
                ui.button("Add expense", on_click=add)
                ui.button("Remove last", variant="secondary", on_click=remove_last,
                          disabled=lambda: not expenses.value)
        with ui.card():
            ui.text_list(expenses, formatter=lambda e: f"{e['description']}: {e['amount']}")
    ui.mount(app)

New ideas:

  • Handlers change state, nothing else. add() never touches the window. Setting description and amount to "" clears the two fields because they are bound.
  • Replace, do not mutate. expenses.set([*expenses.value, item]) builds a new list. expenses.value.append(item) would change the list without telling anyone.
  • disabled=lambda: not expenses.value keeps Remove last disabled while the list is empty.
  • ui.text_list(...) shows one escaped line per item; formatter turns an item into text.
  • Handlers run on the UI's own thread, one at a time; all state changes made in one handler reach the window as one update.

(Complete file: examples/tutorials/python/expenses_step2.py.)

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Step 3: categories and validation
items.text:
Amounts should be numbers, and an empty form should not be addable. Add a category select, an error state shown in an alert, and a computed value that disables the button:

from decimal import Decimal, InvalidOperation

from nativehtmlkit_ui import UI, computed, state

CATEGORIES = {"food": "Food", "transport": "Transport", "home": "Home", "other": "Other"}

    category = state("food")
    error = state("")
    cannot_add = computed(lambda: not description.value.strip() or not amount.value.strip())

    def add(_event):
        try:
            value = Decimal(amount.value.strip().replace(",", "."))
        except InvalidOperation:
            error.set("Amount must be a number, for example 12.50")
            return
        if value <= 0:
            error.set("Amount must be greater than zero")
            return
        expenses.set([*expenses.value, {"description": description.value.strip(),
                                        "amount": value.quantize(Decimal("0.01")),
                                        "category": category.value}])
        description.set("")
        amount.set("")
        error.set("")

and in the form card:

            with ui.row():
                ui.input(description, label="Description", placeholder="Coffee with Sam")
                ui.input(amount, label="Amount", placeholder="0.00")
                ui.select(category, list(CATEGORIES.items()), label="Category")
            with ui.when(error):
                ui.alert(error)
            with ui.row():
                ui.button("Add expense", on_click=add, disabled=cannot_add)

with the list formatter lambda e: f"{e['description']} ({CATEGORIES[e['category']]}): {e['amount']:,.2f}".

New ideas:

  • computed(fn) is a named derived value. Like a bound lambda it tracks what it reads; unlike a lambda it can be shared and read from handlers (cannot_add.value).
  • ui.select(state, [(value, text), ...]) binds the selected option value.
  • with ui.when(error): shows its content only while error is non-empty. The region always exists and is only hidden, so nothing is rebuilt.
  • Money uses Decimal, never float. Input fields always deliver strings; convert them where you use them and report problems through state.

Try it: type three as amount and press Add expense; the alert appears. Fix it and the alert disappears. (Complete file: examples/tutorials/python/expenses_step3.py.)

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Step 4: filter and totals
items.text:
The finished app adds a second card with a Show filter, a badge, a total heading and a per-category summary, all derived from the same two states. With a module-level helper def money(value: Decimal) -> str: return f"{value:,.2f}":

    show = state("all")

    visible = computed(lambda: [e for e in expenses.value if show.value in ("all", e["category"])])
    total = computed(lambda: sum((e["amount"] for e in visible.value), Decimal("0")))
    by_category = computed(lambda: [
        f"{label}: {money(sum((e['amount'] for e in expenses.value if e['category'] == key), Decimal('0')))}"
        for key, label in CATEGORIES.items() if any(e["category"] == key for e in expenses.value)])

        with ui.card():
            with ui.row():
                ui.select(show, [("all", "All categories"), *CATEGORIES.items()], label="Show")
                ui.badge(lambda: f"{len(visible.value)} of {len(expenses.value)} expenses")
            ui.heading(lambda: f"Total: {money(total.value)}", level=2)
            with ui.when(lambda: not visible.value):
                ui.text("No expenses to show yet.", muted=True)
            ui.text_list(visible, formatter=lambda e: (
                f"{e['description']} ({CATEGORIES[e['category']]}): {money(e['amount'])}"))
            ui.text(lambda: " | ".join(by_category.value), muted=True)

Computed values can depend on other computed values (total reads visible). Change the filter and the list, badge, total and empty-state message all update together, in one window update, without a single line of update code.

The complete program is examples/python/expenses.py.

items.title: Tutorial (Python): build a settings editor
items.text:
Python (nativehtmlkit_ui 0.1.1). The same tutorial for PowerShell: build a settings editor.

You will build Settings editor, a small editor for a JSON settings file: bound inputs, live validation, an "Unsaved changes" badge, Save and Revert buttons, and a theme the app itself uses on the next start.

Time: about 25 minutes. You need: nativehtmlkit_ui installed and the first window from getting started working. Both steps are complete programs, verified by the repository's example harness against the real NativeHTMLKit host: examples/tutorials/python/settings_editor_step1.py and the final app examples/python/settings_editor.py.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with the released packages.

items.title: Step 1: a form bound to state
items.text:
Create settings_editor.py:

"""Settings editor tutorial, step 1: a form whose controls are bound to UI state.

Teaches: UI, state(), two-way ui.input / ui.select / ui.checkbox, computed() with automatic
         dependency tracking, a bound ui.text, mount/run/dispose.
Run:     uv run settings_editor_step1.py
Guide:   docs/python/tutorials/settings-editor.md (step 1 of 2)
"""
from nativehtmlkit import Application
from nativehtmlkit_ui import UI, computed, state

THEMES = [("cobalt", "Cobalt"), ("graphite", "Graphite"), ("daylight", "Daylight")]


def main():
    with Application.start(name="Settings editor") as app:
        name = state("Ada")
        email = state("ada@example.org")
        theme = state("cobalt")
        notify = state(True)
        summary = computed(lambda: f"{name.value} <{email.value}>, {theme.value} theme, "
                                   + ("with e-mail notifications" if notify.value else "without notifications"))

        ui = UI(title="Settings editor", theme="cobalt", density="regular", width=560, height=520)
        with ui.column():
            ui.heading("Settings", level=1)
            with ui.card():
                ui.input(name, label="Display name")
                ui.input(email, label="E-mail", kind="email")
                ui.select(theme, THEMES, label="Theme")
                ui.checkbox(notify, label="Send me e-mail notifications")
            ui.text(summary, muted=True)
        try:
            ui.mount(app)
            app.run()
        finally:
            ui.dispose()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run uv run settings_editor.py and edit the fields: the summary below follows every change.

  • Each state() holds one setting. ui.input(name, ...) is two-way; kind="email" gives an e-mail field.
  • ui.select(theme, THEMES, ...) takes (value, text) pairs; ui.checkbox() binds a bool.
  • computed(lambda: ...) records which states it reads (all four here) and recomputes when any of them changes. You never list dependencies.
  • The summary contains < and > around the e-mail address; ui.text() always escapes text, so this is safe.
  • The inputs are inside a card, so they keep their natural height. Labelled inputs placed directly in a column need the B-0014 workaround from the layouts guide.

items.title: Step 2: load, validate, save and revert
items.text:
Replace the file with the final version:

"""Settings editor: edit, validate and save a JSON settings file (settings-editor tutorial, final code).

Teaches: loading initial state from a file, a computed validation message and an "unsaved
changes" badge, buttons that save (atomically) and revert, a status alert, and starting the UI
in the theme the user saved.
Run:     uv run settings_editor.py [PATH]
         (default file: nativehtmlkit-settings.json in your application-data folder:
         %APPDATA% on Windows, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME or ~/.config on Linux)
Guide:   docs/python/tutorials/settings-editor.md (step 2 of 2)
"""
import json
import os
import re
import sys
import tempfile
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

from nativehtmlkit import Application
from nativehtmlkit_ui import UI, computed, state

DEFAULTS = {"DisplayName": "", "Email": "", "Theme": "cobalt", "RefreshSeconds": 60, "Notifications": False}
THEMES = [("cobalt", "Cobalt"), ("graphite", "Graphite"), ("daylight", "Daylight")]
EMAIL = re.compile(r"^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$")


def default_path() -> Path:
    if os.name == "nt":
        base = Path(os.environ.get("APPDATA") or Path.home() / "AppData" / "Roaming")
    else:
        base = Path(os.environ.get("XDG_CONFIG_HOME") or Path.home() / ".config")
    return base / "nativehtmlkit-settings.json"


def read_settings(path: Path) -> dict:
    """Start from the defaults and copy known keys, so a partial or older file still works."""
    result = dict(DEFAULTS)
    if path.is_file():
        data = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        result.update({key: data[key] for key in DEFAULTS if key in data})
    if result["Theme"] not in dict(THEMES):
        result["Theme"] = "cobalt"
    return result


def write_settings(path: Path, values: dict) -> None:
    """Write a temporary file next to the target and replace the target with it."""
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fd, temporary = tempfile.mkstemp(prefix=".settings-", suffix=".tmp", dir=path.parent)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as stream:
            json.dump(values, stream, indent=2)
        os.replace(temporary, path)
    except BaseException:
        Path(temporary).unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise


def main():
    with Application.start(name="Settings editor") as app:
        path = Path(sys.argv[1]).resolve() if len(sys.argv) > 1 else default_path()
        loaded = read_settings(path)

        name = state(str(loaded["DisplayName"]))
        email = state(str(loaded["Email"]))
        theme = state(str(loaded["Theme"]))
        interval = state(str(loaded["RefreshSeconds"]))
        notify = state(bool(loaded["Notifications"]))
        status = state(f"Editing {path}")

        # The values as they would be saved; also used to detect unsaved changes.
        snapshot = computed(lambda: {"DisplayName": name.value.strip(), "Email": email.value.strip(),
                                     "Theme": theme.value, "RefreshSeconds": interval.value.strip(),
                                     "Notifications": notify.value})
        saved = state(snapshot.value)

        def find_problem(values):
            seconds = values["RefreshSeconds"]
            if not values["DisplayName"]:
                return "Enter a display name."
            if not EMAIL.match(values["Email"]):
                return "The e-mail address looks invalid."
            if not (seconds.isdigit() and 5 <= int(seconds) <= 3600):
                return "Refresh interval must be a whole number from 5 to 3600."
            return ""

        problem = computed(lambda: find_problem(snapshot.value))
        changes = computed(lambda: "All changes saved" if snapshot.value == saved.value else "Unsaved changes")

        def save(_event):
            if problem.value:
                status.set("Fix the problem above before saving.")
                return
            values = dict(snapshot.value, RefreshSeconds=int(snapshot.value["RefreshSeconds"]))
            try:
                write_settings(path, values)
            except OSError as error:
                status.set(f"Could not save: {error.strerror or error}")
                return
            saved.set(snapshot.value)
            status.set(f"Saved {datetime.now():%H:%M:%S}")

        def revert(_event):
            try:
                fresh = read_settings(path)
            except (OSError, ValueError) as error:
                status.set(f"Could not read the file: {error}")
                return
            name.set(str(fresh["DisplayName"]))
            email.set(str(fresh["Email"]))
            theme.set(str(fresh["Theme"]))
            interval.set(str(fresh["RefreshSeconds"]))
            notify.set(bool(fresh["Notifications"]))
            status.set("Reverted to the saved file")

        ui = UI(title="Settings editor", theme=loaded["Theme"], density="regular", width=600, height=640)
        with ui.column():
            with ui.row():
                ui.heading("Settings", level=1)
                ui.badge(changes)
            with ui.card():
                ui.input(name, label="Display name")
                ui.input(email, label="E-mail", kind="email")
                ui.input(interval, label="Refresh interval (seconds)", kind="number")
                ui.select(theme, THEMES, label="Theme (applies on next start)")
                ui.checkbox(notify, label="Send me e-mail notifications")
            with ui.when(problem):
                ui.text(problem)
            with ui.row():
                ui.button("Save", on_click=save)
                ui.button("Revert", variant="secondary", on_click=revert)
            ui.alert(status)
        try:
            ui.mount(app)
            app.run()
        finally:
            ui.dispose()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it with uv run settings_editor.py or with a file of your choice: uv run settings_editor.py ./my-settings.json.

  • Without an argument the file is nativehtmlkit-settings.json in your application-data folder (%APPDATA% on Windows, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME or ~/.config on Linux). The PowerShell version of this tutorial uses the same folder and the same JSON keys, so both apps edit the same file.
  • read_settings() starts from defaults and copies known keys from the file, so a partial or older file still works.
  • snapshot is a computed dict of the values as they would be saved. Two computed values use it: problem (a validation message or "") and changes, which compares the snapshot with saved, the snapshot of the last save. Dicts compare by content, so == is enough.
  • with ui.when(problem): shows the message only when there is one.
  • Save refuses to write while there is a problem, writes a temporary file in the same folder and replaces the real one with os.replace(), then updates saved, so the badge returns to "All changes saved". Errors become a status message instead of a traceback.
  • Revert reads the file again and sets every state; the bound inputs update themselves.
  • UI(theme=loaded["Theme"]): the theme is chosen when the UI is built, so a changed theme applies on the next start.
  • Everything runs inside main() because Application.start() runs the script a second time as the backend.

Try it: clear Display name (the message appears and Save refuses), type an e-mail without a dot after the @, set the refresh interval to 2. Fix everything, press Save, change a field and press Revert.
